rows.name: Goryeo white porcelain
rows.period: Goryeo (from the 10th century; style continues in provincial kilns into the 15th)
kilns: Seo-ri, Idong-myeon, Yongin, Gyeonggi (early, with halo-foot bowls)
Jungam-ri, Yeoju, Gyeonggi
Yucheon-ri, Boan-myeon, Buan, North Jeolla (12th-c. inlaid and carved white)
Seoksu-dong, Anyang, Gyeonggi (late 14th c.)
rows.what_it_is: A small production of white wares beside celadon — a tiny fraction of Goryeo output. Most is softer and less vitrified than later Joseon porcelain, and some is inlaid like celadon.
how_to_recognize: Body: often soft, coarse, plaster-like in the 11th c.; better fused in the 12th c.
Glaze: thin, often with fine crackle, and frequently flaking away from the body because the two did not bond — a common feature of Goryeo-type white.
Color: beige-tinged or faintly bluish white; early items have halo feet like early celadon.
Decoration: incised, carved, molded, black inlay (sometimes celadon-clay inlay), iron painting.
Caution: Chinese white and bluish-white (qingbai) wares were imported in quantity and are found in Korean tombs; a Cleveland cup given as a rare Goryeo white item proved to be Song Chinese.

facts.text: Goryeo white was a tiny fraction of production — not even a few hundredths of celadon, per Jeong; nikh calls early white a minor, very small production.
facts.quote_gloss: only very small amounts were produced

facts.text: 11th-century Goryeo white has a weak, plaster-like body and very thin glaze that often did not bond and has flaked off.
facts.quote_gloss: there are many examples where the glaze has fallen away

facts.text: Inlaid white porcelain of the mid-12th century comes mainly from the Yucheon-ri kilns at Buan; Goryeo inlay on white used black clay and sometimes celadon clay.
facts.quote: 부안군 보안면 유천리 가마가 그 대표적인
facts.quote_gloss: the Yucheon-ri kiln at Boan-myeon, Buan, is the representative one

facts.text: Chinese ceramics — mostly white wares, also qingbai, black Jian bowls and Cizhou-type wares — are found in Korean sites; a Cleveland cup donated as rare Goryeo 'white celadon' turned out to be Song Chinese.
facts.quote: turns out to be an imported Song period Chinese example

rows.name: Goryeo black- and iron-glazed wares
rows.hanja: 黑釉 · 鐵釉 · 鐵彩
kilns: Undae-ri, Duwon-myeon, Goheung, South Jeolla (early black glaze)

rows.what_it_is: Dark wares made beside celadon: vessels covered in iron slip under a clear glaze (cheolchae, glossy near-black), iron glazes, and black glazes, sometimes with white inlaid or slip-painted designs such as ginseng leaves.
how_to_recognize: Near-black to dark brown surface from iron slip or glaze on a celadon-type body.
White designs scraped or inlaid through the dark slip, or painted on in white slip (e.g. ginseng leaves).
Caution: Chinese black Jian tea bowls were imported in Goryeo.

facts.quote: 철채(鐵彩) · 철유(鐵釉) · 흑유(黑釉)
facts.quote_gloss: iron-slip, iron glaze, black glaze

facts.text: The NMK iron-slip maebyeong (Treasure former no. 340): iron slip over a celadon body, motif areas thinly cut away and painted with white slip; such wares are rare, and sherds collected at Gangjin suggest they were made with ordinary celadon.
facts.quote_gloss: collected at the Daegu-myeon kilns, Gangjin

facts.text: A small amount of black-glazed ware was made early, at Undae-ri, Goheung.
facts.quote_gloss: black-glazed ware too, in a particular area

rows.name: Buncheong with inlaid decoration
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (inlaid sherds of the mid-15th c.)
rows.what_it_is: The first buncheong: Goryeo-style inlay carried on, with looser, livelier designs and a duller glaze. In the earliest items it is hard to tell from early Joseon inlaid celadon.
how_to_recognize: Black-and-white inlaid lines, and from the mid-15th c. broad area inlay (면상감).
Often combined with stamped bands (e.g. chrysanthemum stamps on the neck of the NMK dragon jar).
Forms: maebyeong with flaring mouth and S-curved profile, jars, bottles, flasks.

Body: gray to gray-black stoneware like late celadon but coarser and darker; a thin, transparent glaze — pale bluish gray-white or faintly yellowish — lets the gray body show through where there is no white slip.
Everything decorative is done with white slip (분장 粉粧) on that dark body: stamped, inlaid, incised, scraped, brushed, painted over, or dipped.

copies.text: Buncheong was revived in Japan by descendants of Korean potters settled there and by Japanese potters; Western museums hold Japanese tea bowls in buncheong manner (e.g. Met 93.1.94, Kyoto ware with inlaid and stamped design, probably 2nd half 17th c.; Met 36.120.518 'Gohon (Korean-style)' tea bowl, 18th c.). Western catalogues sometimes use Japanese trade names: Cleveland labels a 13th-c. Goryeo oil bottle 'painted celadon (Mishima ware)', and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture glosses brushed slip as 刷毛目 (Japanese hakeme). kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).

how_to_recognize: Dense, regular rows of tiny white stamped motifs (chrysanthemum the commonest; also butterflies, rings, lotus petals, ruyi heads).
Peak (Sejo reign, 1455–1468): the whole surface filled, motifs in orderly bands; late (16th c.): stamps shallow, sometimes no slip, slip brushed on and not wiped.
Forms: bowls, dishes, jars, placenta jars.

rows.name: Buncheong with sgraffito (scraped-away background) decoration (bakji)
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
rows.what_it_is: The pot is covered with white slip, a design is drawn, and the slip around the design is scraped away, so a white motif stands on the dark body. Bold peonies, lotus and fish; a Jeolla speciality.
how_to_recognize: White motif left standing in slip against scraped-back dark gray body (sometimes the background is also painted with iron to sharpen the contrast).
Drawn outlines (incised) combined with scraping; motifs peony, lotus, fish.
Forms: flattened bottles (pyeonbyeong), 'turtle' flasks (jarabyeong), jars, janggun (barrel-shaped flasks).

kilns: Hakbong-ri and Hwasan-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong, at the foot of Mount Gyeryong (excavated 1927); white porcelain and other buncheong were fired there too

how_to_recognize: Bold, fast brush marks in white slip; dark body visible between strokes.

Widespread in the 16th c.

Everything decorative is done with white slip (분장 粉粧) on that dark body: stamped, inlaid, incised, scraped, brushed, painted over, or dipped.

facts.text: Gwiyal is a broad paste brush; gwiyal buncheong has white slip brushed on thinly, often with clear, vigorous brush marks.
facts.quote: 넓적한 붓인 귀얄로 백토만을 얇게 바른 것
facts.quote_gloss: only white slip thinly applied with the gwiyal, a broad brush

facts.text: Brushed and dipped buncheong are late phenomena, developed mainly in Honam; brushed slip was widespread in the 16th century.
facts.quote: 귀얄문〔刷毛目〕과 담금분장은 분청사기 후기의 현상

Mostly Jeolla (Kang)
rows.what_it_is: The pot is held by the foot and plunged upside down into liquid white slip, giving a soft, even white coat — buncheong at its closest to white porcelain, and a cheaper substitute for it in the 16th century.
how_to_recognize: Even white slip over the whole outside except the foot area, which was held during dipping and stays dark gray.
Quiet, plain white surface without drawn decoration.
Mainly 16th century.

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain, plain
rows.date_note: Jeong's periods: early 1392–1649/50, middle 1650/51–1751, late 1752–end of Joseon.
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon)
15th-c. upper-grade white also listed at Sangju and Goryeong (North Gyeongsang) in the Sejong sillok jiriji; provincial kilns everywhere from the 16th c.
rows.what_it_is: Undecorated white porcelain, the ware the Joseon court and elite preferred above all; over 90% of white ware was plain from the later 16th century. Grades were made side by side: saggar-fired royal wares and stacked, coarser wares for offices and the market.
how_to_recognize: Early (15th–16th c.), royal grade: snowy white with a faint blue tinge, glaze slightly thick and nearly uncrackled, fired in saggars on fine sand; foot often cut as an inverted triangle.
Early, office / lower grade: pale bluish or light-gray white, often fine crackle, 'bamboo-joint' foot (jukjeol-gup), fired stacked on three to six spurs of body clay or grit (taeto bijim).
17th c.: grayish-white glaze; feet cruder; coarse sand supports; peripheral kilns made concave-footed (ommok-gup) gray wares on coarse sand.
Early 18th c. (Geumsa-ri): milky 'snow white' with faint blue, often a net of crackle; fine sand; new faceted shapes.
Late (Bunwon-ri, from 1752): bluer, thicker, very hard glaze without crackle and with many bubbles; thick walls and wide, deeply cut feet; sand supports, refractory-clay supports at the very end.
Caution: late bluish white is sometimes mistaken for 'qingbai'; Japanese machine-made porcelain flooded Korea from the late 19th century.

copies.text: From the late 19th century machine-made white wares from Kyushu (Japan) — thick, hard, smooth and without variation of line — flooded Korea, and Japanese-owned factories in Korea produced the same kind.

facts.text: From the later 16th century Joseon ceramics were almost all white porcelain, and over 90% of it undecorated.
facts.quote_gloss: plain white porcelain was over 90%

facts.text: Early-Joseon upper-grade white was fired in saggars on fine sand, with a slightly thick, almost uncrackled, faintly blue glaze.
facts.quote_gloss: fired on fine sand supports

facts.text: Royal white wares are snowy white with an inverted-triangle foot, fired in saggars on sand; wares for government offices are pale blue or light gray, with a bamboo-joint foot, fired stacked on body-clay spurs.
facts.quote_gloss: inverted-triangle foot, with sand as the support material

facts.text: Lower-grade early white often keeps throwing marks, has bamboo-joint feet and was fired on body-clay spurs.
facts.quote_gloss: fired on body-clay spurs

facts.text: After the Imjin War the foot, once neatly finished, became cruder and fine sand gave way to coarse sand supports, continuing into the early 17th century.
facts.quote_gloss: changed to firing on coarse sand

facts.text: 17th-century peripheral kilns around the court kilns made gray, impure 'concave-foot' white wares fired on coarse sand; 17th-c. sites (Tanbeol, Hakdong, Sangnim, Seondong, Yusa, Sindae) made much iron-painted ware.
facts.quote_gloss: concave-foot white ware on coarse sand

facts.text: Middle-period (Geumsa-ri) white has very faint blue, often a net-like crackle, and fine sand on a vertical foot.
facts.quote_gloss: often has net-like crackle

facts.text: Late (Bunwon-ri) white is bluer than earlier wares, dense, with no crackle and many bubbles; walls and feet are thick and wide.
facts.quote_gloss: the glaze has no crackle and many bubbles

facts.text: At the end of the Bunwon period refractory-clay supports were used instead of sand.
facts.quote_gloss: at the end, refractory-clay supports are used

facts.text: Late white is so bluish that some people wrongly take it for 'blue-white' (qingbai).
facts.quote_gloss: some misunderstand it as qingbai

facts.text: The court kilns at Gwangju began in the 1460s; scholars place the founding between 1466 and 1469 (Jeon Seungchang: about 1466; Yun Yong-i: about 1467; Kim Young-won: 1467–68; Kang Kyung-sook: after 1469).
facts.quote_gloss: the official kiln was set up in Gwangju between 1466 and 1468

examples.title: Jar with lid, 15th–16th c., porcelain with transparent glaze
백자 상감연화당초문 대접 (white bowl with inlaid lotus scroll, Goryeo-style inlay), 15th c.
Jar, 1700s, glazed porcelain

rows.name: Joseon blue-and-white porcelain
rows.hanja: 靑畵白磁 · 靑華白磁
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon)
18th–19th c. also provincial kilns
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted under the glaze in cobalt blue. For two centuries it was a rare court luxury, because cobalt (回回靑, 'Muslim blue') had to be bought from China; it became abundant only after the Bunwon settled at Bunwon-ri in 1752.
how_to_recognize: Cobalt blue under a clear glaze on white porcelain.
15th–16th c.: few, fine items; Ming-influenced at first, then spare painterly pines, bamboo, plum, birds painted by court painters with much empty space.
17th c.: blue almost absent (cobalt unobtainable); iron-brown used instead.
First half 18th c. (Geumsa-ri): spare sprays of autumn grasses, orchids, pinks, irises; faceted bottles and jars.
Late 18th–19th c. (Bunwon-ri): much more blue-and-white; auspicious motifs, characters 壽 and 福, folk-painting style, often combined with iron and copper red; stationery and ritual vessels.
Color of the blue: imported cobalt (containing arsenic) versus domestic 'earth blue' (iron and manganese rich — blackish or grayish-purple); the difference can be judged by eye only partly.

copies.text: Ming blue-and-white came to Korea as imperial gifts (e.g. 1430) and Chinese polychrome porcelain was imported and admired; whether the blue-and-white wine jar drawn in the Sejong sillok ritual volume is Chinese or Korean is disputed.

facts.text: Blue-and-white reached Korea in the late 14th century and Korean production began about the mid-15th century (Kang; Jeong: imported from the Sejong reign and then fired with imported cobalt), at first strongly influenced by Ming, distinctively Korean by the later 15th century.
facts.quote_gloss: seems to be about the mid-15th century

facts.text: Cobalt (回回靑 / 回靑) was imported from China; when it could not be had, 'earth blue' (土靑) was sought in Korea between 1463 and 1469.
facts.quote_gloss: between 1463 and 1469

facts.text: Chemically, imported cobalt contains arsenic, domestic 'earth blue' much iron and manganese (iron gives a dark blackish tone, manganese grayish-purple); surviving items cannot be clearly sorted, and by eye only partly.
facts.quote: 육안으로 어느 정도 구별이 가능할 뿐이다
facts.quote_gloss: can be distinguished by eye only to some degree

facts.text: The earliest dated Korean blue-and-white is the jar dated 弘治二年 (1489) at Dongguk University Museum.
facts.quote_gloss: a work of 1489 (Seongjong 20)

facts.text: Court painters (화원) were sent each year to the kilns to paint the royal wares, so Joseon blue-and-white follows contemporary painting styles.
facts.quote: 每歲司饔院官率畫員 監造御用之器
facts.quote_gloss: every year a Saongwon official leads court painters to supervise the making of royal wares

facts.text: In the 17th century cobalt could hardly be obtained (war damage, then anti-Qing feeling), so iron-brown took the place of blue for court use.
facts.quote_gloss: iron-painted white ware took its place

facts.text: Geumsa-ri (first half 18th c.) blue-and-white has spare grasses and flowers — pinks, irises, chrysanthemums, orchids — and new faceted forms.
facts.quote_gloss: pinks, irises, chrysanthemums, orchids

facts.text: After the Bunwon settled at Bunwon-ri, blue-and-white production rose rapidly; late wares are popular, with folk-painting motifs and auspicious designs.
facts.quote_gloss: folk-painting style patterns appear clearly

examples.title: 백자 청화'홍치2년'명 송죽문 항아리 (jar with pine and bamboo, dated 1489)
백자 청화매조죽문 유개항아리 (covered jar, plum, bird and bamboo), 15th c.
백자 청화죽문 각병 (faceted bottle with bamboo), first half 18th c.
Faceted jar decorated with plum blossoms and bamboo, end 18th–early 19th c.
Jar with floral roundels and inscriptions, 19th c.
Jar with roundels of tortoises and cranes, 1800–1850

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain with iron-brown painting
rows.period: Joseon (late 15th c. on; flourishing in the 17th c.)
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon) — 17th c. especially Sangnim-ri (from the 1630s), Seondong-ri, Jeongji-ri
Provincial kilns (e.g. 17th-c. iron-brown kilns at Yongyeon-ri, Damyang, South Jeolla, and Jeongsaeng-dong, Daejeon)
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted under the glaze with iron oxide (seokganju), which fires brown to black. Made from the late 15th century, it became the main painted ware in the 17th century when cobalt was unobtainable — dragons, bamboo, plum, grapes, grasses, in bold, often humorous brushwork.
how_to_recognize: Brown to brown-black (sometimes reddish-brown) painting; iron spreads and drags, so tones are hard to grade and lines are heavy.
17th c.: grayish-white glaze, cloud-dragon jars, bamboo and plum; foot often hollowed concave and fired on fine (court) or coarse (peripheral) sand.
Regional kilns: loose, comic dragons on round jars.
Late 18th–19th c.: iron rarely alone, mostly used with blue and copper red.

facts.text: Iron-painted white porcelain began in the later 15th century, was produced in small amounts in the 15th–16th centuries, and reached its distinctive beauty in the mid-17th century.
facts.quote_gloss: radiates a distinctive beauty in the mid-17th century

facts.text: Iron-brown appears at the court kilns from the Sangnim-ri kiln of the 1630s and continues through the mid–late 17th century; in 1634 dragons were painted in seokganju on jars for receiving envoys.
facts.quote_gloss: appears from the Sangnim-ri kiln of the 1630s

facts.text: Seokganju (石間朱) is an iron-oxide mineral pigment found in many places in Korea; on white porcelain it fires brown or reddish-brown, spreads, and drags on the brush, so gradations are hard.
facts.quote_gloss: mostly brown or reddish-brown

facts.text: Iron-brown became popular from the 17th century, especially when cobalt was very expensive or uneven; court items are refined, while regional kilns painted carefree dragons on round jars.

The Ewha iron-painted cloud-dragon jar (Treasure former no. 645) has a concave hollowed foot with fine-sand marks and grayish glaze, features found at the 17th-c. Gwangju kiln sites of Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri and Jeongji-ri.
facts.quote: 가는 모래 받침을 받쳐 구운 흔적
facts.quote_gloss: traces of firing on fine sand

facts.text: From the late 18th century iron is mostly used together with blue; on its own it is very rare.
facts.quote_gloss: examples of independent use are very rare

examples.title: 백자 철화매죽문 항아리 (jar with iron-painted plum and bamboo), late 16th c., Gwaneum-ri
백자 철화포도원숭이문 항아리 (jar with grapes and monkey), first half 18th c.
백자 철화포도문 항아리 (jar with grapevine), 18th c., H. 53.3 cm
백자 철화운룡문 항아리 (jar with cloud dragon), 17th c.
Jar decorated with dragons, 17th c., underglaze iron-brown

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain with copper-red decoration
rows.hanja: 辰砂白磁 · 銅畵白磁
rows.period: Joseon (securely from the later 17th c.; mainly 18th–19th c.)
kilns: Gwangju court kilns (Geumsa-ri, Bunwon-ri), Gyeonggi
Provincial kilns in Gyeonggi; Yeongheung County, South Hamgyeong (North Korea) — sherds found
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted with copper oxide, which fires red in reduction — hard to control, so rarer than blue or iron. Court items combine red with blue and iron; provincial jars and faceted bottles use red alone in bold sprays of bamboo, lotus, grapes or pine and crane.
how_to_recognize: Red painting under the glaze in copper (the 1684 epitaph dishes are described as vermilion-tinged on a grayish-white ground).
Court wares: red together with cobalt blue and iron-brown, sometimes with molded relief.
Provincial wares: round jars and faceted bottles with red alone, bold and free; 19th c. small angled or tall jars with simple red motifs.
Rare variant: whole surface washed red with a reserved white relief design.

facts.text: The earliest securely dated Joseon copper-red items are three epitaph dishes dated 1684 (崇禎後甲子) in the National Museum of Korea; copper red was in use on white porcelain by the later 17th century at the latest.
facts.quote_gloss: inscribed 'gapja after Chongzhen' (1684)

facts.text: Copper-red white porcelain was hard to make: copper needs a higher firing temperature and is more volatile than cobalt or iron.
facts.quote_gloss: it was hard to get good results

facts.text: Successful copper-red items date primarily to the 18th century (Met); Yun says copper red was made at the Bunwon and at provincial kilns in the 18th–19th centuries, in small demand.
facts.quote: dating primarily to the eighteenth century

facts.text: At the court kilns copper red was almost never used alone but with blue, sometimes with iron too; provincial kilns painted round jars and faceted bottles with copper red alone.
facts.quote: 진사와 청화 안료가 함께 사용된 예가 많으며
facts.quote_gloss: there are many examples using copper red and cobalt together

facts.text: Copper-red sherds are known from the Bunwon-ri court kiln and from folk kilns in Yeongheung, South Hamgyeong; 19th-century small copper-red jars are thought to come from Gyeonggi provincial kilns rather than Gwangju.
facts.quote_gloss: folk kilns in the Yeongheung area, South Hamgyeong

examples.title: 백자 청화철채동채초충문 병 (bottle with relief orchid, chrysanthemum and insects in blue, iron and copper red), first half 18th c., Gwangju
Jar with grapevine decoration, mid-18th c., underglaze copper red

rows.name: Moon jar (large round white jar)
rows.hanja: 白磁大壺 (official hanja now 白磁 壺)
rows.period: Joseon (late 17th – mid-18th century, above all c.1700–1750; made on into the 19th)
rows.date_note: KHS: about a century from the late 17th to the early 18th c., especially the first fifty years of the 18th; Met dates its jar to the second half of the 18th c.; V&A dates its jar 1800–1900 and calls moon jars 18th–19th c.; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says by the 19th c. most households had one.
kilns: Gwangju court kilns, Gyeonggi — above all Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon), also Bunwon-ri
rows.what_it_is: A large, nearly spherical white porcelain jar, usually over 40 cm high, thrown in two halves — top and bottom — and joined at the middle. The milky-white color and slightly irregular round shape suggested the full moon, hence the name.
how_to_recognize: Size: usually more than 40 cm high (Busan Museum's is over 50 cm); body diameter about equal to height; short, outward-slanting mouth and a foot of about the same diameter as the mouth.
Construction: upper and lower halves thrown separately and joined; a seam or slight step at the widest point; often lopsided or leaning — not a fault.
Color: milky white (yubaek), cream, snowy or faintly gray or bluish; glaze can pool or melt poorly near the base.
Base: glaze wiped from the foot ring; fired on fine sand; the clay shrinks about 20% in firing.
Unpainted (an iron-painted dragon variant exists).

copies.text: Contemporary Korean potters make moon jars as studio works (V&A: Kim Syyoung 2019, FE.202-2019; Ryu Jongdae 2023, FE.42-2024); Ju Sekyun's 'Tracing Drawing' series imitates designated National Treasures in white stoneware. Sources read give no test for separating a late copy from an 18th-century jar.

facts.text: Moon jars are usually over 40 cm high; their round, milky-white form recalls the full moon, hence the alias 'dal hangari' (moon jar).
facts.quote_gloss: a name given because it resembles the full moon

facts.text: Because of their size they could not be thrown in one item: upper and lower halves were made separately and joined, so many are asymmetrical and show the joint.
facts.quote: 상하 부분을 따로 만든 후, 두 부분을 접합하여
facts.quote_gloss: after making the upper and lower parts separately, joining the two

facts.text: Most were made at the court kilns at Gwangju, chiefly at Geumsa-ri, from the late 17th to the early 18th century, especially in the first half of the 18th century.
facts.quote: 금사리 가마에서 주로 제작된 것으로 추정
facts.quote_gloss: thought to have been made mainly at the Geumsa-ri kiln

facts.text: Round jars became 'moon jars' — mouth, foot, maximum width and height roughly equal — towards the late 17th century; small ones held food, large ones served as ritual flower vessels or for display.
facts.quote_gloss: changed into the so-called moon jar

facts.text: The 1991 National Treasure jar: milky-white glaze evenly applied, glaze wiped from the foot and fired on fine sand; join mark at the middle of the body.
facts.quote_gloss: fired propped on fine sand

facts.text: Joseon white porcelain shrinks about 20% in the kiln, so the 50 cm+ Busan jar was thrown about 65 cm high.
facts.quote_gloss: since it generally shrinks by about 20%

facts.text: Name: designations once called these jars 백자대호 (large white jar); the 1991 National Treasure is called 백자대호 in an the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture entry, while current KHS names are 백자 달항아리 (with hanja 白磁 壺).
facts.quote_gloss: the white large jar designated National Treasure in 1991

facts.text: Moon jars spread from limited production in the middle Joseon to ordinary households by the 19th century.
facts.quote: 어느 가정에서나 한 개쯤 있는 친숙한 세간
facts.quote_gloss: a familiar household item, one in every home

facts.text: The Met's moon jar (1979.413.1) is 38.7 cm high and dated to the second half of the 18th century; the Met essay says moon jars became fashionable in the 18th century.

rows.name: Late Joseon court-kiln porcelain of the Bunwon-ri period
rows.hanja: 分院里 白磁 (分院 沙器)
rows.period: Late Joseon (1752 – 1884, privatised kiln to the 1900s)
kilns: Bunwon-ri, Namjong-myeon, Gwangju, Gyeonggi — on the Han River where the North and South Han meet (site now under a school, damaged in the colonial period)
rows.what_it_is: After 1752 the court kiln stopped moving and stayed at Bunwon-ri, so 'Bunwon ware' usually means late Joseon court porcelain: hard, bluish white wares, much more blue-and-white, many scholar's desk items, ritual vessels, bottles and jars. In 1884 the kiln was handed to merchant-contractors and lost out to Japanese and Chinese imports.
how_to_recognize: Bluish, hard, dense glaze without crackle; thick walls and wide feet; sand supports.
Many stationery items (brush holders, often openwork; water droppers), ritual vessels, faceted and molded items.
Blue-and-white dominant; blue with iron and copper red; auspicious motifs and characters in the 19th century.

facts.text: The court kiln moved roughly every ten years in search of firewood until 1752, when it was fixed at Bunwon-ri, convenient for water transport where the North and South Han rivers meet.
facts.quote_gloss: moved to Bunwon-ri in spring 1752 (Yeongjo 28)

facts.text: Geumsa-ri, the court kiln before Bunwon-ri: c.1720/1721–1752 per Yun and nikh; Kim Kyoung-joong (2022) puts the Gwaneum-ri no.19 area at 1721–1733 and Geumsa-ri at 1734–1751.
facts.quote_gloss: Geumsa-ri (1734–1751)

facts.text: End of the court kiln: 1882 (Kang), 1883 (Jeong; Yun in 광주 요지; Ju In-taek; Im Eung-geuk), or 1884 (Yun in 관요; nikh/Bang Byeong-seon, citing the 1884 regulations 分院磁器貢所節目, which turned it into a contractor-run 'gongso' still supplying the court). The Met says the 1880s.
facts.quote_gloss: changed into the Bunwon gongso in 1884

facts.text: Bunwon-ri produced mostly stationery, ritual vessels, bottles and jars, with bluish white glaze; most surviving late white and blue-and-white wares were made there.
facts.quote: 문방구, 제기, 병, 호 등이 많이 제작되었다
facts.quote_gloss: many stationery items, ritual vessels, bottles and jars were made

facts.text: Saggar-fired top-grade ware (gapbeon), meant for the court, was by 1793 used for tableware even by commoners despite repeated bans.
facts.quote_gloss: even the lowly (used) saggar wares

facts.text: After 1884: the contractors failed; c.1897 a porcelain company (燔磁會社) with Seoul capital took over, and in 1895 a Japanese set up a kiln in Korea and supplied wares for a state funeral.
facts.quote_gloss: in 1895 a Japanese even set up a kiln in Joseon

examples.title: Openwork jar with peonies, late 18th–early 19th c.

rows.name: Provincial (folk) porcelain and brown-glazed wares, 18th–19th century
rows.hanja: 地方窯 白磁 · 民窯 · 石間硃
kilns: Provincial kilns of Gyeonggi and other provinces; Yeongheung, South Hamgyeong (copper red)
rows.what_it_is: Porcelain made outside the court kiln for the growing market: thicker, grayer white wares with free painting in iron, copper red or blue, and dark-brown glazed (seokganju) jars and bottles for storage.
how_to_recognize: Copper-red painting alone on round jars, faceted bottles, small angled or tall jars — simple, bold or naive.
Iron-brown dragons and plants painted loosely on round jars.
Seokganju (石間硃): dark brown to black-brown iron glaze, often on faceted jars and bottles — storage vessels of late Joseon.
Caution: from the late 19th century Japanese and Chinese imported porcelain circulated widely; Japanese machine-made Kyushu wares are thick, hard, smooth and uniform in line.

facts.text: Provincial kilns painted round jars and faceted bottles with copper red alone; 19th-century angled and small tall jars with naive copper-red motifs are thought to come from Gyeonggi provincial kilns, not Gwangju.
facts.quote: 지방가마에서는 둥근 항아리와 각병(角甁)에 진사로만
facts.quote_gloss: provincial kilns use copper red alone on round jars and faceted bottles

facts.text: Seokganju (dark-brown black-glazed) jars and bottles, mostly faceted, were made from the end of the middle period and much used in late Joseon as storage vessels.
facts.quote_gloss: much used as storage vessels in late Joseon

facts.text: From the late 19th century machine-made Japanese (Kyushu) porcelain — thick, hard, smooth, with no variation in line — flooded Korea; Japanese and Chinese imports circulated ever more widely.
facts.quote_gloss: mass-produced by machine

examples.title: Jar, 1800–1850, underglaze blue roundels

rows.name: Onggi (brown-glazed earthenware storage jars)
rows.period: Late Joseon to the present (glazed onggi from the 17th century)
kilns: Everywhere; 17th-c. finds at the iron-brown porcelain kilns of Yongyeon-ri, Damyang (South Jeolla) and Jeongsaeng-dong, Daejeon; Mapo and Noryangjin (Seoul) named as pot-making places in the early Joseon
rows.what_it_is: Everyday earthenware coated with a yellow-brown glaze (yakto) — kimchi and soy jars, steamers, water jars, chamber pots, barrel flasks. Porous walls 'breathe', which suits fermentation.
how_to_recognize: Coarse earthenware with a yellow-brown glaze (yakto); walls porous ('breathing vessel').
Forms: soy and kimchi jars (jangdok), water jars, rice jars, steamers (siru), water-carrying jars (dongi), vinegar bottles, barrel flasks (janggun), chamber pots.
20th c.: red lead (gwangmyeongdan, 光明丹) glaze used from the colonial period and widely after the 1960s.
Colonial-era liquor-brewery jars may be incised with capacity and inspection words such as 第 號 石 斗 年 月 檢定.

facts.text: Onggi: earthenware coated with a yellow-brown glaze called yakto (藥土); the term covers jars, steamers, vinegar bottles, chamber pots and many other glazed household vessels.
facts.quote: 약토(藥土)라는 황갈색의 유약을 입힌 질그릇
facts.quote_gloss: earthenware coated with the yellow-brown glaze called yakto

facts.text: Yellow-brown glazed onggi has not been found at 15th–16th-century kiln sites but appears at 17th-century iron-painted porcelain kilns (Damyang Yongyeon-ri, Daejeon Jeongsaeng-dong), so glazed onggi seems to begin after the 1592–1637 wars.
facts.quote_gloss: 17th-century iron-painted white porcelain kiln sites

facts.text: Red lead (光明丹, lead oxide) began to be used on onggi under Japanese rule and was widely used from the 1960s.
facts.quote_gloss: gwangmyeongdan (lead oxide)

facts.text: Colonial-era liquor jars from licensed breweries carry characters for number, capacity and inspection (第·號·石·數·斗·幷·年·月·檢定), sometimes a cyclical date or the brewery name.
facts.quote_gloss: inspection (passed)

facts.text: In the early Joseon Seong Hyeon's Yongjae chonghwa names Mapo and Noryangjin as places making earthenware jars.
facts.quote: 마포, 노량진 등지에서는 진흙 굽는 것을 업으로
facts.quote_gloss: at Mapo, Noryangjin and so on, firing clay is the trade

rows.name: Colonial-period ceramics (1910–1945): Japanese factories and 'Korai' (Goryeo-style) reproductions
kilns: Seoul: Hanyang Goryeo-so (漢陽高麗燒), Goryeo-style ceramics made for the retailer Haesi Sanghoe in the 1910s–20s
Busan: Japan Hard Pottery (日本硬質陶器) factory from 1917
Mokpo (Haengnamsa, 1942), Miryang (1942), Bucheon and Daegu (1943)
rows.what_it_is: After the court kiln closed, Japanese porcelain and Japanese-run factories in Korea took over the market, while workshops such as Hanyang Goryeo-so in Seoul made 'Goryeo-style' (高麗燒) ceramics for retailers. The Gangjin Goryeo kilns were found and surveyed in these same years (1913–14). Their makers' marks are in the inscriptions explorer.
how_to_recognize: Factory wares: machine-thrown or molded, thick, smooth, uniform.
Goryeo-style celadon of this period exists, but the sources read give no physical tests for separating it from Goryeo items.

copies.text: Goryeo-style celadon was made commercially in the colonial period (e.g. Hanyang Goryeo-so for Haesi Sanghoe, 1910s–20s). No source read states how to tell such items from Goryeo originals.

facts.text: In 1917 the Japanese company Japan Hard Pottery set up a factory in Busan with modern kilns and mechanical wheels; by 1945 there were 16 ceramics factories in Korea (9 in the south, 7 in the north).
facts.quote_gloss: 16 ceramics factories in operation

facts.text: The Seoul retailer Haesi Sanghoe had its ceramics made by Hanyang Goryeo-so (漢陽高麗燒) in the 1910s–20s.
facts.quote_gloss: Hanyang Goryeo-so

facts.text: After the Bunwon closed, the flood of Japanese ceramics nearly cut the Korean tradition; reproducing celadon became a matter of national pride.
facts.quote_gloss: with the flood of Japanese ceramics

facts.text: The Sadang-ri kiln site at Gangjin became known in 1913 when a Japanese policeman found celadon sherds; the Yi Royal Household Museum surveyed it the next year, and Gangjin was listed as a historic site in 1939.
facts.quote_gloss: the next year the Yi Royal Household Museum surveyed the site

rows.name: Post-1945 celadon and porcelain revival (Icheon, Gangjin)
kilns: Sindun-myeon, Icheon, Gyeonggi (e.g. Yu Geun-hyeong 'Haegang', Ji Sun-tak, Jo So-su)
Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, South Jeolla (Gangjin county kiln from 1977; Gangjin Celadon Museum workshops)
Gwangju (Jeolla): Mudeung-yo of Jo Gi-jeong (1966 on)
rows.what_it_is: Studios and county workshops that set out to reproduce Goryeo celadon and Joseon white wares after liberation — a local in Icheon recalls Japanese visitors buying up pottery by the hundreds each week after the 1965 Korea–Japan treaty. Their makers' marks are in the inscriptions explorer.
how_to_recognize: Makers' marks: see the inscriptions explorer.
Quality ranges from cheap souvenirs to fine studio work; side by side, glaze color and precision of pattern differ (Nakamura).

copies.text: These are the modern reproductions that most often stand in for Goryeo celadon in Western homes; the sources read do not give connoisseurship tests beyond marks and the period features listed under each Goryeo ware.

facts.text: In Icheon (Sindun-myeon) Yu Geun-hyeong, Ji Sun-tak, Jo So-su and others reproduced Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain around two surviving kilns after the war; Yu (Haegang) is said to have restored Goryeo celadon in 1959.
facts.quote_gloss: achieved its restoration in 1959

facts.text: Gangjin county formed a Goryeo celadon reproduction committee in 1977, built a wood-fired 'Gangjin official kiln' and in February 1978 first succeeded in reproducing Goryeo celadon with natural glaze.
facts.quote: 천연유약을 사용한 고려청자 재현사업을 국내 최초로 성공
facts.quote_gloss: first in Korea to succeed in reproducing Goryeo celadon with natural glaze

facts.text: Modern Goryeo-style celadon is sold everywhere in Korean souvenir shops, from very cheap cups to expensive items; seen side by side, they differ in glaze color and accuracy of design.
facts.quote: 並べてみると、その釉薬の色合いから模様の正確さ
facts.quote_gloss: placed side by side, from the glaze colour to the accuracy of the pattern…

rows.name: Bandaji: front-opening chest (general type)
rows.period: Joseon (most surviving items late 18th–early 20th century); still made through the 20th century
rows.date_note: Sources describe the type without a start date; the earliest firmly dated Western-collected bandaji-type chests are 1880s–1890s accessions. Typical surviving examples are 19th–early 20th c.
kilns: All provinces of Joseon Korea; strong regional styles (see regional rows): Ganghwa (Incheon), Gaeseong (North Hwanghae, DPRK), Pyongyang and Bakcheon (North Pyongan, DPRK), Jeonju and Namwon (North Jeolla), Naju (South Jeolla), Tongyeong, Miryang, Jinju and others (South Gyeongsang), Jeju
rows.what_it_is: A rectangular single-level chest whose front is split horizontally: the upper half is a board that hinges down (drops forward) to open, the lower half is fixed. Used for clothes, bedding, documents, books, brassware and ritual vessels; bedding was often stacked on top. The most common Korean chest in Western homes.
how_to_recognize: Construction: six thick solid boards; Bae describes the top joined to the back and sides with plain butt joints and the sides joined to front and back with interlocking 'four-way' corner joints (사개물림) — look at the corners for these interlocking fingers rather than nails or screws.
Proportions (Bae's standard sizes): height 60–100 cm, front 65–90 cm, depth 30–45 cm; northern chests taller, Gyeongsang chests low.

Hardware: one long lock strap (뻗침대) hangs from the top over the center of the drop-front onto a lock plate; long hinges on the drop-front; ring or crescent handles on the sides; corner and edge straps (감잡이) and round-head nails (광두정). Iron (무쇠) or brass in older work; white brass (백동) on many late items.
Interior: some regional types have small drawers or a shelf inside the top (Ganghwa, Pyongyang).
Wood: pine and zelkova in the center and south; linden (피나무) in the north (wood-anatomy study).
Wear: rounded front edges and hand-wear around the lock plate; old dark staining around fittings that fades without hard borders (dealer guidance).

facts.text: Bandaji is defined as a rectangular single-level clothes chest whose front upper half opens up and down.
facts.quote: 전면(前面) 상반부를 상하로 열고 닫는 문판
facts.quote_gloss: a door board on the upper half of the front that opens up and down

facts.text: Besides clothing, bandaji held scrolls, books, brass and ritual vessels; ordinary households also stacked bedding on top.
facts.quote_gloss: stacking bedding on top

facts.text: Bandaji styles differ by region in materials and metal fittings because heavy woodwork was rarely traded over long distances.
facts.quote_gloss: because woodwork was hard to distribute far

facts.text: In a wood-anatomy study of mainly 19th-century furniture, northern bandaji used linden and pine, central-southern bandaji pine and zelkova.
Large chests (궤) were usually built of solid boards over 2 cm thick with interlocking corner joints, reinforced with iron straps; side handles and locks were mainly iron.
facts.quote_gloss: solid boards over 2 cm, corner-locked

facts.text: For bandaji and rice chests, black iron (거멍쇠) fittings continued to be used even after white brass became fashionable for other furniture.
facts.quote_gloss: black iron continued to be used

facts.text: Foreign buyers in early-20th-century Seoul called the bandaji a 'cash box' because it was used to store strings of coins.

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Chest, Joseon dynasty, 19th century; carved wood with iron fittings
Korean chest, Joseon dynasty; pine, oak and brass
Wooden chests, late Joseon (bandaji and small chest)

rows.name: Ganghwa bandaji
rows.date_note: No dated examples found; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture describes it without dates.
kilns: Ganghwa Island, Ganghwa-gun, Incheon
rows.what_it_is: The most prized regional bandaji: tall, near-square, heavy-boarded chests from Ganghwa Island, said to have been made for palace use, with finely cut iron and brass fittings.
how_to_recognize: Proportions: often closer to square and tall (Bae: height 80–100 cm, front 90–100 cm, depth 45–50 cm).
Boards: all six faces of the same heavy thickness; interlocking corner joints.
Lock strap: runs straight down from the top board instead of bending at a right angle as on ordinary bandaji, so the upper interior stays usable.

Fittings: iron and brass; long 'yakgwa'-shaped hinges pierced with 亞 and 卍 patterns; often a single gourd-shaped (호리병) hinge in the center; bat and 'herb of immortality' (불로초) corner items, taeguk motifs; around forty different ornament shapes recorded.
Interior: an open shelf, drawers or a letter rack under the top.
Base: low, heavy stand with gently curved cut-outs (풍혈).

facts.text: Ganghwa bandaji are ranked the finest and most expensive bandaji and were largely made for royal use.
facts.quote_gloss: counted the top grade among bandaji

facts.text: Its lock strap comes straight down from the top board rather than bending in an L as on ordinary bandaji.
facts.quote_gloss: comes straight down from the top board

facts.text: Ganghwa fittings are mainly iron and brass, with long yakgwa-shaped hinges pierced with 亞/卍 and a single gourd-shaped central hinge.
facts.quote_gloss: one gourd-shaped hinge

rows.name: Gaeseong (Songdo) bandaji
rows.date_note: Only a dealer pamphlet of after 1910 describes it.
kilns: Gaeseong (Kaesong), North Hwanghae Province, DPRK
rows.what_it_is: Chest style of the merchant city of Gaeseong. A Seoul dealer describes the door opening in the center between two small drawers set at the top on either side, with less brass, a plain lower front, and hinges engraved with characters for longevity, prosperity and wealth. The National Folk Museum's chests of this name have the center opening and the small top drawers, but several are heavily fitted in brass.
how_to_recognize: (single dealer source) center opening flanked by two small top drawers; fewer fittings; lower front plain; engraved character hinges.
Museum examples (National Folk Museum) are often brass-rich, with gourd-shaped hinges and bat and 囍 plates: less brass is not a reliable sign.

facts.text: A Seoul dealer described Songdo (Gaeseong) chests as opening in the center between two small top drawers rather than across the whole front.
Gaeseong, a commercial city, is also where the gakgesuri strong-box developed.
facts.quote_gloss: developed in the commercial city of Gaeseong

facts.text: The National Folk Museum's chests catalogued as 개성반닫이 (민속 24344, 24348, 24361, 24362) include brass-rich ones with gourd-shaped hinges and bat and 囍 plates; two (24361, 24362) open in the center between small top drawers.

rows.name: Pyongyang bandaji
rows.date_note: Undated in sources; brass and white-brass fittings suggest 19th–early 20th c.
kilns: Pyongyang and surroundings, DPRK
rows.what_it_is: A very large, tall, heavy northern bandaji used as a clothes chest and as a stand for thick bedding.
how_to_recognize: Size: much bigger and taller than southern chests (Bae: height 90–120 cm, front 90–115 cm).
Boards: thick, hard zelkova, corners locked with interlocking joints; the drop-front framed with a border (문변자).
Interior: three small drawers with little pulls under the top.

Fittings: abundant tin-brass (주석) and white-brass (백동) plates; six to eight long yakgwa- or gourd-shaped hinges in a row; a 'Namdaemun-gate' or carp-shaped center plate; many square round-head nails in symmetrical rows.

facts.text: Pyongyang bandaji are larger and taller than those of other regions and are built of thick zelkova.
facts.quote_gloss: very heavy, big and tall

facts.text: Their fronts carry many tin-brass and white-brass fittings, with six to eight long hinges side by side.
facts.quote_gloss: six to eight long hinges side by side

facts.text: Northern chests were taller because northern houses had small windows and chests stood against the wall.
facts.quote_gloss: characteristically tall

rows.name: Bakcheon bandaji ('sungsung-i' pierced-iron chest)
rows.date_note: Bae's general article claims perforated-iron items already in 'early Joseon' — unsupported elsewhere (see disputed). Song & Park's Bakcheon samples are in a mainly 19th-century collection.
kilns: Bakcheon-gun, North Pyongan Province, DPRK
rows.what_it_is: A tall northern bandaji covered with black iron plates pierced (punched) into dense geometric scroll patterns, over a dark or red-painted linden body.
how_to_recognize: Black iron hinges and corner plates pierced with a sharp punch into lace-like geometric scroll patterns.
Body of close-grained, figure-less linden (피나무) or walnut, painted dark or red so the iron lace stands out.
One large crescent handle at the bottom center of the front and smaller ones at the top corners of the door; Bakcheon chests also used handles on front and back, not only the sides.
Later items: seven or eight long brass yakgwa hinges side by side (Bae).
Museums use 숭숭이 (pierced iron) for chests from Ganghwa, Haeju and Pyongan too: pierced iron alone does not make a chest a Bakcheon one.

facts.text: Bakcheon chests are decorated with black iron plates pierced with a sharp punch, a style nicknamed 'sungsung-i bandaji'.
facts.quote_gloss: 'holey' bandaji

facts.text: The body is of grainless linden (or walnut), stained dark or red to set off the pierced iron.
facts.quote_gloss: little-figured linden and walnut

facts.text: Wood identification found linden in Hwanghae and Bakcheon chests, a cold-climate species, indicating northern origin of the wood.
Unusually, Bakcheon bandaji carry lifting handles on the front and back as well as the sides.
facts.quote_gloss: examples used on the front and back boards

facts.text: Museums give the name 숭숭이 to pierced-iron chests from more places than Bakcheon: Ganghwa (National Museum of Korea, 건희 4602), Haeju (National Folk Museum, 민속 62484) and Pyongan province (National Museum of Korea, 건희 4630).
Bakcheon chests are not all linden: the National Museum of Korea's (구 8703) is linden, but the National Folk Museum records one (민속 70664) as paulownia.

rows.name: Jeonju bandaji (two-section chest)
rows.date_note: Baik & Lim compare late-Joseon and colonial-period Jeonju chests.
kilns: Jeonju, North Jeolla Province (Jeonbuk State)
rows.what_it_is: A Jeonju chest built in two stacked sections: a drop-front bandaji below and a section with small double doors above, often with a row of drawers under the top.
how_to_recognize: Two-part front: bandaji drop-front below, small side-hinged double doors above (Wright & Pai).

Late-Joseon Jeonju chests: boards bound together, single-board bottom, front frame members few or small, 3–4 drawers under the top, drawers and shelf behind the doors; cast-iron and yellow-brass fittings.
Colonial-period Jeonju chests: framed side panels, more panel divisions, separate legs, top board projecting farther; nickel (white-metal) fittings with more engraving.

facts.text: The Jeonju bandaji is two stacked compartments, a bandaji door below and small double doors above.
Late-Joseon Jeonju chests used cast iron and yellow brass fittings; colonial-period ones mainly nickel, with more engraved pattern.
Colonial-period Jeonju chests have framed side panels, separate legs and a top board projecting farther at the sides.

examples.title: Korean storage chest (Jeonju bandaji), Joseon dynasty, late 19th century; elm, oak, pine and metal

rows.name: Gyeongsang (South Gyeongsang) bandaji: Miryang, Tongyeong, Jinju, Namhae, Yangsan, Gimhae
rows.hanja: 慶尙道半닫이 (密陽·統營·晉州·南海·梁山·金海)
rows.rr: Gyeongsang-do bandaji (Miryang, Tongyeong, Jinju, Namhae, Yangsan, Gimhae)
rows.mr: Kyŏngsang-do pandaji (Miryang, T'ongyŏng, Chinju, Namhae, Yangsan, Kimhae)
rows.date_note: Kim 2017 studies late-Joseon chests.
kilns: South Gyeongsang Province: Miryang, Tongyeong, Jinju, Namhae, Yangsan, Gimhae
rows.what_it_is: Southern bandaji that are low and small for their width, with fewer fittings so the grain of pine or zelkova shows.
how_to_recognize: Low and small (Bae, Miryang: height 50–60 cm, front 65–80 cm).
Sparse iron fittings; wood grain is the decoration.

Miryang: no separate stand, only foot rails; relatively more iron, simplified 'herb of immortality' hinges, 卍/亞 strapwork, chrysanthemum-head nails; crescent handles on the sides or one at the bottom center; pierced iron work (Kim).

Jinju: cicada-shaped hinges and decorative iron hooks. Namhae: lotus-bud hinges, yin-yang and number patterns in the piercing. Yangsan: 'violin-shaped' hinges. Gimhae: tin and cast-iron rivets and locks (Kim).
Southern boards are thinner than northern ones (Choi, Jeju article).

facts.text: Gyeongsang bandaji are low for their width, use little iron and let the wood grain show.
facts.quote_gloss: low relative to width

facts.text: Kim distinguishes six Gyeongnam sub-styles: Tongyeong, Jinju, Miryang, Namhae, Yangsan and Gimhae.
Miryang chests have no stand, only foot rails, and chrysanthemum-shaped round-head nails.
facts.quote: 마대(馬薹 : 받침다리)가 없고 족대(足臺)만
facts.quote_gloss: no stand, only foot rails

facts.text: Miryang chests are mainly pine, sometimes zelkova with good figure.
facts.quote_gloss: pine is the main wood

facts.text: Regional names are given to later chests too: the National Folk Museum dates its 밀양반닫이 민속 74534 and 진주반닫이 민속 74535 after 1945, while its 밀양반닫이 70665 and 김해반닫이 74511 are Joseon.

rows.name: Jeju bandaji
rows.date_note: Choi notes fittings grow larger and more numerous in later items.
kilns: Jeju Island (Jeju Special Self-Governing Province)
rows.what_it_is: Island bandaji used for books, writing things and ritual vessels; tall for its width, of thin zelkova boards, with three big iron hinges.
how_to_recognize: Nearly as tall as wide (taller-looking than mainland chests).
Three large 'herb of immortality' long hinges of thick black iron; the hinge/lock plates often widen into a rounded 'beoseon' (sock-toe) shape like Jangheung and Haenam work.
Iron crescent handles on the sides; chrysanthemum-shaped clasps; lozenge round-head nails at the corners.
Thin boards, mostly zelkova.
Door does not span the whole front (Wright & Pai).
Older items: thin edge straps; later: broad flat iron straps, bigger and more numerous fittings.

facts.text: Jeju bandaji are tall relative to their width, with three large iron 'herb of immortality' hinges and iron crescent side handles.
facts.quote_gloss: three large herb-of-immortality hinges

facts.text: Later Jeju chests have bigger and more numerous fittings, and broad flat iron straps replace thin early ones.
facts.quote_gloss: fittings grow larger

facts.text: Jeju chests are mostly zelkova with thin boards.
facts.quote_gloss: zelkova was much used

facts.text: Wright & Pai group the Jeju and Gyeonggi bandaji as types whose door does not run across the whole front.
The National Folk Museum's records overlap Jeju and southwest Jeolla: one chest (민속 51402) is called 전라도, 장흥 and 제주도 반닫이, another (49821) 제주도 and 해남 반닫이; most of its Jeju chests are zelkova.

rows.name: Namwon, Naju and Tongyeong bandaji (names only)
kilns: Namwon (North Jeolla), Naju (South Jeolla), Tongyeong (South Gyeongsang)
rows.what_it_is: Regional names used in the Korean trade and literature. Within the search budget no source describing Namwon or Naju bandaji was found; Tongyeong is listed by Kim (2017) as one of six Gyeongnam sub-styles without details in the abstract.

facts.text: Tongyeong is one of six Gyeongnam bandaji areas in Kim's classification, alongside Jinju, Miryang, Namhae, Yangsan and Gimhae.
The National Museum of Korea's 남원 반닫이 (신수 13557, colonial period, persimmon wood) is a tall two-part chest with a tier of drawers and open compartments, not a plain box chest.

rows.name: Nong: stacked clothing chest of separate boxes
rows.date_note: Choi: since modern times the nong largely gave way to the jang and the names merged.
kilns: Nationwide; women's quarters (anbang)
rows.what_it_is: A clothes chest made of two or three separate box sections stacked on each other (often on a separate stand), each with its own front doors. Unlike a jang, the sides are not one continuous board and there is no projecting top board.
how_to_recognize: Lift test: each tier is a separate box that lifts off; the sides break at each tier.
Top flush with the body (no overhanging top board) unless a later 'gaepan-nong'.
Joints: tongue-and-hole (촉짜임) board joints; every corner reinforced with brass clasps, often 'chilli-leaf' shaped; a large crescent handle under the door and on each side.
Wood: light, insect-resistant paulownia; for the anbang also figured persimmon or zelkova; some with mother-of-pearl, painted oiled paper, or bamboo veneer.
Proportions: Wright & Pai describe nong as separate stacked sections on a separate stand, used for longer-term storage.

facts.text: The jang and nong are distinguished by the top board: the nong has none and its tiers separate, the jang has a projecting top and one continuous body.
facts.quote: 장과 농(籠)은 개판(蓋板: …)에 의해 구별
facts.quote_gloss: jang and nong are told apart by the top board

facts.text: Since the modern period the nong has largely given way to the jang and the names 'jang' and 'nong' have been used loosely (jangnong).
facts.quote_gloss: the strict distinction in names disappeared

facts.text: Nong were favoured in light, insect-resistant paulownia, and in figured persimmon and zelkova for the women's room.
facts.quote_gloss: light, moth-proof paulownia

facts.text: Corner joints of the nong were reinforced with chilli-leaf or other brass clasps, and a large crescent handle hangs under the door and on each side.
facts.quote_gloss: chilli-leaf-shaped clasps

examples.holder: unrecorded Korean museum (photo by Motoko C. K., Commons)
examples.title: 2층 농 (two-tier nong), Joseon, 19th century, paulownia

rows.name: Jang: two- and three-tier clothing cabinet (icheungjang, samcheungjang)
rows.date_note: Dated anchors: NMNH E77008 three-tier chest collected in Seoul 1884–85 with white-brass fittings; Guimet items given 1891.
kilns: Nationwide; regional types e.g. Jeonju-jang (see bandaji_jeonju)
rows.what_it_is: A tall clothes cabinet of two or three (sometimes four) levels built as ONE frame with continuous side boards, a top board overhanging the body by a few centimetres, and double doors on each level; often a row of small drawers and a cut-out stand.
how_to_recognize: Continuous sides from top to bottom (vs separate boxes in a nong); top board projects ~3–4 cm left and right.
Frame-and-panel construction: posts and rails joined with tenons (촉짜임), mitred corners (연귀짜임), panels let into grooves (턱솔짜임) so they can move; door panels framed (문변자).

Woods: anbang items in zelkova, pine and paulownia, often with figured burl (용목) or persimmon panels in mirror-matched pairs; painted (화초장), ox-horn (화각장), embroidered (수장) and mother-of-pearl (나전장) versions for women.

Hardware changes with date: plain brass or iron in earlier items; white brass (백동) with symbolic cut-out shapes and 囍 'double joy' plates on later ones; fittings become larger and showier around 1900.

facts.text: A jang has a top board wider than the body by about 3–4 cm on each side and a body not split by tiers; doors in the center of each level.
facts.quote_gloss: 3–4 cm wider than the body each side

facts.text: Panels are fitted into grooves in the frame to stop warping and shrinkage damage.
facts.quote: 판재가 휘거나 수축하는 것을 막기 위해
facts.quote_gloss: to keep boards from warping or shrinking

facts.text: A three-tier chest collected in Seoul in 1884–85 by Ensign J. B. Bernadou has white-brass (baekdong) fittings and 囍 'double joy' appliqués of silver inlaid in copper.
facts.quote: white brass known in Korean as baekdong

facts.text: Around 1900 furniture workshops displayed signboards reading 粧籠, and metal fittings became larger and showier than before.
facts.quote_gloss: metal fittings became large and showy

facts.text: Matched 'mirror-image' panels sawn from one slab were used to balance chest fronts.
Door panels were chosen for figure: burl (용목), persimmon and other patterned woods.
facts.quote_gloss: burl with beautiful grain

facts.text: In the bridal 'mandarin-duck' cabinet (wonangjang) one level holds a lockable gakgesuri of drawers; fronts are zelkova burl veneered on paulownia.

examples.title: Three-Tiered Storage Chest (Samcheung-Jang), collected in Seoul 1884–85 by J. B. Bernadou
Two-tier wardrobe, late Joseon

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Three-Tiered Cabinet with Flowers, 19th century; red lacquer, painted decoration, brass fittings

rows.name: Uigeorijang: hanging wardrobe
rows.date_note: Kim Samdae-ja dates its appearance to the late 18th century; bandaji-base versions late 19th c.; burl-veneer, mother-of-pearl and imported-mirror versions early 1900s.
kilns: Nationwide (sarangbang and later anbang)
rows.what_it_is: A tall two-part cabinet with a hanging rail inside the upper two-thirds (for officials' robes) and a lower third for hats and boots.
how_to_recognize: Looks like a bookcase but deeper (about 46 cm vs 40 cm) with a hanging rail instead of shelves; the floor sits lower than the door opening so clothes do not catch.
Earliest: paulownia panels on pear or chamjuk (Toona) posts, sometimes paulownia surface scorched (낙동법) to raise the grain; lattice-door versions in pine papered inside.
Late 19th c.: built over a bandaji base for the women's room.
Early 1900s: rosewood-type (화류) veneer, mother-of-pearl, and imported mirrors set in — bridal furniture of wealthy families.
Hidden hinges appear only on late (post-Joseon-style) uigeorijang and mungap.

facts.text: The uigeorijang appeared in the late 18th century when hanging rails were fitted inside a bookcase-type cabinet to keep official robes uncrushed.
facts.quote: 18세기 말 책장 양식의 가구 내면에 횟대를
facts.quote_gloss: late 18th c., a hanging rail inside a bookcase-type cabinet

facts.text: In the early 1900s uigeorijang were veneered with rosewood-type wood, inlaid with mother-of-pearl and fitted with imported mirrors as wedding furniture for wealthy families.
facts.quote_gloss: fitting imported mirrors

facts.text: Concealed hinges are found only occasionally, on uigeorijang and mungap made from the end of Joseon onward; exposed hinges are the rule on Joseon furniture.
facts.quote: 조선 말기 이후에 제작된 의걸이장이나 문갑
facts.quote_gloss: uigeorijang or mungap made from late Joseon on

examples.title: 시명 의걸이장 (wardrobe with inscribed poem panels), 19th century

rows.name: Meoritjang: bedside chest (incl. beoseonjang, aegijang)
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: A low single-level chest kept at the head of the sleeping place; in the men's room a square chest with one or two doors and drawers above (or the scroll-topped gyeongchukjang), in the women's room a miniature wardrobe for socks and small things.
how_to_recognize: Low, single storey (Wright & Pai: mŏrijang and pŏsŏnjang are one level).
Sarangbang: plain figured paulownia, persimmon or pine fronts.
Anbang: ash (물푸레나무) or decorated with ox-horn, embroidery or mother-of-pearl.

facts.text: Meoritjang are low single-level chests kept at the head of the bed; the women's versions are called aegijang or beoseonjang.
facts.quote_gloss: called aegijang or beoseonjang

rows.name: Mungap: low document cabinet
kilns: Nationwide; sarangbang and anbang
rows.what_it_is: A long low cabinet set beside the floor cushion or under a window for letters, papers and small valuables, its top used to display items; made singly or as a matching pair.
how_to_recognize: Pair type: front filled with 3–4 sliding panels without hinges; only one panel is lockable — lift it up and out (its slot is cut 7–10 mm deeper), then slide the others along to remove them.
Single type: taller, mixing open space, drawers and doors.
Men's: plain pine, paulownia, persimmon, pear; women's: richer woods incl. 'hwaryu' (rosewood-type) with mother-of-pearl.
Concealed hinges only on late (end-of-Joseon onward) mungap.

facts.text: Mungap front panels have no hinges; the one lockable panel is lifted out and the others slid across and removed, so one lock secures all.
facts.quote_gloss: lifting the panel up

facts.text: A mungap is a low rectangular chest for stationery, writing materials and sometimes valuables, set at desk height.

rows.name: Seoan: scholar's low writing desk
rows.date_note: Lee Jong-seok: pre-19th-century seoan are rare; a Dosan Seowon desk is an exception with Ming-style apron cut-outs.
kilns: Nationwide; sarangbang
rows.what_it_is: A long, narrow floor-height desk for reading and writing, placed between the master and visitors in the men's room; usually paired with a separate inkstone stand (연상).
how_to_recognize: Long and narrow; low for floor sitting; top sometimes with raised ends.
Plain figured wood, unlacquered, polished with oil or scorched; little carving — Joseon manuals advised against red lacquer and fuss.
Woods named in old texts: Jeju sanyuja, Honam persimmon, aged mulberry from Daecheong-do; also torreya, elm, ash.
Hidden lock mechanisms (은혈자물쇠) were used mainly on seoan.

facts.text: Seoan made before the 19th century are rare, so their earlier form is known mainly from paintings and a few survivals.
facts.quote_gloss: pre-19th-c. seoan are rare

facts.text: Joseon manuals (Sallim gyeongje, Iunji) recommended plain figured wood without carving or red lacquer for scholars' desks.
facts.quote_gloss: avoid fussy decoration

facts.text: Hidden-keyhole locks (eunhyeol jamulsoe) were used mainly on seoan.
facts.quote_gloss: used mainly on seoan

facts.text: Wright & Pai call individual desks sŏan or ch'aeksang, or kyŏngsang when in temple-desk style; offering tables are similar but sometimes taller.

examples.title: Desk for literati, wood, Joseon period, 18th century

rows.name: Gyeongsang: scroll-ended sutra or reading desk
rows.date_note: LACMA dates its examples 18th and 19th century.
kilns: Nationwide; temples and wealthy sarangbang
rows.what_it_is: A low desk whose top curls up at both ends like a scroll, on curved (tiger-paw) legs, with one or two drawers; derived from Buddhist sutra desks.
how_to_recognize: Top ends roll up in a scroll; either a separately cut scroll item glued onto a tongue, or let into a groove.
Tiger-paw legs carved with cloud scrolls or bamboo joints; incised 'eye' (안상) or ruyi motifs front and back.
Lower and lighter than Chinese altar tables, for floor sitting.
Hardware: older items have round black-iron ring pulls, more recent ones butterfly-type brass (주석) fittings (Kim — single source).
Best wood: figured zelkova (괴목); also pine, paulownia, linden, spruce, sanyuja.

facts.text: The gyeongsang has scroll-curled top ends and tiger-paw legs and derives from Buddhist sutra and altar tables.
facts.quote_gloss: both ends of the top roll like a scroll

facts.text: On gyeongsang, older items tend to have round black-iron ring pulls and later ones brass fittings.
facts.quote_gloss: the older, the more likely black-iron round rings
