examples.title: Reading Table with Bats, 19th century; carved wood, red lacquer, brass fittings

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Reading Table, 18th century; carved wood with metal fittings, 27.9 × 58.4 × 27.9 cm

rows.name: Sabangtakja and takja: open display shelves (incl. takjajang)
rows.hanja: 四方卓子 · 卓子 · 卓子欌
rows.date_note: Bae: from the late 19th century hinges become bigger and decoration showier.
kilns: Nationwide; sarangbang (books, scrolls) and anbang (display)
rows.what_it_is: Tall, slender shelving of four thin posts and shelf boards, open on all sides (sabangtakja) or with closed sides/back or a cupboard at the bottom (takjajang).
how_to_recognize: Thin posts and rails in fine proportion; square plan (rectangular ones are jangtakja/chaektakja).
Few fittings: concealed or small square hinges on the cupboard; after the late 19th century bigger hinges and more decoration.
Surface: wood scorched or rubbed with ash to kill shine and raise the grain; frames of chamjuk (Toona), pine or pear, panels of paulownia or pine.
Wright & Pai: two to five levels, bottom usually enclosed with double doors.

facts.text: Sabangtakja are open on all four sides, built of posts and shelf boards, with any cupboard at the bottom.
facts.quote_gloss: multi-level stand open on four sides

facts.text: Sabangtakja carried few fittings, but from the late 19th century hinges grew larger and decoration showier.
facts.quote_gloss: after the late 19th c. hinges grow larger

facts.text: Takja wood was scorched or rubbed with ash to remove shine and bring out the grain.
facts.quote_gloss: scorched or rubbed with ash

examples.title: Exhibit Cabinet (Sabang-Takja), gift of the Republic of Korea, accessioned 15 Aug 1964 (indexed '1960s')

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Three-Tiered Cabinet (takjajang type), 18th century; carved wood, red and black lacquer, brass fittings

rows.name: Chaekjang: bookcase
rows.date_note: Dated anchor: Guimet MG 15566 given by Victor Collin de Plancy in 1891.
kilns: Nationwide; sarangbang
rows.what_it_is: A tall cabinet for books and scrolls (Bae: H 110–160 cm), with big doors hung directly on the posts so they open wide; inside, shelves.
how_to_recognize: Doors hinged straight onto the posts (no narrow side panels), no rail panel below the doors.
Frames of hard chamjuk (Toona) or pine; panels paulownia or pine; little iron; a plain, unglossy look.
Shallower (about 40 cm) than an uigeorijang (about 46 cm).

facts.text: Bookcase doors are hinged directly to the posts so they open fully, without side panels or a rail panel below.
facts.quote: 경첩(…)을 문판(門板)과 기둥에 직접 부착
facts.quote_gloss: hinges fixed directly to door and post

facts.text: A bookcase is about 40 cm deep, an uigeorijang about 46 cm.

examples.title: Bookcase (ch'aekjang), wood, burl board, copper; Joseon, 19th century; gift of Victor Collin de Plancy, 1891; H 145 cm
Yangban book cabinet, early 19th century; pine, sandalwood and brass

rows.name: Yeonsang: inkstone and brush stand
rows.date_note: Bae: later items often carry relief-carved peony, ten-longevity or crane designs on lid and drawer.
kilns: Nationwide; sarangbang
rows.what_it_is: A small two-level stand: a lidded box on top for the inkstone, an open stand below, sometimes a drawer for ink and brushes; used next to the seoan.
how_to_recognize: Mitred board joints with bamboo pegs; lid framed (문변자) with a floating panel.
Ginkgo, pine or persimmon outside, paulownia drawer insides; iron ring pull, almost no other metal.
Later items: relief carving on lid and drawer front.

facts.text: Yeonsang are mostly of ginkgo, pine or persimmon, with paulownia inside the drawers and almost no metal beyond an iron ring.
facts.quote_gloss: ginkgo, pine and persimmon most used

examples.title: Lacquered inkstone table inlaid with mother-of-pearl, Joseon, 19th century
Stand for Writing Accessories (Yongsang), gift of the Republic of Korea 1964

rows.name: Gakgesuri: strong-box cabinet
rows.hanja: 角其所里 (Sillok transcription); Japanese 懸硯 kakesuzuri; 甲開修理 (National Museum of Korea catalogue)
rows.date_note: The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture dates use to 1711 from a 1722 Sillok interrogation recalling eight 角其所里 made while the speaker's father was naval commander (통제사).
kilns: Developed in Gaeseong; nationwide
rows.what_it_is: A single-level cabinet with two front doors enclosing many small drawers, used as a safe for valuables and documents (sometimes as a medicine chest).
how_to_recognize: Double doors locking over a nest of small drawers.
Frame of figured burl (용목) with interlocking corners; several hinges across the front; corners wrapped with iron caps (고깔싸개).
Scholars preferred black-iron fittings (Jeungbo sallim gyeongje).

facts.text: The gakgesuri is a single-level strong-box: two doors over many drawers for valuables and documents; it developed in Gaeseong.
facts.quote_gloss: a safe in the form of a single-level cabinet

facts.text: The name derives from the Japanese kakesuzuri (懸硯) and settled as 'gakkesuri' during the colonial period; Joseon texts also say 정궤 or 천안주.
facts.quote: 일본의 현연(懸硯; がけすずり)에서 유래
facts.quote_gloss: from the Japanese kakesuzuri

facts.text: A 1722 Sillok record mentions eight 角其所里 made to hold valuables sent as bribes; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture identifies these as gakgesuri.
facts.quote_gloss: made eight gakgisori

facts.text: The Republic of Korea gave the Smithsonian a 'Kek-ge-suri' chest with lock and key (H 86 × W 97 × D 51 cm) in 1964.
The National Museum of Korea also catalogues the type as 갑게수리 and writes it 甲開修理 (건희 4470, 4350); the National Folk Museum writes 가께수리, with 각게수리 among its other spellings.

examples.title: Chest (Kek-Ge-Suri) with lock and key; gift of the Republic of Korea, accessioned 15 Aug 1964 (indexed '1960s')

rows.name: Yakjang: medicine chest
rows.period: Joseon – 20th century (still made for herbal wholesalers)
rows.date_note: Kim Gwae-jeong: small, few and shallow drawers indicate older types; modern wholesalers' chests are very large.
kilns: Nationwide; Chungcheong, Gyeonggi and Jeolla types named
rows.what_it_is: A cabinet of many small drawers (commonly 50–70, up to 150–200) for sorting herbal medicines, each drawer front labelled with the drug name; larger lockable drawers at the bottom for bulk, precious or poisonous drugs.
how_to_recognize: Drawer fronts carved, inlaid with white paste, or written with drug names on the right side; red ink for poisons.
Korean chests have partitions both above/below AND left/right of each drawer; most Japanese medicine chests lack the side partitions; Chinese ones are sometimes revolving.
Woods: commonly pine and paulownia; drawer fronts often of hard zelkova, jujube, persimmon or pagoda tree; elite items in figured paulownia, black persimmon or burl.
Pulls: knotted cord or leather, or brass/iron peach, ring, bat, half-moon, cicada, petal, ㄷ or 卍 shapes; few or no lock plates on the front.
Older types: smaller, fewer and shallower drawers; some aromatic-drug drawers have inner lids with small holes.

facts.text: Medicine chests usually have 50–70 drawers, each with the drug name on the front, and larger lockable drawers below for bulk, precious or poisonous drugs.
facts.quote_gloss: usually 50–70

facts.text: Korean medicine chests are partitioned on all sides between drawers; Japanese ones mostly lack the side partitions and can be told at a glance.
facts.quote_gloss: mostly without the side partitions

facts.text: Smaller, fewer and shallower drawers indicate an older type.
facts.quote_gloss: the older style

rows.name: Soban: small individual dining table (general)
rows.date_note: Dated anchors: NMNH 'Eating Table' from P. L. Jouy, accessioned 1887; NMNH soban 1966.
kilns: Nationwide; named regional types Tongyeong, Naju, Haeju, Chungju, Anju; leg types by region: bamboo-joint legs in Gyeongsang, tiger legs in Jeolla, dog legs in Gangwon and Gyeonggi (Bae)
rows.what_it_is: A low, portable tray-table on which one person's meal was carried from kitchen to room and eaten; Joseon etiquette favoured individual tables. About sixty kinds by region, shape and use.
how_to_recognize: Top: one solid board with a raised rim; shapes square, rectangular, 8- or 12-sided, round, half-moon, lotus-leaf, flower.
Under the top: an apron (운각) often pierced; legs joined by a middle stretcher (중대) and foot rails (족대).
Legs: dog-leg (구족), tiger-leg (호족), bamboo-joint (죽절), single central leg, or side boards (Haeju).
Woods: tops of ginkgo, walnut, Manchurian walnut, paulownia, linden or zelkova; legs pine, maple, willow.
Finish: raw lacquer, red or black lacquer, or vegetable oil; sometimes ochre, iron-red earth or gardenia tint, or mother-of-pearl.

facts.text: Soban are classed into some sixty kinds by region, shape and use; the Tongyeong, Naju and Haeju types are the most distinctive.
facts.quote_gloss: classed into about sixty kinds

facts.text: Small individual tables suited the floor-sitting ondol room, the distance between kitchen and rooms, and Confucian separation at meals.
facts.quote_gloss: individual rather than shared tables

facts.text: Ginkgo and linden were the commonest soban woods; ginkgo tables (haengjaban) are light and take lacquer well.
facts.quote_gloss: ginkgo and linden most used

facts.text: There was no separate soban-maker post in Joseon workshops; soban were made by general cabinetmakers (somokjang).
facts.quote_gloss: generally the cabinetmaker made such things

examples.title: Eating Table, donor Pierre L. Jouy, accessioned 26 May 1887
Small Table (Soban), donor Prof. Doo-Hyun Lee, 1966
A Korean man servant holding a small meal table (watercolor, c. 1890)

rows.name: Haeju-ban: board-legged soban
kilns: Haeju, South Hwanghae Province, DPRK
rows.what_it_is: A rectangular soban standing on two wide side boards instead of four legs, the boards and front aprons pierced with cloud, fret, 卍 or bat patterns.
how_to_recognize: Two pierced side boards (판각) tenoned into long grooves under the top; the unused groove ends filled with wood strips that often show as diagonals under the top — a short-cut for volume production (Bae).
Long triangular apron boards front and back, often pierced.
Top mostly ginkgo (also linden or pine); leg boards of hard Manchurian walnut.
Raw lacquer with light coloring. Bae: about H 26–29, 30–35 × 42–45 cm.

facts.text: Haeju-ban stand on two side boards instead of four legs.
facts.quote: 반면(盤面) 양측에 판각을 한 개씩
facts.quote_gloss: one board-leg on each side of the top

facts.text: The filled grooves visible under Haeju-ban tops were a technique for convenience in volume production.
facts.quote_gloss: a technique for ease of mass production

rows.name: Naju-ban
rows.date_note: Naju soban-making designated intangible heritage (Kim Chun-sik, provincial 1986; national 소반장 1992).
kilns: Naju, South Jeolla (now 전남광주통합특별시)
rows.what_it_is: A rectangular or polygonal soban with softly rounded corners, a separately applied thick rim, a pierced apron, and legs braced by the distinctive raised 'ring' stretcher.
how_to_recognize: Rim (전) cut separately and attached, thick for its size.
Legs tenoned into the apron; a raised, stepped middle stretcher (凸형 중대, 'garakji') on all four sides.
Legs bamboo-joint, dog, cat or tiger form, splaying out then turning in at the foot.
Top of ginkgo (best) or zelkova; legs willow or pine; sometimes lacquered.

facts.text: Naju-ban have a raised ring-like stretcher on all four sides between the legs.
facts.quote_gloss: the Naju-specific raised stretcher

facts.text: Naju soban-making is a designated intangible heritage; Kim Chun-sik was named holder (South Jeolla, 1986).

rows.name: Tongyeong-ban
rows.date_note: Bae: practical and sturdy, still widely used in homes in her time.
kilns: Tongyeong, South Gyeongsang (a lacquer and mother-of-pearl center)
rows.what_it_is: A sturdy rectangular soban with rounded corners, a top carved from one thick block including the rim, straight cylindrical legs and two stretchers.
how_to_recognize: Rim carved in one item with the thick top; sometimes a carved center motif (phoenix, cranes, peaches, auspicious characters).
Straight round legs; an apron of relief-carved scroll or peony between the legs; an upper stretcher and a second lower stretcher 5–6 cm below.
Top of zelkova or ginkgo (linden sometimes); legs pine or zelkova. Bae: H 25–28, 38–47 × 28–38 cm.
Museum examples vary: the National Folk Museum's Joseon Tongyeong table has bamboo-jointed legs and one stretcher above foot rails.

facts.text: Tongyeong-ban tops are thick single boards carved together with the rim; legs are straight and round with two stretchers.
facts.quote_gloss: carved continuously with the rim

facts.text: The National Folk Museum's Joseon Tongyeong table (민속 29166) has bamboo-jointed legs and a single stretcher above foot rails, not straight round legs with two stretchers.

rows.name: Gujokban / gaedari soban: dog-leg soban (Chungju-ban)
kilns: Chungju, North Chungcheong; dog legs typical of Gangwon and Gyeonggi (Bae)
rows.what_it_is: A soban, typically 8- to 12-sided, whose four plain square legs bow outward then curve back in like a dog's legs; no middle stretcher.
how_to_recognize: No middle stretcher; legs attach right under the top, thick above and tapering, swelling out then turning in onto two foot rails.
Polygonal top (8–12 sides) with rounded edges; little ornament.
Ginkgo or zelkova top; legs of tough mixed wood.

facts.text: The Chungju soban, called 'dog-leg soban', has four plain legs that bow out and turn in, with no middle stretcher.
facts.quote_gloss: also called dog-leg soban

rows.name: Hojokban: tiger-leg soban
rows.date_note: LACMA's example is dated early 20th century.
kilns: Nationwide; 'Naju style' construction; tiger legs typical of Jeolla (Bae)
rows.what_it_is: A round or polygonal soban on curved tiger legs, used for royal meals, palace rites and formal occasions.
how_to_recognize: Legs heavy at the 'shoulder', curving and tapering, splayed, with the foot flicked up like a sock toe onto two foot rails.
Plain, or with bamboo-joint and scroll-carved aprons.
Palace items red lacquer; court ritual black lacquer; common items raw lacquer; small wine tables black lacquer with mother-of-pearl. Bae: H 28–38, diameter 35–38 cm.

facts.text: Tiger-leg soban served royal and formal use: red lacquer for palace meals, black for court rites, raw lacquer for commoners.
facts.quote_gloss: palace pieces in red lacquer

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Tiger-legged Table with Phoenix Design using Shark Skin, early 20th century; brown lacquer, shark skin inlay, brass fittings

rows.name: Gyeongdae: dressing box with folding mirror
rows.date_note: Park Jin-kyung: became a mirror-box after glass mirrors reached Korea in late Joseon; shown in 18th–19th-century genre paintings.
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: A small box for cosmetics, combs and hair ornaments whose hinged lid lifts to stand up a mirror; drawers or small doors below. Used by women and by men for topknots.
how_to_recognize: Folded, it looks like a small box; the lid hinges up to show a mirror.
Two or three drawers, sometimes small doors in front.
Plain wood, or ox-horn (화각), mother-of-pearl, black or red lacquer with metal fittings.

facts.text: The gyeongdae developed from the mirror-and-toilet box once glass mirrors came into late-Joseon Korea; its lid folds up to hold the mirror.
facts.quote_gloss: as glass mirrors came in

facts.text: The National Folk Museum uses 경대 and 빗접 (comb box) for the same items (민속 63595, 40319, 40320), and also calls a standing mirror on a stand 경대 (민속 105766).

rows.name: Dwiju: rice and grain chest
rows.date_note: NMNH example collected in Gimhae, 1972.
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: A wooden chest for rice or grain, either a hollowed log or four posts with boarded walls; the top in two parts, the back half fixed and the front half opening, with a lock.
how_to_recognize: Heavy posts, thick boards; top split, front half lifts.
Usually pine; black-iron fittings persisted on rice chests even when white brass was fashionable.
Stood on the maru (wooden-floored hall).

facts.text: A dwiju has a two-part lid: the back half fixed, the front half opening, with iron fittings and a lock.
facts.quote_gloss: the top in two leaves

facts.text: Rice chests and bandaji kept black-iron fittings even after white brass spread.

examples.title: Rice Storage Chest 'Ss'al Dwiji', collected 1972 in Samjeong-dong, Gimhae, South Gyeongsang

rows.name: Mother-of-pearl and ox-horn furniture (brief; see the lacquer/najeon reference)
rows.date_note: furniture-dating points only.
kilns: e.g. Tongyeong, long known for lacquer and mother-of-pearl (Bae, 통영반)
rows.what_it_is: Chests, boxes, cabinets and tables decorated with mother-of-pearl set in lacquer (najeon) or with painted ox-horn sheets (hwagak) — women's-room furniture.
how_to_recognize: 19th c.: more naturalistic pictures, landscapes, tortoise-shell geometric 'cut-thread' (끊음질) grounds.
From 1920: fret-saw (실톱) cut shell with smooth, even outlines and designs from painters' drawings; Japanese-style motifs and maki-e appear in the colonial period.
After 1945: cashew substitute lacquer appears.
Hwagak: small items (boxes, small chests, mirror boxes) because the technique is laborious.

facts.text: After a 1920 stay in Japan by Jeon Seong-gyu, fret-saw cutting of shell entered Korean najeon, giving smooth even outlines; colonial-era furniture took Japanese-style forms and ornament.
facts.quote_gloss: as the fret saw came in

facts.text: The red-lacquer najeon furniture attributed to Empress Sunjeonghyo, probably by Kim Jin-gap in the 1930s, has paulownia interiors and white-brass fittings.
facts.quote_gloss: the metal fittings are white brass

facts.text: After liberation (1945) a cashew-based substitute lacquer spread in Korean lacquerware.
facts.quote_gloss: a substitute lacquer called cashew

examples.title: Inlaid Chest (Ja-Ga-Son-Que): lacquer with mother-of-pearl, Korean brass lock; P. L. Jouy, 1890
Ox-horn bridal chest (hwagak-ham), Korean Commission, World's Columbian Exposition, 1893–94
Pair of chests, 18th–19th century; lacquer, metal wire, gold, silver, mother-of-pearl
Small chest of drawers decorated with flowers, birds, and insects, early 20th century; lacquer inlaid with mother-of-pearl

examples.holder: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco
examples.title: Two-tiered chest with stand, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, c. 1800–1850
Low cupboard, wood, horn and bamboo marquetry, 19th century; gift of Victor Collin de Plancy, 1891

rows.name: Zelkova (neutinamu; 'goemok')
kilns: Central and southern Korea
rows.what_it_is: Zelkova serrata: hard, fine-grained, often strongly figured; prized for chest fronts, soban tops and frames. Burl or root-cut figure is called yongmok (용목).
how_to_recognize: Ring-porous, warm brown, strong flame or burl figure; heavy.
In the 82-piece Seoul Museum of History study zelkova was 9% of identified woods, used for frames and panels with hard pine and chamjuk.
Old Western dealer texts call it 'Quimuk' (괴목) and compare root-cut figure to curly maple.

facts.text: Zelkova (Zelkova serrata) is also written 괴목/규목/궤목 and its fine, hard wood was used for tables and furniture.
facts.quote_gloss: fine and hard, used for tables and furniture

facts.text: Zelkova made up 9% of 19th-century items examined at the Seoul Museum of History and was a main structural wood with hard pine and chamjuk.
An early-20th-century Seoul dealer called the prized chest wood 'Quimuk', said no stains or oils were used on old chests, and that their color came from age and polishing.
The National Folk Museum writes 괴목 with 槐 in its titles, e.g. 槐木三層饌欌 (민속 4988): a catalogue title, not a wood identification.

rows.name: Black-streaked persimmon (meokgam)
kilns: Honam (Jeolla) named as the source of good persimmon in Joseon texts (Lee)
rows.what_it_is: Persimmon heartwood with black, ink-like streaks; used as thin decorative panels on chests, nong, mungap, medicine chests and stationery items.
how_to_recognize: Pale wood with dramatic black clouds and streaks, usually as thin, mirror-matched panels in a frame of another wood.
Rare as a structural wood (3% of the Seoul Museum of History sample).

facts.text: Figured black persimmon was used for panels of women's-room chests, nong, mungap and stationery items.
facts.quote_gloss: persimmon with beautiful grain

facts.text: Persimmon (Diospyros) was 3% of identified woods in 82 late-Joseon items.
Joseon texts name Honam persimmon among the best desk woods.
facts.quote_gloss: Honam black persimmon

rows.name: Paulownia (odong)
kilns: Cultivated south of the central region
rows.what_it_is: Very light, soft, pale wood resistant to damp and insects; used for drawers, chest bodies, nong and wardrobes, often scorched to bring up the grain.
how_to_recognize: Very light in the hand; soft (dents easily); silvery-gray when new.
Often surface-scorched (낙동법) and brushed so the grain stands up dark.
Typical for drawers and drawer linings (with linden).

facts.text: Paulownia is light and resists damp and insects, so it was used for chests and boxes; families planted one at a daughter's birth to make her wedding chest.
facts.quote_gloss: planting a paulownia when a daughter was born

facts.text: Light, low-shrinkage woods — paulownia and linden — were chosen for drawers.
On early uigeorijang the paulownia surface was scorched with an iron (낙동법) to emphasise the grain.
facts.quote_gloss: scorching paulownia with an iron

rows.name: Pine (sonamu)
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Korean red pine: the commonest furniture wood — chest bodies, rice chests, kitchen cupboards, bookcases, soban legs.
how_to_recognize: Pale yellow sapwood, red-brown heartwood, distinct growth rings; resinous.
Hard pines were 43% of identified woods in 82 late-Joseon items.

facts.text: Pine was used for chests, wardrobes, rice chests, cupboards and bookcases.
facts.quote_gloss: wardrobes, rice chests, cupboards, bookcases

facts.text: Hard pines made up 43% of the woods identified in 82 late-Joseon items.

rows.name: Ginkgo (eunhaeng; 'haengjamok')
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Fine, even, slightly elastic pale wood; the classic soban top and stationery-box wood.
how_to_recognize: Pale, even, featureless grain; light; takes lacquer well.
5% of identified woods in the Seoul Museum of History sample — high for furniture.

facts.text: Ginkgo is fine-grained, dense and elastic and is used for furniture and dining tables.
facts.quote_gloss: furniture, carving, go boards, tables

facts.text: Ginkgo was 5% of identified woods in 82 late-Joseon items.

rows.name: Black iron fittings
rows.period: all periods; dominant on bandaji, rice chests and in some regions
rows.date_note: Choi: iron in antiquity; later still used on bandaji and dwiju whatever the fashion.
kilns: Nationwide; Bakcheon pierced iron; Jeju heavy iron
rows.what_it_is: Hand-forged iron hinges, straps, handles, lock plates and nails, blackened; the oldest and most persistent Korean furniture metal.
how_to_recognize: Hand-cut, slightly irregular shapes; nails with hand-forged heads of varying size (dealer).
Old surfaces: stable dark patina, not fresh black paint (dealer).
Older gyeongsang have round iron ring pulls (Kim, single source).

facts.text: Early fittings were mainly functional iron; bandaji and rice chests kept iron even after white brass became general.
facts.quote_gloss: in antiquity mainly functional iron fittings

facts.text: Late-Joseon Jeonju chests used cast iron and yellow brass fittings.

examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.title: Chest, 19th century; carved wood with iron fittings

rows.name: Yellow brass (duseok) fittings
rows.hanja: 豆錫 · 黃銅 · 朱錫
rows.period: Joseon to the late 19th century as the main fine-furniture metal
rows.date_note: Choi: brass fittings throughout Joseon until late in the dynasty.
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Copper-alloy fittings hammered from sheet and cut out; the name duseok comes from the Joseon government metalworkers (두석장) listed in the Gyeongguk daejeon.
how_to_recognize: Mellow, warm yellow when old; hard bright yellow suggests new metal; a reddish tint can mean chemical ageing (dealer).
Shapes: yakgwa (oblong cookie), gourd, butterfly, bat, swallow-tail, cloud, 卍, herb of immortality, carp, 'Namdaemun gate'.
Hand-chased line engraving; slight differences from item to item (dealer).

facts.text: Duseok is named after the Joseon government brass-smiths (두석장) of the Gyeongguk daejeon; it was a copper alloy, though exactly which is debated.
facts.quote_gloss: the capital craftsmen of the Board of Works in the Gyeongguk daejeon

facts.text: Through most of the Joseon period brass fittings were applied sparingly to suit each item's structure.
facts.quote: 황동제 장석이 가구의 구조에 따라 간결하고
facts.quote_gloss: brass fittings simply, following the structure

facts.text: Lifting handles fixed by a single eye-pin are mainly found on furniture before the late Joseon; two-pin handles come later.
facts.quote: 배목 한 개의 들쇠가 조선 후기 이전의
facts.quote_gloss: one-pin handles on pre-late-Joseon furniture

examples.title: Korean chest; pine, oak and brass (gourd hinges, 囍 roundels, bat lock plate)

rows.name: White brass (baekdong / paektong) fittings
rows.date_note: Lee: fashion probably began in the late 19th century; NMNH: already on a chest collected in Seoul 1884–85; Baik & Lim: nickel dominant on Jeonju chests in the colonial period (1910–45); 1930s royal najeon furniture uses white brass.
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Silvery copper–nickel alloy fittings, often large, profuse and cut into auspicious symbols (bats, butterflies, 囍, 壽福), sometimes inlaid with silver or dark copper (오동).
how_to_recognize: Silver-white metal; many and large plates covering much of the front.
Auspicious or apotropaic symbols increase from the end of Joseon.
Later work may be press-stamped rather than hand-cut (Lee: modern makers use presses).

facts.text: From the end of Joseon, white brass (copper–nickel) became the main fitting metal.
facts.quote: 구리와 니켈의 합금인 백동이 장석 재료의 대종
facts.quote_gloss: copper-nickel white brass became the main fitting material

facts.text: The white-brass fashion probably began in the late 19th century; today's metalworkers work almost only in white brass.
facts.quote_gloss: probably began from the late 19th c.

facts.text: A three-tier chest collected in Seoul in 1884–85 already has white-brass fittings.
Jeonju chests of the colonial period mainly use nickel fittings with more engraved ornament, unlike late-Joseon cast iron and yellow brass.
With the wider market of late Joseon came auspicious and apotropaic motifs and over-decoration with silver and dark-copper inlay, which Choi calls a decline.
facts.quote_gloss: falling into excessive decoration

facts.text: Modern makers stamp fittings with presses instead of hand-forging.
facts.quote_gloss: stamped out with a press

examples.title: Three-tiered chest with white-brass fittings, collected in Seoul 1884–85

rows.name: Fitting shapes and symbols: bat, butterfly, gourd, 囍, fish
rows.hanja: 蝙蝠 · 蝶 · 囍 · 壽福
rows.date_note: Choi: auspicious/apotropaic motifs dominate from the end of Joseon.
kilns: Nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Named hinge, handle, clasp and lock shapes. Bats stand for blessing and protection; carp for sons and advancement ('carp becomes dragon'); 囍 for double joy.
how_to_recognize: Hinges: round, yakgwa, folding-screen, swallow-tail, cloud, herb of immortality, orchid, 卍, gourd, name-tag, 'Namdaemun', butterfly, bat, cloisonné (Choi).
Locks: tube locks, 'watermelon' locks, figural locks in carp, dragon, bat or bamboo shape (Choi).
Bae lists 卍, 囍, 壽福 characters and gourd, swallow-tail, bat and herb shapes as the most common.

facts.text: Bats in fittings stand for blessing and warding off evil; carp for sons and success.
facts.quote_gloss: the bat, seeking fortune and repelling evil

facts.text: Gourd, swallow-tail, bat and herb-of-immortality shapes and 卍, 囍, 壽福 characters are the commonest fitting designs.
facts.quote_gloss: gourd, swallow-tail, bat, herb shapes

examples.title: Brass-fitted chest with gourd hinges, 囍 roundels and a bat-shaped lock plate

rows.name: 20th-century export, tourist and reproduction furniture
rows.rr: suchullyong gagu, gwangwangyong gagu, jaehyeon gagu
rows.mr: such'ullyong kagu, kwan'gwangyong kagu, chaehyŏn kagu
rows.date_note: Earliest documented: a Seoul curio dealer's catalogue (after 1910) of new 'modern type' chests for foreigners. Mid-century: plywood and veneer (dealer: widespread by the 1970s). Official gifts of new traditional-style furniture by the Republic of Korea (Smithsonian, 1962–77).
kilns: Seoul (curio shops selling to foreigners)
workshops nationwide
rows.what_it_is: Furniture in traditional Korean form made for foreign buyers, tourists, diplomats and the modern Korean market — from hand-made 'old style' chests with Western interiors (1910s–30s) to machine-made veneered chests with stamped brass (later 20th c.). Not fakes in themselves, but often sold or inherited as 'antique'.
how_to_recognize: Western-use interiors: lined drawers, desk or silver-cabinet fittings, 'mahogany' or other stains (Ye Olde Curio Shoppe new chests).
Materials: plywood or pressed board under thin veneer; thin, shiny, identical yellow-brass plates; machine-cut or press-stamped fittings; new wire nails or screws (dealer; Lee).
Fake age: black paint or stain around fittings with hard edges; chemical reddening of brass; glossy uniform finish; fresh wood visible in cracks; new paper lining the back or inside (dealer).
'Married' or rebuilt items: old bodies with new fittings, or new chests built from old boards (dealer; Ye Olde 'reconstructed cash boxes').
Dimensions and names drifting from traditional norms and Japanese-style details mixed in (Lee & Park 2004, for the 2000s Korean market).

Export history: Korea's cultural-property law (enacted c. 1962, replaced by the 국가유산 laws in 2024) controls export; today items of cultural value made 50+ years ago need permission, checked at airport and port inspection offices. When the 50-year rule began was not established. Any surviving export paperwork is a lead (our inference, not a source statement).

facts.text: A Seoul curio dealer after 1910 sold new chests 'following the old lines' with modern interiors and stains, alongside antiques and chests 'reconstructed' from old material.
In the 19th century and later, furniture-making spread to a mass market with specialised shops, and quality became uneven.
facts.quote_gloss: as mass production set in

facts.text: Late-19th-century imports brought Western-style furniture; the colonial period brought Japanese forms and ornament, and new chests of many drawers.
facts.quote_gloss: into Japanese-style forms and ornament

facts.text: Modern metalworkers stamp fittings with presses rather than hand-forging them.
facts.quote_gloss: stamped out with a press

facts.text: Plywood came into furniture in the mid-20th century and was widespread by the 1970s.
Items at least 50 years old with historical, artistic or scholarly value (일반동산문화재) need government permission to leave Korea; airport and port inspection offices check them.
facts.quote_gloss: made 50+ years ago and in good condition

facts.text: Edward Reynolds Wright formed his Korean furniture collection while living in Seoul 1967–78, when many displaced families were selling household goods.
A 2004 study of reproduced 'traditional' furniture on the Korean market found confused names, changed dimensions and Japanese-style mixing.

examples.title: Set of traditional-type furniture, gift of the Republic of Korea, accessioned 15 Aug 1964 (indexed '1960s')
Lacquer and pearl chest, U.S. State Department, 1977

rows.name: Goryeo bronze mirrors (including the 煌丕昌天 ship mirrors)
rows.hanja: 高麗銅鏡 · 煌丕昌天銘鏡
rows.period: Goryeo (918–1392); Joseon mirrors noted for contrast
kilns: Production centres not established. Find-spots recorded only as 'near Gaeseong' (Kaesong, North Korea) or 'near Ganghwa Island' (Ganghwa County, Incheon).
rows.what_it_is: Cast bronze mirrors: the face was polished to reflect, the back carries a central knob for a cord and cast decoration or auspicious words. Shapes include round, square, six- and eight-lobed, bell-shaped and handled. Many entered Western museums in the 1910s–20s (Met, Freer and Cleveland acquisitions of 1911–1932).
how_to_recognize: Back with a central knob, a zone around it and an outer rim; the face is plain (often corroded).
Shapes: round, square, lobed (six- or eight-foil), bell-shaped, with a handle, or made to hang.
The 煌丕昌天 type: eight-lobed, a ship riding stormy waves with sea creatures, and four seal-script characters above the knob; thick-bodied with high relief.

A few carry a stamped cartouche 高麗國造 ('made in Goryeo') in the inner zone; Jin-dynasty official inspection inscriptions (北京驗記官, 西京官記 and the like) are finely scratched on the rims of some mirrors said to come from Goryeo tombs.
Being found in a Goryeo tomb does not make a mirror Korean: Han, Tang, Song, Liao, Jin and Yuan mirrors, and recasts or imitations of them, were all buried in Goryeo.
Joseon mirrors tend to be larger and thinner, often with Sanskrit letters or chrysanthemum designs; Japanese Edo-period mirrors also arrived then.

copies.text: Re-casts (再鑄) and imitations (倣製) of Han, Tang and Song mirrors were made and buried in Goryeo; copying blurred or altered the designs (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 동경).
No source found on modern reproductions or physical tests for them.

facts.text: Korean bronze mirrors were used until glass mirrors replaced them in modern times; the back carries designs or auspicious words around a central knob.
facts.quote_gloss: were used until replaced by glass mirrors

facts.text: Most mirrors from Goryeo tombs lost their find data because early excavators cared only for celadon; they are known only as 'found near Gaeseong' or 'near Ganghwa Island'.
facts.quote: 개성 부근 출토, 강화도 부근 출토라는 단서만으로
facts.quote_gloss: only with the clue 'excavated near Gaeseong' or 'near Ganghwa'

facts.text: Goryeo tombs contained imported Tang, Song, Jin and Yuan mirrors and re-casts or imitations of them, so picking out mirrors actually made in Goryeo is difficult; museums still hedge attributions (Cleveland catalogues one as 'China, Jin dynasty or Korea, Goryeo').
facts.quote: 고려시대의 독자적인 동경을 가려내는 데는 많은 문제가
facts.quote_gloss: there are many problems in picking out Goryeo's own mirrors

facts.text: A few mirrors carry a square stamped mark 高麗國造 ('made in Goryeo') in the inner zone; most inscribed examples of the Jin type have their inscriptions finely incised on the rim. NMK holds at least two catalogued under this name (덕수 89; 건희 5787).
facts.quote_gloss: a square stamped mark 高麗國造

facts.text: Jin official inspection inscriptions such as 北京驗記官 and 西京官記 occur on mirrors said to be from Goryeo tombs, evidence of heavy traffic in Jin mirrors.
facts.quote: 금대의 것으로 인정되는 명문을 가진 동경
facts.quote_gloss: mirrors with inscriptions accepted as Jin

facts.text: Under the Jin (1115–1234), mirrors were made in state workshops (offices such as 銅院, 鏡子局, 鑄鏡所) centered on the capital Shangjing, partly to control copper supply.
facts.quote: 동원(銅院), 경자국(鏡子局), 주경소(鑄鏡所)
facts.quote_gloss: the offices Dongwon, Gyeongjaguk, Jugyeongso

facts.text: 煌丕昌天 means roughly 'bright and resplendent is the heaven' (Cleveland: 'Great and resplendent is the heaven').
facts.quote_gloss: means 'the bright, flourishing heaven'

facts.text: 煌丕昌天 mirrors are thick and in near-high relief; examples are almost unknown from excavations in China or Japan, and whether they are Goryeo's own invention needs further study. Identical examples were among the finds from the Sinan shipwreck.
facts.quote: 경태가 두껍고 고육조(高肉彫)에 가까운 문양
facts.quote_gloss: thick body, decoration close to high relief

facts.text: The 煌丕昌天 type survives in Korea in the largest numbers of any Goryeo mirror type; it is described as introduced from China and also made in Goryeo, with round Goryeo versions developing new designs.
facts.quote: 고려시대에 국내로 유입되어 성행·제작된 것으로 보인다
facts.quote_gloss: seems to have been introduced, flourished and been made in Goryeo

facts.text: Dating rests on indirect evidence: with no records and many heirloom (never-buried) items, 煌丕昌天 mirrors are usually placed in the 12th–14th centuries, partly from coins found with them.
facts.quote_gloss: explained as 12th–14th century

facts.text: Cleveland's label reports that on the seventh day of the New Year (the 'Day of Humans') the Goryeo king gave officials bronze mirrors with auspicious symbols, which would explain how many mirrors reached elite tombs.
In the Joseon period mirrors became larger and thinner and often carry Sanskrit letters or chrysanthemums; Japanese (Edo) mirrors also came in.
facts.quote: 동경이 대형화하고 얇아지며 범자(梵字) · 국화문
facts.quote_gloss: mirrors became larger and thinner, Sanskrit and chrysanthemum designs

examples.title: Mirror decorated with a ship in a stormy sea (煌丕昌天 type)
Octafoil-shaped Mirror Featuring Ci Fei, the Dragon Slayer (煌丕昌天)
「황비창천」이 새겨진 항해도 무늬 거울 (銅製海舶魚龍鏡, 煌丕昌天鏡)
『고려국조』명동제원형경 (『高麗國造』銘銅製圓形鏡)
Mirror with dragon, cassia tree, and pavilion design, 11th–12th c.
Mirror decorated with phoenixes and flowers, first half 12th c.

rows.name: Goryeo and Joseon Buddhist bronzes and ritual vessels (censers, bells, sutra cases)
rows.hanja: 香垸 · 梵鐘 · 佛具
kilns: Gaegyeong (Kaesong, North Korea): Goryeo court metal office 掌冶署 (Jangyaseo)
Hanyang (Seoul): Joseon capital craftsmen 京工匠 under the Ministry of Works 工曹 and the Royal Wardrobe 尙衣院
rows.what_it_is: Bronze vessels made for temples: above all the hyangwan, a censer with a wide flat rim on a trumpet-shaped foot, often inlaid with silver wire; also small hanging bells, ritual handbells, incense boxes, sutra cases and kundikas (separate entry).
how_to_recognize: Goryeo hyangwan: bowl-shaped body with a broad horizontal rim, on a flaring trumpet foot with a disc base; height and width roughly equal.
Silver-wire inlay of Sanskrit syllables in roundels, cloud scrolls, dragons and phoenixes, lotus scrolls; on one Leeum censer, the willow-and-waterfowl scene usual on kundikas.
Many carry inlaid or incised inscriptions naming a temple, donor and a cyclical year; inscriptions call the inlay 含銀, 入銀, 納銀, 銀絲 or 入絲.
Joseon censers keep the form; museums catalogue silver-inlaid censers into the Joseon period (e.g. the Cheonggok-sa censer).

copies.text: NMK catalogues a silver-inlaid bronze hyangwan in the Lee Kun-hee gift as post-1945 (건희 3240): the form has been made again in modern times. No source gives tests for telling such items from Goryeo ones.

facts.text: A censer with a wide rim and trumpet-shaped foot was specially called hyangwan (香垸) in the Goryeo period; it was used on altars and in rituals at temples.
facts.quote_gloss: in Goryeo it was specially called hyangwan

facts.text: The Pyochungsa censer (National Treasure) bears a 57-character silver-inlaid inscription dating it to 1177; it is the oldest surviving Korean hyangwan and a fixed point for dating the type. Its inscription also shows it first belonged to Yongheung-sa, Changnyeong.
facts.quote: 고려 명종 7년(1177)에 제작된 것임을 알 수 있다
facts.quote_gloss: it was made in the 7th year of King Myeongjong (1177)

facts.text: The Heungwang-sa censer (National Treasure, Leeum) carries a 34-character inscription round the foot whose cyclical year 己丑 places it about 1289.
facts.quote_gloss: through the cyclical year gichuk

facts.text: Goryeo censer inscriptions name the inlay technique in several ways: 含銀 (Pyochungsa), 入銀 and 納銀 (Geumsan-sa), 銀絲 (Baekjang-sa, Donghwa-sa) and 入絲 (Geonbong-sa, Cheonggok-sa).
facts.quote_gloss: the Pyochungsa censer has 含銀

facts.text: Goryeo metalworkers of this kind belonged to the court office 掌冶署; in Joseon, inlay craftsmen were capital craftsmen (京工匠) of the Ministry of Works and the Royal Wardrobe.
facts.quote_gloss: in Goryeo, the Jangyaseo

facts.text: Goryeo inlay motifs include ruyi heads, Sanskrit letters, willows and waterfowl, lotus and honeysuckle scrolls.
facts.quote_gloss: ruyi heads, Sanskrit letters, willow-and-waterfowl, lotus scroll

facts.text: The willow-and-waterfowl design is common on kundikas but, among censers, appears only on the Leeum censer (Treasure); its 34-character inscription gives no date and it is placed in the 13th century on style.
facts.quote_gloss: among censers it appears only on this piece

facts.text: A small cast-bronze temple bell at Cleveland is dated 1226 by its inscription.

examples.title: 「함평궁주방」이 새겨진 청동 은입사 향완 (「咸平宮主房」銘銅製銀象嵌香垸)
「지정 26년 진종사」가 새겨진 청동 은입사 향완

표충사 청동 은입사 향완, 1177
흥왕사명 청동 은입사 향완, c. 1289

rows.name: Kundika (ritual water sprinkler), bronze with silver inlay
rows.hanja: 淨甁 · 靑銅銀入絲蒲柳水禽文淨甁
rows.rr: jeongbyeong · cheongdong eunipsa poryu sugeummun jeongbyeong
rows.mr: chŏngbyŏng · ch'ŏngdong ŭnipsa p'oryu sugŭmmun chŏngbyŏng
kilns: Not recorded; Goryeo court and temple workshops (see buddhist_bronzes)
rows.what_it_is: A tall water bottle for pure water used in Buddhist ritual and held by the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara. The Goryeo form has a long neck with a ring, a slender pointed spout on top and a lidded spout on the shoulder. The finest are bronze inlaid with silver wire showing a waterside scene.
how_to_recognize: Two openings: a tall, thin tube rising from a disc on the neck, and a short spout on the shoulder with a small lid.
Silver-wire inlay of willows, reeds, ducks and geese, sometimes a boatman and distant birds (蒲柳水禽文); ruyi borders at shoulder and foot.
Bronze now covered with green-blue patina; the same shape and scene occur in celadon.
Plain bronze kundikas without inlay are also held in the West (Cleveland 1991.58 and 1992.141, Met 23.115).

facts.text: The jeongbyeong derives from the Sanskrit kundika: a bottle for the purest water, which became an offering vessel on Buddhist altars and an attribute of Avalokitesvara.
facts.quote_gloss: derived from Sanskrit kundika

facts.text: Kundikas were made of pottery, gold and silver, but mainly of bronze and ceramics; in Goryeo they were produced in quantity as essential Buddhist implements.
facts.quote_gloss: bronze and ceramics were mainly used

facts.text: The characteristic Korean form has a long neck with a ring, a tall pointed top and a lidded spout on the shoulder; the National Treasure silver-inlaid kundika in NMK is its type item.
facts.quote: 몸체의 넓은 어깨에는 주둥이가 나와 있는 형태
facts.quote_gloss: a spout comes out on the broad shoulder

facts.text: Bronze and ceramic kundikas share the same waterside decoration of willows, reeds, ducks and geese; among metalwork the scene is mainly found on kundikas.
facts.quote_gloss: willow-and-waterfowl and willow-reed-waterfowl designs

facts.text: On the National Treasure kundika (37.5 cm) the design was cut into the bronze and silver hammered into the grooves; the spout lid is openwork and the neck cover is pierced silver sheet.
facts.quote: 문양 부분을 파낸 뒤 은을 박아 장식한
facts.quote_gloss: decorated by cutting out the design and setting in silver

facts.text: Several Goryeo silver-inlaid kundikas are known; the National Treasure item is regarded as the finest.
facts.quote: 현존하는 고려시대 은입사정병은 여러 점이 알려져
facts.quote_gloss: several surviving Goryeo silver-inlaid kundikas are known

examples.title: 청동 은입사 물가풍경무늬 정병 (靑銅銀入絲蒲柳水禽文淨甁)
청동 은입사 물가 풍경 무늬 정병
청동 은입사 물가풍경무늬 정병

Water Ewer for Rituals (Kundika), 1100s

rows.name: Iron inlaid with silver (ipsa): tobacco boxes, braziers, candlesticks, horse gear
rows.period: mid-Joseon to the 20th century (earlier iron items exist)
kilns: Hanyang (Seoul): capital inlay craftsmen (入絲匠, 京工匠); later the Yi Royal Household art workshop at Gwanghwamun, Seoul, through which the craft lineage passed
rows.what_it_is: Dark iron items whose surface was chiselled into a fine criss-cross texture and then covered with silver (sometimes gold) wire or thin sheet hammered on, making silver patterns, characters and scenes. Common forms: tobacco boxes, incense boxes, braziers, candlesticks, maces, stirrups and saddle fittings.
how_to_recognize: Iron (black to brown, may rust) rather than bronze; the silver lies on a finely roughened, hatched ground rather than in single cut grooves.
Typical Joseon motifs: longevity symbols, the characters 壽 and 福, swastika (卍) and key frets; plum, orchid, chrysanthemum, bamboo, crane, deer, bat, tiger, pine.
Tobacco boxes (煙盒) usually rectangular with a lid, often with brass fittings.
Goryeo inlay is different: bronze with silver wire set into cut grooves (see kundika, buddhist_bronzes).

copies.text: The technique never stopped: it passed through the Yi Royal Household art workshop to masters designated from 1983, so 20th-century and new items exist. No source gives tests for dating them.

facts.text: Korean inlay has two methods: from Goryeo, silver wire hammered into grooves cut in bronze; from the mid-Joseon period, iron inlay, in which the iron surface is chiselled criss-cross until rough and thin gold or silver sheet or wire is laid on and hammered down.
facts.quote_gloss: iron inlay, handed down from the mid-Joseon period on

facts.text: Early Korean inlay pressed silver wire into chiselled grooves ('kkium ipsa'); the late-Joseon method chiselled the ground densely and laid silver on it, which craftsmen called yeopsa (葉絲); it allowed freer designs.
facts.quote_gloss: craftsmen of the time called it yeopsa

facts.text: In Joseon, inlay spread from Buddhist items to everyday things: braziers, candlesticks and tobacco boxes.
facts.quote: 화로 , 촛대, 담배함 등 일상 유물에서도
facts.quote_gloss: also on everyday objects such as braziers, candlesticks, tobacco boxes

facts.text: Joseon inlay motifs are mostly longevity and good-fortune symbols: the ten longevity symbols, demon masks, the seven treasures, and the characters 壽 and 福.
facts.quote_gloss: character designs such as su and bok

facts.text: The late-18th-century 『京都雜志』 says court officials always carried a tobacco box of iron engraved with plum and bamboo in silver.
facts.quote: 쇠로 만들었는데 매화와 대나무를 은으로 새겼다
facts.quote_gloss: made of iron, with plum and bamboo in silver

facts.text: Tobacco reached Korea after the Imjin War (1592–98), so tobacco boxes and pipes post-date about 1600.
facts.quote: 임진왜란 후 일본을 통해 담배가 전래되면서
facts.quote_gloss: with tobacco introduced via Japan after the Imjin War

facts.text: The 『經國大典』 forbade officials below the dangha rank to have silver-inlaid saddles, and silver-inlaid swords are recorded; Joseon saddles were iron.
facts.quote: 당하관의 신분으로 말안장에 은입사하는 것을 금한다
facts.quote_gloss: forbids those of dangha rank silver inlay on saddles

facts.text: The ipsa craft lineage in Seoul ran through the Yi Royal Household art workshop; ipsajang was designated a national intangible heritage in 1983.
facts.quote: 이왕직미술품제작소(李王職美術品製作所) 를 통하여
facts.quote_gloss: through the Yi Royal Household art workshop

facts.text: The Met dates an iron incense box inlaid with gold and silver to the 14th–15th century (early Joseon): iron inlay is not only a late form.

examples.title: Tobacco box, 19th c., iron inlaid with silver; brass fittings
Incense box, 14th–15th c., iron inlaid with gold and silver
철제은입사육각형합 (鐵製銀入絲六角形盒)
Spirit House, late 1800s, iron inlaid with silver and copper

rows.name: Yugi brassware: hammered bangjja and cast jumul (Napcheong, Anseong)
rows.hanja: 鍮器 · 方字 · 鑄物
rows.period: Goryeo to the 20th century; everyday ware above all in the 18th–20th centuries
kilns: Napcheong (納淸): Cheongjeong-dong, Masan-myeon, Jeongju County, North Pyongan (North Korea) — hammered bangjja
Anseong, Gyeonggi Province — cast ware ('Anseong-matchum')
Gaeseong (Kaesong, North Korea) — cast ware
Bonghwa, North Gyeongsang — cast ware
Suncheon, South Jeolla — half-bangjja
also Gimcheon, Namwon, Jeonju, Hongseong, Bakcheon, Pyongyang, Sariwon, Seoul
rows.what_it_is: Yellow copper-alloy tableware and ritual ware (rice bowls, lidded bowls, basins, spoons, candlesticks, censers, braziers) and gongs. Two methods: bangjja, a high-tin bronze forged hot by a team with hammers; and jumul, molten metal poured into molds, often a zinc brass.
how_to_recognize: Bangjja: hammer marks often left on the surface; does not bend or crack readily and tarnishes less; gongs, cymbals, basins and large yangpun were bangjja.
Cast: smoother, mold-made shapes (candlesticks, censers, braziers); zinc brass or mixed metals; bends, cracks and tarnishes more easily.
Goryeo yugi is thin and tough.
Tarnish and green patina form with time; households scoured it with ground roof-tile powder.

copies.text: From the 20th century cheap cast zinc brass that looks like bangjja displaced it (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 유기장). Both methods are still practised by designated masters (Anseong, Bonghwa and others).

facts.text: Bangjja uses copper and tin only; any other metal makes it crack under the hammer.
facts.quote: 다른 물질이 들어가면 두들겨 기형을 만드는 과정에서 깨어지기
facts.quote_gloss: if any other substance gets in it breaks while being hammered

facts.text: The classic recipe is one geun of copper to four nyang of tin, as given in 『五洲書種博物考辨』.
facts.quote: 구리 한 근에 주석 4냥을 합치면 된다
facts.quote_gloss: combine one geun of copper with four nyang of tin

facts.text: Bangjja is forged hot from a flat disc of alloy (badaegi) by a team of eleven working in turn.
facts.quote_gloss: a team of eleven hammering while heating

facts.text: On bangjja the hammer marks are often left to show the method.
facts.quote_gloss: the hammer marks are left as they are

facts.text: Cast yugi is made by pouring copper alloyed with tin or zinc (about 7:3) into molds, then finishing and polishing; Anseong was famous for it.
facts.quote_gloss: copper with tin or zinc in a 7:3 ratio

facts.text: Gongs, cymbals, basins, yangpun, tableware and spoons are bangjja; candlesticks, censers and braziers are cast in zinc alloy.
facts.quote_gloss: zinc-alloy cast yugi such as candlesticks, censers, braziers

facts.text: Rich households used bangjja lidded bowls (hap), commoners cast ones; cast items of brass or mixed metals bend, break and discolor more easily.
facts.quote: 잘 휘거나 깨지며 쉽게 변색되는 단점
facts.quote_gloss: the drawback that they bend, break and discolour easily

facts.text: Anseong yugi gave rise to the saying 'Anseong-matchum' (made to order in Anseong, i.e. a perfect fit); 『임원경제지』 ranks it above Gurye, Gaeseong and Jeongju ware.
facts.quote_gloss: said Anseong yugi was the best

facts.text: Napcheong in Jeongju, North Pyongan, was the home of large hammered vessels; bangjja was called 'yangdae Napcheong seonggi' (良大納淸成器), yangdae being the northern word for bangjja.
facts.quote_gloss: yangdae Napcheong seonggi

facts.text: Goryeo yugi is thin, tough and lustrous.
facts.quote: 고려시대의 유기는 동체가 얇고 질긴 것이 특징
facts.quote_gloss: Goryeo yugi is characterised by thin, tough bodies

facts.text: Joseon state craftsmen made yugi: the Gyeongguk daejeon lists yujang (鍮匠) in the Ministry of Works, the Royal Treasury (內需司) and the Royal Wardrobe, with others in provincial offices.
facts.quote: 유기를 전담하여 놋그릇을 생산하는 유장(鍮匠)
facts.quote_gloss: yujang who specialised in making brassware

facts.text: Yugi went out of use after the Korean War: coal-briquette fumes tarnished it, and stainless steel and plastic replaced it.
facts.quote_gloss: brass's tendency to tarnish in briquette gas

facts.text: A first-birthday brass bowl with spoon and chopsticks, inscribed in hangeul, is catalogued by the National Hangeul Museum as colonial period.

examples.title: '돌맞이~' 명 유기 주발과 수저 (colonial period)
Wine Cup (pair), brass, 1900s
Bowl, bronze, 1700s
유기 국그릇 (鍮器大楪)

rows.name: White brass (baekdong) and furniture fittings (jangseok, duseok)
rows.hanja: 白銅 · 裝錫 · 豆錫
rows.period: Joseon; white baekdong fittings above all from the late 19th century
kilns: Hanyang (Seoul): capital fitting-makers (豆錫匠)
pipe-making centres for baekdong: Dongnae (Busan), Gimcheon, Namwon, Anseong; also Gyeongju, Yeonghae, Ulsan, Yecheon
rows.what_it_is: Metal hardware on wooden furniture (hinges, handles, corner plates, lock plates, locks, decorative nail heads) and the white copper alloy, baekdong, used for the showier late fittings and for tobacco pipes.
how_to_recognize: Yellow brass fittings, few and restrained, are the Joseon norm; white (silvery) baekdong fittings in profusion, with bats, butterflies, fish and auspicious characters, are a late-Joseon and later fashion.
Fittings were hammered to sheet about 0.5 mm thick, cut out, filed and engraved, then polished.
Late fittings may be inlaid with silver or odong (烏銅, a dark gold- or silver-copper alloy).
Baekdong is whiter the more nickel it holds; pipes (yeonjuk) were forged cold from it.

copies.text: Chests with profuse white-brass fittings continued to be made after 1945 (the National Folk Museum holds North Korean examples shown in 2006). No source gives tests for the age of fittings.

facts.text: Furniture fittings were long called duseok (豆錫), from the alloy used by the Joseon capital craftsmen who made them; jangseok is the newer term.
facts.quote_gloss: originally the word duseok was used

facts.text: Kinds of fitting include hinges, drop handles, rings, strap plates, corner items, locks, lock plates and dome-headed nails.
facts.quote: 경첩 · 들쇠 · 고리 · 감잡이 · 귀장식 · 자물쇠
facts.quote_gloss: hinges, drop handles, rings, straps, corner pieces, locks

facts.text: Until the late Joseon period fittings were brass, attached sparingly to suit the furniture's structure; from the end of the period they turned to baekdong, with auspicious and protective motifs and sometimes too many fittings.
facts.quote: 재료도 백동으로 바뀌는 새로운 경향이 대두되었다
facts.quote_gloss: a new tendency arose for the material to change to baekdong

facts.text: For more luxurious fittings baekdong rather than brass was used.
facts.quote: 보다 사치스러운 장석으로 꾸미기 위해서는 백동을 쓴다
facts.quote_gloss: for more luxurious fittings baekdong is used

facts.text: At the end of Joseon, copper-nickel baekdong became the main fitting material.
facts.quote: 구리와 니켈 의 합금인 백동이 장석 재료의 대종
facts.quote_gloss: copper-nickel baekdong became the mainstay of fitting materials

facts.text: 'Baekdong' has meant different things: today a copper-nickel alloy, but in older texts also copper with tin, zinc, lead or arsenic, or simply a white metal; nickel entered Korea between the end of Joseon and the modern period.
facts.quote: 니켈이 우리나라에 도입된 시기는 조선 말기에서 근대기로
facts.quote_gloss: nickel was introduced to Korea between late Joseon and the modern period

facts.text: Fittings were made by hammering the metal into sheet about 0.5 mm thick, cutting with chisels, filing, engraving and polishing with ceramic powder.
facts.quote_gloss: hammered out into sheet 0.5 mm thick

facts.text: Baekdong tobacco pipes were made by hammering and soldering sheet; plain ones are minjuk, decorated ones byeoljuk, ornamented with odong, gold or silver.
facts.quote_gloss: a plain baekdong pipe is a minjuk

facts.text: Noted pipe centres were Dongnae, Gimcheon, Namwon and Anseong; Dongnae was also known for pipes decorated with enamel (paran).
facts.quote_gloss: Dongnae's enamel-decorated pipes

examples.title: 백동장식궤(白銅裝飾櫃) — Gaeseong bandaji, post-1945 North Korean item
바늘집 (needle case, 백동, Joseon)
진유제 붕어모양 자물쇠 (brass fish-shaped lock)
Document box with brass fitting, ca. 1850

rows.name: Joseon silver: hairpins, pendants, knives, small vessels; the Yi Royal Household workshop
rows.hanja: 銀器 · 銀簪 · 銀粧刀 · 李王職美術品製作所
rows.rr: eungi · eunbinyeo · eunjangdo · Iwangjik Misulpum Jejakso
rows.mr: ŭn'gi · ŭnpinyŏ · ŭnjangdo · Iwangjik Misulp'um Chejakso
kilns: Hanyang (Seoul): eight state silversmiths (銀匠) of the Ministry of Works; silver shops (銀房)
Seoul, Gwanggyo stream (today Jongno 1-ga): cluster of silver shops around the colonial period
Seoul, Gwanghwamun crossroads: the Hanseong / Yi Royal Household art workshop, 1908–c. 1937
rows.what_it_is: Personal silver above all: hairpins (binyeo), pendants (norigae), ornamental knives (jangdo), buttons, spoons; fewer vessels (ewers, cups, bowls). Silver was state-controlled and long restricted to the court and upper class. Marks on silver are covered in the silver/ folder.
how_to_recognize: Hairpins named by the head: phoenix, dragon, mandarin duck, plum-and-bamboo, peony, mushroom, etc.; phoenix and dragon pins for royal ceremony and weddings.
Norigae of silver, often in sets of three (samjak), in shapes such as a mortar-leg, knife, arrow-vase, bat, butterfly, gourd, purse, or with pierced characters.
Gilding and enamel (chilbo) are frequent on silver jewelry.
Yi Royal Household workshop products carried the plum-blossom (李花) emblem; its metal section made small silver souvenirs copying Chinese bronze ritual vessels (see silver/ for marks).

copies.text: The Yi Royal Household workshop (from 1922 a Japanese-owned company) reproduced older forms in silver to be sold; NMK records a silver ewer by its successor company 조선미술품제작소.

facts.text: Silver was a precious metal and a currency, so the state managed its use; the eight silversmiths (銀匠) were capital craftsmen of the Ministry of Works.
facts.quote_gloss: eight were kept in the Ministry and the state controlled it

facts.text: Silver goods were limited to special classes until the craftsman system decayed after the late 18th century, when they spread to ordinary people.
facts.quote: 18세기말 이후에는 일반 대중 속으로 서서히 확산
facts.quote_gloss: after the late 18th century gradually spread among the public

facts.text: Sumptuary rules repeatedly targeted silver: a 1498 law forbade commoners silver knives, and in 1670 wearers among commoners were to be prosecuted.
facts.quote_gloss: the 1498 sumptuary law forbade commoners silver knives

facts.text: Hairpins were made of gold, silver, white brass, brass, jade, coral, wood, horn and bone; commoners used wood, horn and bone.
facts.quote_gloss: gold, silver, white-brass and brass hairpins

facts.text: Ordinary families mostly wore silver three-piece norigae, kept wrapped and brought out for family weddings.
facts.quote_gloss: among the people, mainly silver samjak were worn

facts.text: The royal workshop was founded in 1908 as 漢城美術品製作所, renamed 李王職美術品製作所 in 1911, and from 1922 became 株式會社 朝鮮美術品製作所 under Japanese management, producing to be sold; it ran until about 1937.
facts.quote_gloss: from 1922 'Joseon Art Works Co. Ltd.'

facts.text: Its metal section mainly made small silver souvenirs reproducing Chinese bronze ritual-vessel forms, and all products carried the Yi family's plum-blossom emblem.
facts.quote_gloss: engraved with the Yi family's plum-blossom emblem

facts.text: Craftsmen trained at the workshop were later designated intangible-heritage holders (e.g. the first jogakjang, Kim Jeong-seop).
facts.quote_gloss: Kim Jeong-seop also trained here

facts.text: NMK records a colonial-period silver ewer whose maker is given as 조선미술품제작소.

examples.title: Filigree scent container, 19th c., silver
은제 주자 (maker: 조선미술품제작소; colonial period)
용비녀 (silver dragon hairpin)
은제 칠보 밀화 비녀 (銀製七寶蜜花簪)

rows.name: Spoons and chopsticks (sujeo): Goryeo bronze to Joseon silver
kilns: Not recorded
rows.what_it_is: A spoon and a pair of chopsticks forming a set, used together at Korean meals. Goryeo examples are bronze, sometimes silver; later ones brass, white brass and silver. Cleveland calls bronze spoons the commonest Goryeo burial goods, and holds dozens.
how_to_recognize: Early Goryeo: handle strongly curved.
Mid-Goryeo: handle end split into a 'swallow-tail' (fish-tail).
Early Joseon: swallow-tail gone, less curve, leaf-shaped oval bowl; later the handle grows long, thick and straight and the bowl round.
Later silver sets often have auspicious characters or flowers in enamel at the top of the handle and chopsticks.
Double-ended spoons with one small bowl occur in Goryeo.

copies.text: The fish-tail handle is not only Korean: Liao and Jin spoons share it (Cleveland).

facts.text: Using spoon and chopsticks together became a distinctively Korean habit, while China and Japan came to rely on chopsticks.
facts.quote: 숟가락과 젓가락을 병용하는 관습은 우리 나라의 독특한 관습
facts.quote_gloss: using both is a custom peculiar to Korea

facts.text: Materials changed from bronze to brass, white brass and silver.
facts.quote_gloss: changed to brass, white-brass and silver

facts.text: Early Goryeo spoon handles curve strongly; mid-Goryeo ones end in a swallow-tail; in early Joseon the swallow-tail disappears, the curve lessens and the bowl is leaf-shaped.
facts.quote: 중기의 것은 자루 끝이 제비꼬리의 형태
facts.quote_gloss: mid-period handles end in a swallow-tail

facts.text: The fish-tail handle end is also found in the Liao and Jin territories, reflecting Goryeo's contacts with the northern states.
Bronze spoons are the commonest Goryeo burial goods; double-headed spoons have one small bowl thought to be for liquid medicine.
Handle tops were often decorated with auspicious characters or flowers in enamel (chilbo).
facts.quote: 길한 의미의 글자나 꽃을 칠보로 입히는 경우가 많다
facts.quote_gloss: often coated with auspicious characters or flowers in enamel

facts.text: A child received its own spoon at the first birthday; a bride brought the couple's spoons with their bowls at marriage, and these were used for life.
facts.quote_gloss: on the first birthday a personal spoon was prepared

examples.title: Spoon with Fish-Tail Design, silver bronze, Goryeo
Spoon, silver with partial gilding, 12th–13th c.

rows.name: Enamel on silver (chilbo; older name paran), including 20th-century cloisonné
rows.period: Joseon jewelry (paran) and 20th-century enamel and cloisonné
kilns: Dongnae (Busan): enamel-decorated tobacco pipes
Seoul, Nakseonjae (Changdeokgung): enamel workshop run by Lee Bang-ja (Princess Masako) after her return to Korea
rows.what_it_is: Colored glass fused onto metal, mainly silver. In Joseon, small touches of paran in a few strong colors decorated hairpins, pendants, knives, buttons and spoon handles. In the 20th century, studio and commercial enamelling (including cloisonné with wire cells) spread widely in Korea.
how_to_recognize: Traditional paran: a small range of unmixed colors (deep yellow, dark navy, blue-green, purple), thinly applied on thin silver, often over chased or wire-drawn auspicious designs.
20th-century work: wider palettes, thicker enamel, techniques such as cloisonné (wire cells), stencilled, marbled, plique-à-jour and foil enamel.
Enamel often appears with gilding, coral, amber or jade on the same item.

copies.text: Enamel jewelry and souvenirs have been produced in quantity since the 1970s with domestically made enamels; no source gives tests for separating them from older paran.

facts.text: Korean enamel was formerly called paran.
facts.quote_gloss: in Korea it was also called paran

facts.text: Traditional paran was imported from China as stick-shaped lumps, ground and fired; in the Three Kingdoms period it was blue only and melted below about 500 °C.
facts.quote_gloss: lumps like toffee sticks imported from China

facts.text: In Joseon four colors were used — deep yellow, navy, blue-green and purple — never mixed, so the contrasts are strong.
facts.quote: 황색(짙은 노랑), 검정과 남색의 중간색인 감색
facts.quote_gloss: yellow (deep yellow), gam (between black and indigo)

facts.text: Because the base metal was very thin, the enamel was applied thinly and fired quickly.
facts.quote_gloss: thinly applied glaze is a characteristic

facts.text: Silver jewelry was chased or decorated with (sometimes twisted) silver wire in auspicious designs and then covered with transparent enamel.
facts.quote: 은선(銀線, 때로는 꼰 은선)으로 길상문양
facts.quote_gloss: auspicious designs in silver wire, sometimes twisted

facts.text: Enamel was used on hairpins, norigae pendants and spoon handles.
facts.quote: 금속세공품에 금을 올리거나 칠보 를 올린 것
facts.quote_gloss: metalwork with gold or enamel applied

facts.text: A record says the Kyoto metalworker Hirata learned enamelling from a Korean (1596–1615) and became an Edo-period enameller.
facts.quote_gloss: learned enamel technique from a Korean

facts.text: Modern Korean enamel: Kim Ki-ryeon exhibited enamel in 1963 and founded an enamel art society in 1972; domestic enamel production followed; Lee Bang-ja ran an enamel workshop at Nakseonjae; the Korean Enamel Artists Association was founded in 1983.
facts.quote: 낙선재(樂善齋)에서 명휘원(明徽園)의 박애사업 후원
facts.quote_gloss: at Nakseonjae, supporting the Myeonghwiwon charity

facts.text: Wire-partitioned enamel (cloisonné) is named among the modern techniques, as 有線七寶.
facts.quote: 유선칠보(有線七寶)는 소지에 금속선을 세워
facts.quote_gloss: cloisonné sets metal wires on the base

facts.text: NMK catalogues an enamelled silver ewer and cups as colonial period.
