은칠보 단추 (Joseon)
단추 (silver, enamel, plum-blossom design; post-1945)
은제 산호장 도금 칠보 비녀

rows.name: Goryeo mother-of-pearl lacquer (najeon)
rows.hanja: 螺鈿漆器 · 螺鈿玳瑁菊唐草文
rows.period: Goryeo, 12th–14th century; the style lingers to about 1500
kilns: Gaegyeong (Kaesong, North Korea): royal workshop 中尙署 (供造署); temporary office 鈿函造成都監 for sutra boxes
rows.what_it_is: Black lacquer on wood (with cloth and bone-ash ground), inlaid with tiny cut items of shell forming dense chrysanthemum and peony scrolls, with tortoiseshell painted red or yellow from behind and twisted metal wire. Forms: sutra boxes, rosary boxes, cosmetic boxes, a fly-whisk. Extremely rare.
how_to_recognize: Very small, regular shell items in repeating chrysanthemum-scroll and lattice bands on black lacquer; borders of tiny shell dots.
Tortoiseshell items painted on the underside (伏彩) so the color shows through.
Twisted or single metal wire (silver, copper, tin, brass) for stems and border lines.
Sutra boxes: rectangular with bevelled lid edges, metal fittings; iron nails at the joints.

copies.text: No source found on modern copies of Goryeo najeon; early Joseon items continue the Goryeo repertoire (Cleveland).

facts.text: In 1123 the Song envoy Xu Jing wrote that Goryeo lacquer work was not very good but its mother-of-pearl work was fine and precious.
facts.quote: 나전 일은 세밀하여 귀하다고 할 만하다
facts.quote_gloss: the mother-of-pearl work is fine and may be called precious (Xu Jing: 而螺鈿之工 細密可貴)

facts.text: Royal najeon was made in the court workshop (中尙署 / 供造署), and a temporary office (鈿函造成都監) was set up to make inlaid sutra boxes.
facts.quote_gloss: the office for making inlaid boxes

facts.text: Goryeo najeon is black lacquer inlaid with shell, tortoiseshell and silver or copper wire.
facts.quote: 흑칠 위에 나전 · 대모 · 은사 · 동사를 감입하여
facts.quote_gloss: inlaid with shell, tortoiseshell, silver and copper wire on black lacquer

facts.text: Tortoiseshell was shaved thin and painted red or yellow on the back so the color shows through (伏彩 / 伏紅).
facts.quote: 복홍(伏紅) 또는 복채(伏彩)라고도 일컫는다
facts.quote_gloss: also called bokhong or bokchae

facts.text: Metal wire (silver, copper, tin) for scroll stems and borders is a Goryeo hallmark; twisted brass wire, introduced in the 12th century, is believed to have been used in high-quality lacquer until the end of the 15th century.
facts.quote_gloss: mainly silver, copper and tin wire was used

facts.text: The NMK sutra box (Treasure, 2018) has iron nails at its joints and a ground of cloth and bone ash under the shell and lacquer.
facts.quote_gloss: iron nails driven into each joint

facts.text: Early Joseon najeon kept Goryeo designs but more coarsely, with bold single peony or lotus scrolls and looser symmetry; large designs replaced Goryeo's fine mosaic-like patterns.
facts.quote_gloss: peony scrolls with big, bold petals and leaves

examples.title: Trefoil-shaped covered box with decoration of chrysanthemums, ca. 12th c.
나전경함 (螺鈿經函)

examples.holder: 當麻寺 (Taima-dera), on deposit at Nara National Museum
examples.title: 螺鈿玳瑁菊唐草文念珠盒
Hexafoil-Shaped Table with Mother-of-Pearl Inlay, late 1400s–early 1500s
Foliate-Shaped Tray with Mother-of-Pearl Inlay, late 1400s–early 1500s

rows.name: Joseon mother-of-pearl lacquer: boxes, trays, chests; kkeuneumjil and jureumjil
kilns: Hanyang (Seoul): capital najeon craftsmen (2 in the Ministry of Works, 1 in the Royal Wardrobe)
Tongyeong (統營), South Gyeongsang: workshops of the Three-Province Naval Command (統制營) after the Imjin War
rows.what_it_is: Black (sometimes red) lacquer on wood inlaid with abalone shell (jagae), used for stationery and clothing boxes, sewing trays, small tables and, increasingly, furniture. Two cutting techniques: jureumjil (shapes cut and filed from shell) and kkeuneumjil (fine strips cut and broken off to form lines and geometric patterns).
how_to_recognize: 15th–16th c.: large peony or lotus scrolls over the whole surface, looser and coarser than Goryeo; wire use fades.
After the Imjin War (1592–98): pictorial motifs — the ten longevity symbols, pine, bamboo, plum, deer, crane, flowers and birds, grapes, the four gentlemen; boxes give way to furniture.
19th c.: more naturalistic scenes and landscapes; geometric kkeuneumjil (tortoiseshell hexagons etc.) covering whole surfaces.
Shell: iridescent blue-green abalone from the south coast and Jeju.
Jureumjil leaves cut-out pictorial shapes; kkeuneumjil shows thin parallel strips set edge to edge.

copies.text: See najeon_modern for 20th-century production and its tell-tale materials and tools.

facts.text: Joseon najeon craftsmen were capital craftsmen (two in the Ministry of Works, one in the Royal Wardrobe); after the Imjin War tribute najeon was also made at Tongyeong.
facts.quote_gloss: two in the Ministry of Works, one in the Royal Wardrobe

facts.text: The Tongyeong naval command's twelve workshops made tribute crafts, especially najeon, in quantity; this tradition and local abalone explain why so many najeon makers come from Tongyeong.
facts.quote_gloss: in the twelve workshops under the naval command

facts.text: Najeon was made by a division of labour: a joiner (白骨匠) made the wooden core, a lacquerer (漆匠) lacquered it, the najeon craftsman cut and applied the shell; then repeated lacquering, grinding and polishing.
facts.quote: 백골장(白骨匠)과 칠장(漆匠), 나전장의 분업으로
facts.quote_gloss: by the division of labour of joiner, lacquerer and najeon craftsman

facts.text: Korean craftsmen preferred iridescent blue-green abalone from the south coast; early inlay elsewhere used whiter turban shell.
facts.quote_gloss: used abalone shell from the south coast

facts.text: Kkeuneumjil: shell cut into thread-like strips (sangsa) and broken off with a knife point as they are laid, making mainly straight-line geometric patterns; jureumjil: shapes sawn or filed from shell for pictorial motifs.
facts.quote: 끊음질은 얇게 켠 자개껍질을 직선으로 재단하기 때문에
facts.quote_gloss: since kkeuneumjil cuts thin shell in straight lines

facts.text: After the Imjin War, scroll, double-phoenix and double-dragon designs receded and ten-longevity motifs (pine, bamboo, plum, deer, crane) took over; najeon moved into cosmetic boxes, sewing boxes, small tables and wardrobes.
facts.quote: 십장생을 주제로 하는 서정적인 도안이 부각
facts.quote_gloss: lyrical designs on the ten longevity symbols came forward

facts.text: In the 19th century realistic scenes and landscapes increased and kkeuneumjil geometric patterns such as tortoiseshell hexagons were spread over whole items.
facts.quote: 끊음질수법으로 귀갑문(龜甲紋) 같은 기하학적인 무늬
facts.quote_gloss: geometric patterns like tortoiseshell hexagons by kkeuneumjil

facts.text: Cleveland describes a 19th-century sewing tray with a leather core, on which the design was cut into the dry lacquer and shell inserted.

examples.title: Stationery box decorated with peony scrolls, 15th–16th c.
Clothing box decorated with peony scrolls, 17th c.
Box decorated with flowers and clouds, 18th c.
Scroll Box with Dragon and Phoenix Design, 1800s
Tray for Sewing Tools with Mother-of-Pearl Inlay, 1800s

rows.name: Tongyeong and 20th-century mother-of-pearl lacquer
kilns: Tongyeong, South Gyeongsang: industrial training school, many private workshops; Tongyeong Lacquer Co.
Seoul: Yi Royal Household art workshop (najeon section); Jeon Seong-gyu's workshop in Samcheong-dong; 1970s–80s main market
Takaoka, Toyama (Japan): 朝鮮螺鈿社, 1920
Taecheon, North Pyongan (North Korea): lacquer works, 1940
Wonju, Gangwon: lacquer production; Kim Bong-ryong's institute, 1969
Busan, Jwacheon-dong: 'jagae alley' furniture dealers, 1970s
rows.what_it_is: Mother-of-pearl lacquer made under the Yi Royal Household workshop and Japanese-run firms in the colonial period, for American servicemen in the 1950s, and in large volume for Korean homes and export in the 1960s–80s: boxes, trays, chests, wardrobes and souvenirs.
how_to_recognize: Fretsaw-cut shell (from the 1920s): smooth, slick, even outlines instead of the rougher knife- and file-cut edges of older work.
Pictures drawn from design drawings (도안), sometimes after named painters; Japanese-taste motifs in the 1920s–40s, sometimes combined with maki-e.
Imported shell from the late 1960s: larger, more colorful items (green snail, pearl oyster, 'Mexican' abalone, winged pearl shell); dyed cultured-pearl shell from Japan.
Identical motifs repeated from die-cut machine production.
Cashew resin instead of true lacquer (ot-chil) after 1945.
1960s–70s motifs of 'cultural treasures' (Buddha images, celadon, pagodas), engraved and etched shell; very large wardrobes of the 1970s–80s.

copies.text: This entry is itself the later production against which older najeon is judged; earlier styles (Goryeo chrysanthemum scrolls, Joseon peony scrolls, ten longevity symbols) were reproduced throughout.

facts.text: Under the Japanese colonial government the Yi Royal Household workshop had a najeon section that gathered old craftsmen and trained young ones, working to designs drawn by Japanese; in 1922 it became the Joseon Art Works company.
facts.quote: 그들이 그려 주는 도안에 따라 나전칠기를 제작하였다
facts.quote_gloss: made najeon according to designs they drew

facts.text: Tongyeong had an industrial training school teaching najeon and countless small private workshops; a lacquer works also opened at Taecheon, North Pyongan, in 1940.
facts.quote: 통영에 공업전수소(工業傳修所)가 일찍부터 개설되어
facts.quote_gloss: an industrial training school opened early in Tongyeong

facts.text: In 1920 Jeon Seong-gyu, regarded as the last Joseon najeon master, was invited to the 朝鮮螺鈿社 at Takaoka, Japan; on his return the fretsaw was adopted, giving smooth, practised lines, and design drawings (도안) came into use.
facts.quote: 실톱이 유입되면서 매끈하고 능숙한 선을 표현
facts.quote_gloss: with the fretsaw, smooth and skilled lines could be made

facts.text: Kim Bong-ryong learned the watchmaker's hand fretsaw in Japan in 1920 and used it to cut shell, transforming jureumjil.
facts.quote_gloss: learned to use the metalworking hand saw

facts.text: From the 1920s to the 1940s production and sales were controlled by the Japanese government and many designs followed Japanese taste; customers were mainly Japanese.
facts.quote: 일본의 취향을 따른 문양 도안이 많다
facts.quote_gloss: many pattern designs followed Japanese taste

facts.text: A set of red-lacquer najeon furniture said to have belonged to Empress Sunjeonghyo is attributed to Kim Jin-gap in the 1930s; it combines many kinds of shell with maki-e in silver powder, uses white-brass fittings, and reproduces paintings by named artists.
facts.quote: 마키에[蒔絵] 기법도 볼 수 있다
facts.quote_gloss: the maki-e technique can also be seen

facts.text: In the 1950s American servicemen became new customers, and small accessories with 'Korean' motifs were popular.
facts.quote_gloss: American forces appeared as a new class of customers

facts.text: From the late 1960s imported shell — larger and more colorful than Korean — came into use; motifs of cultural treasures appeared, with new engraving and etching techniques.
facts.quote_gloss: as foreign shell was imported and use increased

facts.text: Shell used today is mostly imported (green snail, pearl oyster, winged pearl, trochus); Korean abalone is more colorful but small. Dyed by-product shell from Japanese cultured pearls has been used since the 1960s, and die-cut motifs are machine-repeated.
facts.quote: 금형으로 그 무늬를 만들어 기계에 설치한 뒤 반복 작업
facts.quote_gloss: patterns made in dies, set in machines and repeated

facts.text: After 1945 a substitute lacquer, cashew, came in; craftsmen of lacquer and najeon merged roles as demand fell.
facts.quote_gloss: the appearance of a substitute lacquer called cashew

facts.text: Demand rose from the 1960s and peaked in the 1970s–80s, with factory-style division of labour, professional designers and large wardrobes; some makers exported incense boxes and tea caddies to Japan. Built-in and Western furniture ended the boom from the 1980s.
facts.quote_gloss: the 1970s–80s, the boom years of modern Korean najeon

facts.text: Najeonjang was designated national intangible heritage in 1966 (Kim Bong-ryong); kkeuneumjil was designated separately in 1975 and 1979, and merged back into najeonjang in 1995.
facts.quote_gloss: in 1995 the kkeuneumjil and jureumjil skills were combined

examples.title: Small chest of drawers decorated with flowers, birds, and insects, early 20th c.
Chest decorated with phoenixes, colored roundels (taegeuk), and flowers, early 20th c.
Chest decorated with phoenixes, colored roundels (taegeuk), and flowers, early 20th c.
자개박이 백동장식궤 (post-1945, North Korean)

rows.name: Hwagak: painted ox horn
rows.hanja: 華角 (also 畵角 · 花角 · 火角 · 畫刻)
kilns: Yanghwajin / Yanghwado (today Mangwon-dong, Mapo-gu, Seoul): about 60 hwagak workshops in the 1910s
Jeonju, North Jeolla: 'Jeonju hwagak ware' named in 『閨閤叢書』
Incheon: present-day designated master
rows.what_it_is: Ox horn softened, split and flattened into translucent sheets 0.3–0.4 mm thick, painted on the back in strong mineral colors and glued face-down onto a wooden core, the joints covered with strips of bone. Used for women's things: boxes, combs, rulers, spools, mirror stands, pillow ends, small chests.
how_to_recognize: Small square panels (about 10–13 cm, older up to 18 cm) set in a grid, each with its own picture, divided by white bone strips.
Bright red-dominated colors with white or black outlines, seen through the glossy horn (painted on the reverse).
Folk-painting style: ten longevity symbols, flowers and birds, tigers, dragons, auspicious characters.
Fragile: the water-based pigments lift or rub off where damp has reached them; areas not covered with horn are lacquered; metal fittings of brass or white brass.

copies.text: The craft continues under a national intangible-heritage designation (1996); no source discusses copies or imitation materials.

facts.text: Hwagak is made by flattening translucent ox horn as thin as paper, painting designs on its back in dancheong pigments and attaching it to a wooden core; areas not covered are lacquered.
facts.quote: 투명도가 높은 쇠뿔을 종잇장처럼 얇게 펴
facts.quote_gloss: spreading highly translucent ox horn thin as paper

facts.text: Horn from bulls of middle age is used: young horn has white spots and old horn a dark core; the finished sheet is about 0.3–0.4 mm thick.
facts.quote_gloss: the horn sheet is then about 0.3–0.4 mm

facts.text: Panels are about 10–13 cm square; red predominates, outlined in white or black; bone strips are set in grooves between the panels.
facts.quote_gloss: each piece is 10–13 cm square, repeated

facts.text: Because materials were scarce and the process demanding, hwagak was a luxury for the upper class, chiefly women's articles.
facts.quote_gloss: used as favourite possessions of a special elite

facts.text: The water-based pigments, bound with animal glue, are weak against damp and can rub off.
facts.quote_gloss: very weak against moisture

facts.text: Hwagak craftsmen are not listed among Joseon state craftsmen; the only early record is 'Jeonju hwagak ware' in 『閨閤叢書』 by Lady Bingheogak Yi (1759–1824).
facts.quote_gloss: 'Jeonju hwagak ware' is the only known example

facts.text: In the 1910s Yanghwado (Mangwon-dong, Seoul) had about 60 hwagak workshops; Yanghwajin was the main production area up to the loss of sovereignty.
facts.quote_gloss: in the 1910s Yanghwado had some 60 workshops

facts.text: Painted tortoiseshell (伏彩) on Goryeo najeon is the precursor; items decorated with hwagak alone developed from the mid-Joseon period.
facts.quote: 조선 중기 이후부터는 화각으로만 장식한 화각공예품이 발달
facts.quote_gloss: from mid-Joseon, works decorated only with hwagak developed

examples.title: Box decorated with auspicious symbols, 19th c., lacquered wood inlaid with flattened and painted ox horn
화각함 (華角函)
화각 필통 (華角十長生文筆筒)
Ruler, late 19th–early 20th c., wood, bone, painted ox horn (not open access)

rows.name: Red and black lacquer (chilgi): juchil and heukchil
rows.hanja: 漆器 · 朱漆 · 黑漆 · 紙繩漆器
rows.period: from the 1st century BCE; for owners chiefly Joseon and later
kilns: Wonju, Gangwon: known for fine lacquer (ot-chil)
Joseon lacquer tribute from producing areas nationwide; lacquerers in capital and provincial offices
rows.what_it_is: Items coated in Korean lacquer (ot, the sap of Toxicodendron vernicifluum): plain raw, black or red lacquer, without shell. Cores include wood, bamboo, hemp cloth (dry lacquer), twisted paper cord (jiseung), paper, ceramic, metal and leather. Typical heirlooms: small tables (soban), document and stationery boxes, trays, bowls.
how_to_recognize: Korean lacquer is plain compared with Chinese or Japanese: raw (brownish), black, red, plus shell inlay — little carved, painted or gold lacquer.
Red lacquer pigmented with iron oxides (seokganju) on some 20th-century furniture.
Twisted-paper (jiseung) trays and boxes show a woven-cord texture under the lacquer.
Since 1945 cashew resin has often replaced true lacquer.

copies.text: Cashew substitute lacquer and imported refined lacquer after 1945 (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 칠장).

facts.text: The earliest substantial lacquer in Korea comes from the 1st century BCE (the Daho-ri tombs, Changwon); traces go back to the 3rd century BCE.
facts.quote: 본격적인 유물이 출토된 것은 기원전 1세기 경부터
facts.quote_gloss: substantial finds date from about the 1st century BCE

facts.text: Silla had a central office, the 漆典, for lacquer.
facts.quote_gloss: there was a separate Chiljeon

facts.text: Korean lacquer is simpler than Chinese or Japanese, using mostly raw, black and red lacquer and shell; its strengths are good lacquer and skilled shell work.
facts.quote: 생칠 · 흑칠 · 주칠(朱漆)과 자개를 활용하는 것이 고작이었다
facts.quote_gloss: using raw, black and red lacquer and shell was about all

facts.text: In Joseon lacquer became more widely used; the state collected lacquer tribute from producing areas and lacquerers worked for capital and provincial offices.
facts.quote_gloss: received the lacquer produced as tribute

facts.text: Lacquerware is named by its core: wood, bamboo, hemp (dry lacquer), twisted paper (jiseung), paper, ceramic, metal and leather.
facts.quote: 종이를 꼬아 기물을 만든 뒤 그 위에 옻칠을 도장해서
facts.quote_gloss: twisting paper into a vessel and lacquering it

facts.text: Paper was widely used from the 1800s for stationery and storage boxes; Cleveland's footed tray is lacquer over twisted and coiled paper.
In the modern period demand collapsed, cashew substitutes appeared and refined lacquer even had to be imported for a time.
facts.quote_gloss: came to the point of importing refined lacquer for a time

facts.text: The red-black lacquer of a 1930s najeon furniture set used seokganju (red iron-oxide earth) and iron oxide.
facts.quote_gloss: the red-black lacquer used seokganju and iron oxide

examples.title: Red lacquer box for an inkstone, 19th c.
주칠문서함 (朱漆四角函)
나전주칠학문호족반 (螺鈿朱漆鶴文虎足盤)
Footed Tray, 1900s, lacquer over twisted and coiled paper

rows.name: 20th-century export and tourist lacquer and brass: how to recognize
rows.hanja: 觀光民藝品 · 輸出工藝品
kilns: Tongyeong and Seoul (najeon)
Busan, Jwacheon-dong (najeon furniture trade)
state-promoted rural 'Saemaeul' factories (1970s tourist crafts)
rows.what_it_is: Crafts made for American servicemen after the Korean War and, from the 1960s, for export and tourists under state policy: mother-of-pearl boxes, jewelry boxes, trays and furniture; enamel jewelry; brass. These were made for foreign buyers: servicemen, tourists and importers.
how_to_recognize: Najeon: fretsaw-smooth shell outlines; large, very colorful imported shell (green snail, pearl oyster, 'Mexican' abalone) or dyed shell; repeated die-cut motifs; motifs of Korean 'cultural treasures' (Buddha images, celadon, pagodas); engraved and etched shell; cashew instead of true lacquer.
Designs chosen to look 'traditional' and 'Korean' for foreign buyers.
Brass: no source found describing export or tourist brass; cheap cast zinc brass imitating bangjja is documented for the domestic market (see yugi_brass).

copies.text: This type is the main body of later material that resembles older items.

facts.text: In the 1950s American servicemen became a new market for najeon, buying small accessories decorated with 'Korean' motifs.
facts.quote_gloss: American forces appeared as a new class of customers

facts.text: In the 1960s–70s government policy (Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Ministry of Transportation) restructured crafts for export to earn foreign currency; by the 1970s 'crafts' had largely come to mean tourist folk crafts, deliberately showing traditional, folk and local elements to foreigners.
facts.quote_gloss: the sense of 'tourist folk crafts' was greatly strengthened

facts.text: Imported shell, larger and more colorful than Korean, came into use from the late 1960s, with new engraving and etching techniques and motifs of cultural treasures.
facts.quote: 조각법, 부식법 등의 새로운 기법도 등장
facts.quote_gloss: new techniques such as engraving and etching appeared

facts.text: Die-cut machine production repeats identical shell motifs; dyed cultured-pearl shell from Japan was used from the 1960s.
facts.quote: 양식진주패(mop shell)를 염색 가공하여 사용하는 예도
facts.quote_gloss: dyed cultured pearl-oyster shell is also used

facts.text: After 1945 the cashew substitute lacquer contributed to najeon's decline in quality.
facts.quote_gloss: the appearance of a substitute lacquer called cashew

facts.text: Some 1970s–80s najeon makers exported incense boxes and tea caddies to Japan.
facts.quote_gloss: exported incense boxes, tea caddies and the like to Japan

facts.text: In the 20th century cheap cast zinc brass, looking like bangjja, displaced it.
facts.quote: 아연합금의 주물이 언뜻 보기에 황색과 비슷하고 값도 싸
facts.quote_gloss: zinc-alloy castings look similar in yellow and are cheap

rows.name: Minhwa (Korean folk painting) — the genre as a whole
rows.period: Late Joseon to the mid-20th century (main period late 18th c.–early/mid 20th c.)
rows.date_note: Yoo Jeong-seo (2025): popular from the late 18th century to the early-to-mid 20th century; the traditional lineage broke between Liberation (1945) and the Korean War (1950–53). Earlier roots are claimed (Kim Cheol-sun) but almost all surviving items are 19th–20th century.
rows.what_it_is: Anonymous, practical paintings made to decorate houses and to bring luck or keep evil away: New Year door pictures, screens for weddings and birthdays, pictures for walls, cupboards and shrines. The same subjects were repeated for generations (tiger and magpie, books and scholar's things, character paintings, flowers and birds, longevity symbols). Painters ranged from court-trained men and their pupils to provincial and itinerant painters and amateurs. The word 'minhwa' is modern: it was coined by the Japanese critic Yanagi Muneyoshi.
how_to_recognize: Support: mostly paper (single sheets pasted to walls/doors, or mounted as hanging scrolls and folding screens); finer commissioned and court-style items are on silk.

Pigments: bright opaque colors; from the mid/late 19th century imported synthetic emerald green and synthetic ultramarine appear alongside traditional mineral and plant colors (see modern_production).
Mounting: folding screens (8 panels most common), hanging scrolls, or unmounted sheets; New Year door pictures (sehwa/munbae) were replaced yearly, so old ones are rare.

Iconography: repeated auspicious subjects (tiger/magpie, chaekgeori, munjado, birds and flowers, ten longevity symbols, peonies, fish, landscapes such as Geumgangsan), flattened space, strong color, humour.
Script: usually no signature or seal (anonymity is a defining trait); hanja appear as subject matter (character paintings) rather than as signatures.

copies.text: Printed bird-and-flower screens were mass-produced from the 1920s and used until the 1980s at weddings and 60th-birthday parties; folk painters copied their (partly Japanese-style) motifs.
1970s 'export minhwa workshops' (수출용 민화 공방) boomed, and from the 1990s amateurs learned minhwa by copying old pictures from templates, producing reproductions.

facts.text: The term minhwa was first used by the Japanese Yanagi Muneyoshi (柳宗悅), who defined it as painting born among, painted for and bought by the common people.
facts.quote: 민화라는 용어를 처음 사용한 사람은 일본인 야나기
facts.quote_gloss: the first person to use the term minhwa was the Japanese Yanagi

facts.text: Makers ranged from Dohwaseo court painters and their pupils to provincial painters, painter-monks, itinerant painters and amateurs, mostly of low status; court styles reached private workshops through model drawings (hwabon/choebon).
facts.quote: 민화의 작가는 도화서 화원과 화원의 제자에서부터
facts.quote_gloss: the painters of minhwa range from Dohwaseo court painters and their pupils …

facts.text: Minhwa flourished among commoners from the late 18th to the early-mid 20th century; the tradition broke off between 1945 and the Korean War, and the present-day 'contemporary minhwa' scene was built from the 1960s–70s by people unconnected with the old painters.
facts.quote_gloss: broken off in the period from Liberation to the Korean War

facts.text: New Year pictures (sehwa, also munbae 'door pictures') were made by the Dohwaseo for the court and handed out by rank; commoners bought theirs at paper shops; because they were replaced every year, old examples are rare.
facts.quote: 해마다 새로운 것으로 갈아 붙였기 때문에 오래된 유물이 드물다
facts.quote_gloss: because they were renewed every year, old examples are rare

facts.text: A fierce tiger image was traditionally pasted on entrance doors on New Year's Eve to ward off evil; in folk custom chickens, dogs, lions and tigers were the protective door animals.
Painted decorative pictures (flowers and birds above all) were the most numerous kind of minhwa, made for screens, walls, wall-cupboards and lofts.
facts.quote_gloss: flower-and-bird paintings are the majority

examples.title: 호피장막도 (tiger-skin curtain painting), 1800s, color on paper, 128×355 cm

rows.name: Chaekgeori / chaekgado / munbangdo — paintings of books and scholar's things
rows.hanja: 冊架圖 · 文房圖 (책거리 written 冊巨里 in the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture)
rows.period: Late 18th century (court) to the 20th century (folk and later)
rows.date_note: Met: an established genre by the 1780s; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: begun under King Jeongjo (r. 1776–1800); court and folk versions continue into the early 20th century and the genre is still painted today.
rows.what_it_is: Still-life screens of books with scholar's and luxury items: brushes, inkstones, archaic bronzes, ceramics, flowers, fruit, clocks and spectacles. The court 'bookshelf' type shows a whole cabinet painted with Western-style perspective and shading; folk versions drop the shelf and pile the books and items on each panel.
how_to_recognize: Support: court bookshelf screens are usually on silk (Cleveland 2011.37, NPMK 창덕6499, Met 2005.385); many folk screens are on paper (Met 2024.89.6, Cleveland 2017.6).
Pigments/technique: court bookshelf type uses linear perspective and shading for recessed shelves; folk versions are flatter, crowded, sometimes in 'reversed perspective' (far items drawn larger).
Mounting: 6-, 8- or 10-panel folding screens; in the bookshelf type the shelf runs continuously across all panels; in stacked/isolated types each panel is a separate composition.

Iconography: books in wrappers, Qing archaistic bronzes, blue-and-white vessels, peacock feathers, coral, clocks and watches (Western goods), fruits full of seeds (watermelon, pomegranate) for many sons, eggplant for long life.

Script: the characters 壽 (su, long life) and 福 (bok, fortune) often appear on painted vessels; some court screens carry a hidden artist's seal on a painted item (e.g. Yi Taek-gyun, Cleveland 2011.37); folk screens are unsigned.

copies.text: Bookshelf-type screens of the late 19th and early 20th centuries are fewer and become increasingly graphic and abstract, while stacked and isolated types multiply; the Met dates its stacked screen (2005.385) to the early 20th century as a 'continuation and transformation' of the genre.

facts.text: Chaekgado probably began in the late 18th century with court painters working to King Jeongjo's plan to govern through books; the word chaekga first appears as a painting topic in the Jeongjo-era examinations for court painters on special duty (차비대령화원).
facts.quote: 정조(正祖)의 구상에 의해 화원이 제작한 것이 시초
facts.quote_gloss: began as works by court painters following King Jeongjo's plan

facts.text: The genre was established by the 1780s and originated at court; the bookshelf form reflects Qing 'many treasures' display cabinets (duobaoge/다보격).
In the 19th century, chaekgeori without shelves became more common than shelf types as the subject spread to folk painting, because folk screens were small and crowded many items into flat space.
facts.quote_gloss: chaekgeori without shelves became more prevalent

facts.text: Court painter Yi Hyeong-nok (b. 1808) changed his name to Yi Eung-nok (1864) and Yi Taek-gyun (1871); works under the name Yi Taek-gyun have a blue background; a Cleveland screen carries a hidden seal of Yi Taek-gyun on its third panel.
facts.quote_gloss: the background treated in blue

facts.text: Terminology differs: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture treats chaekgeori (책거리) as the wider term that includes paintings without shelves, with chaekgado as the shelf type; the Met essay uses munbangdo (文房圖) for the whole genre and restricts chaekgeori/chaekgado to the bookshelf type.
facts.quote_gloss: chaekgeori is the broader concept than chaekgado

facts.text: Folk chaekgeori often use reversed perspective (distant items larger) and pile auspicious motifs, suggesting use as household talismans as well as studio decoration.
Representative folk chaekgeori are held in the Japan Folk Crafts Museum, the Koryo Museum (Kyoto), Sunmoon University Museum and the National Folk Museum of Korea.

rows.name: Munjado — character paintings (eight Confucian virtues and blessing characters)
rows.hanja: 文字圖 · 孝悌文字圖
rows.date_note: No source gave firm dates; surviving examples cited are 19th–early 20th century (Cleveland 2017.6: early 1900s).
rows.what_it_is: Paintings in which each panel shows one large Chinese character whose strokes are filled or replaced with pictures of the stories and emblems linked to that virtue. The standard set is the eight Confucian virtues 孝悌忠信禮義廉恥 (filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, trust, propriety, righteousness, integrity, sense of shame); other sets spell blessings such as 壽福康寧 or 百壽百福.
how_to_recognize: Support: usually paper; one character per panel, typically eight panels read right to left.
Pigments: bright colors; some regional types use pale ink washes inside the strokes.
Mounting: folding screens or single hanging panels; combined munja-chaekgeori screens put a still life below each character (early 1900s, Cleveland 2017.6).
Iconography: emblem-filled strokes, e.g. for 孝 the carp and bamboo shoots of the filial sons Wang Xiang and Meng Zong, a fan, oranges, a zither.

Script: the characters themselves, as written on the item; sources write the sixth either 禮義 or 禮儀 — record what is painted. Regional variants: Gangwon (two tiers with landscapes), Andong (on the back of literati paintings), Jeju (three tiers, stroke ends shaped as bird beaks).

facts.text: The usual munjado is the 'hyoje munjado' of eight Confucian virtues 孝悌忠信 禮儀廉恥, each character linked to stories and emblems; other sets include 壽福康寧 富貴多男 and blessing types such as 百壽百福 萬壽無疆, 囍 and 龍虎.
facts.quote: 효제충신 예의염치(孝悌忠信 禮儀廉恥)
facts.quote_gloss: the eight virtues hyo-je-chung-sin ye-ui-yeom-chi

facts.text: Cleveland's munja-chaekgeori screen (early 1900s) reads right to left; the eight characters mean filial piety, brotherly love, loyalty, trust, propriety, righteousness, modesty/integrity and humility/sense of shame; the Met notes munbangdo imagery was increasingly paired with munjado.
facts.quote: Read from far right to left

facts.text: Regional styles: Gangwon munjado have a two-tier format with landscapes (Geumgangsan, Gwandong Palgyeong); Andong examples are painted on the back of literati-style paintings; Jeju munjado have three tiers, drop the narrative emblems, fill strokes with flowers, clouds or waves and end the strokes in bird beaks.
facts.quote: 자획의 끝 부분은 새의 부리로 표현하였다
facts.quote_gloss: the ends of the strokes are shaped as birds' beaks

facts.text: Character paintings for blessings (수복문자도, 백수전도) were also embroidered as screens.
facts.quote_gloss: 'character picture of longevity and fortune'

rows.name: Hojakdo / kkachi horangi — tiger and magpie
rows.period: Late 16th century (Ming-derived prototypes) to 20th century; folk versions mainly 19th century
rows.date_note: The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: the subject came from Ming China around the Imjin War (1592); Hong Seon-pyo (2006) treats a work dated 1592 as the source of the Korean type. Folk versions flourish in the 19th century.
rows.what_it_is: A tiger under a pine with a magpie on a branch. The tiger drives off bad luck and the magpie brings good news; in 19th-century folk versions the tiger is comic and the magpie bold, which some read as a satire on officials. Often paired with a dragon painting, from the New Year custom of pasting a tiger and a dragon on the two leaves of the gate.
how_to_recognize: Support: paper, as hanging scrolls or single sheets; some on silk.
Pigments: strong colors, patterned stripes or leopard-like spots (tiger and leopard skins are often mixed).
Mounting: hanging scroll or sheet; often a pair with a cloud-dragon picture (용호문배도).
Iconography: pine, magpie, tiger with comic face; Ming-style versions are soft and detailed, 17th-c. versions flatter, 19th-c. folk versions cartoon-like.
Script: usually none.

copies.text: 20th-century tigers in temple mountain-god paintings changed under the influence of Japanese tiger painting into roaring, teeth-baring beasts (as opposed to the cat-like folk tiger).

facts.text: Tiger paintings with magpies derive from Yuan and Ming tiger paintings (子母虎圖, 乳虎圖) and reached Korea from Ming China around the Imjin War.
facts.quote_gloss: came to Korea from Ming around the Imjin War

facts.text: In 19th-century folk versions the tiger is drawn foolish and the magpie confident, read as a fable of commoners mocking the powerful.
facts.quote_gloss: the tiger is shown flustered before the magpie

facts.text: At New Year a dragon-and-tiger door picture (용호문배도) was pasted on the gate: the tiger to chase away the three calamities, the dragon to bring the five blessings; tiger images on doors warded off evil.
facts.quote_gloss: they pasted the 'dragon-and-tiger door picture' on the gate

facts.text: Well-known folk examples are in Japanese collections (Kurashiki Mingeikan, Nihon Mingeikan, Koryo Museum Kyoto) and the Leeum.

examples.holder: Hoam Museum (photo: Academy of Korean Studies, KOGL 1)
examples.title: 까치호랑이 (magpie and tiger)

rows.name: Hwajodo — flower-and-bird painting (incl. peony screens)
rows.date_note: Met 1993.255 label: screens of this subject became prevalent in the late Joseon period and stayed popular into the 20th century; surviving court peony screens are mostly 19th century or later (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 모란도).
rows.what_it_is: Screens and panels of flowering plants with pairs of birds (mandarin ducks, pheasants, cranes, magpies), insects and fish, standing for married harmony, many children, wealth and rank. Peony screens were also court ceremonial screens and were widely copied for private use.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk for court and fine private screens (Met 1993.255), paper for most folk screens.
Pigments: bright colors; peonies drawn as frontal full blooms, side blooms, opening flowers and buds in deep/pale red, deep/pale blue, yellow and white (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 모란도).
Mounting: 8- or 10-panel folding screens; double-sided screens (both faces painted) appear in the late 19th–early 20th c. (Cleveland 2022.59).

Iconography: male-female bird pairs (suitable for weddings), peony = wealth and honour, pomegranate = many sons; 20th-c. printed screens add pine-and-crane, tiger-and-bamboo, peony-and-peacock, eagles, flocks of chickens.
Script: usually none; court peony screens are unsigned.

copies.text: Printed bird-and-flower screens, mass-produced from the 1920s to the 1980s and used at weddings and 60th birthdays, show Japanese influence in composition and style.

facts.text: Flower-and-bird pictures were the most numerous type of minhwa; pairs of birds expressed the wish that husband and wife stay together and that the family multiply.
facts.quote: 다른 어떠한 종류보다도 그 수효가 많았다
facts.quote_gloss: were more numerous than any other kind

facts.text: In Korea flower-and-bird folding screens became prevalent in the late Joseon period and remained popular in the 20th century; male-female pairs such as mandarin ducks made them suitable for weddings or the bridal room.

Peony screens were used in court rites from at least 1627 (Sohyeon Seja garye dogam uigwe); surviving court peony screens are mostly 19th century or later, and private workshops produced many imitations of the court type with a vertical peony on each panel.
facts.quote: 민간에서도 궁중의 모란도 병풍을 모방한 작품이 다량 제작되었다
facts.quote_gloss: privately, many imitations of court peony screens were produced

facts.text: By the late 19th century peony paintings with bold, graphic stylisation were increasingly produced for and bought by the middle class, e.g. for weddings.

Peonies, early 1900s, eight-panel screen (painted on both sides), ink and color on silk

rows.name: Sipjangsaengdo — the ten symbols of longevity
rows.period: Recorded from late Goryeo; surviving screens mostly late Joseon (19th–early 20th c.)
rows.date_note: Earliest record: Yi Saek (1328–1396), 「歲畫十長生」; surviving paintings mostly from the later Joseon period; the University of Oregon screen is firmly dated 1880 by its list of officials (Park Bon-su 2008).
rows.what_it_is: A paradise landscape gathering the symbols of long life — sun, clouds, mountains, water, rocks, pine, crane, deer, turtle and the fungus of immortality (lingzhi), often with bamboo and peaches — painted as large blue-and-green screens for royal birthday and wedding banquets and as New Year gifts, and copied in simpler folk versions.
how_to_recognize: Support: court screens on silk; folk versions on paper or silk.
Pigments: blue-and-green landscape colors (malachite and azurite greens/blues in court work; synthetic colors in later items).
Mounting: mostly 8- or 10-panel folding screens; also window/door panels (창호) at court; 1880 Oregon screen has a list of officials (좌목) attached.

Iconography: typically starts at right, deer and cranes center, sea and turtles at left; late 19th-century screens: masses of multicolored clouds, red-dotted peaches, upturned leaves, big moss dots on pine trunks (Park Jeong-hye).
Script: usually none; commemorative court screens (계병) may carry a list of names.

facts.text: The usual ten are sun, clouds, mountains, water, rocks, crane, deer, turtle, pine and the fungus of immortality, but bamboo and peaches are so often added that most paintings show more than ten.
facts.quote: 대나무와 천도(天桃)가 많이 다루어져 열 가지가 넘는 것이 대부분
facts.quote_gloss: bamboo and peaches are often included, so most have more than ten

facts.text: Making the longevity symbols into a fixed set of ten as an independent picture subject is considered a Korean invention, not found in China or Japan.
facts.quote: 중국이나 일본에 없는 한국 고유의 착안
facts.quote_gloss: a uniquely Korean idea not found in China or Japan

facts.text: Yi Saek's (1328–1396) poem on a New Year 'ten longevity' painting is the earliest record of the subject in Korea.

At court the screens stood behind the queen's or crown prince's seat at events praying for health and were used at royal weddings and 60th-birthday banquets; they were also given as New Year paintings and used privately for 60th birthdays.
facts.quote_gloss: set up behind the seat of the queen or crown prince

facts.text: Screens decorated with many multicolored clouds became fashionable in the late 19th century; formalised details (red dots on peaches, upturned leaves, large moss dots on pine trunks) indicate a late-19th-century date.
facts.quote_gloss: was in fashion around the late 19th century

facts.text: Court-made ten-longevity screens survive in numbers and are distinguished by good materials and skilled execution; freer, more decorative versions are later or folk work.
facts.quote_gloss: the materials are good and the workmanship excellent

facts.text: A ten-longevity screen sold in 1924 by a Seoul trader to the University of Oregon museum was made in 1880 to commemorate the crown prince's recovery from smallpox — one of very few court decorative screens with a known date.

rows.name: Irworobongdo / obongbyeong — sun, moon and five peaks screen
rows.hanja: 日月五峯圖 · 五峯屛 (variants 日月五峰圖, 五峰山屛)
rows.period: Joseon court, 17th century to 1910 (surviving screens mostly 19th–early 20th c.)
rows.date_note: No example earlier than late Joseon is known (the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture); dated items include a 1857 six-panel screen and an 1883 screen from the Bukgwanwangmyo; NPMK screens are catalogued 19th–early 20th c.
rows.what_it_is: The royal screen placed behind the king's throne: five stylised peaks, a red sun and white moon, waterfalls, red-trunked pines and patterned waves. It marked the king's presence and was also set up in mortuary halls, spirit halls and portrait shrines. It is court art, not folk painting.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk (NPMK 창덕6420, 6421) or paper (the Gyeongbokgung Geunjeongjeon screen, per the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture media caption); very large (NPMK 6420: 222 × 485.6 cm).
Pigments: vivid dancheong-type blue, red, green, white and black (NPMK); one analyzed screen used synthetic ultramarine, emerald green and lead white or titanium oxide (Han & Hong 2005).

Mounting: 4-, 6- or 8-panel folding screens, single insert screens in stands (삽병), sets of four window panels (창호); ceremonial screens bordered in green silk with gilt floral ornament (Park Yoon-hee 2022).

Iconography: central large peak flanked by two pairs; sun to the right and moon to the left (reversed on seven works of 1760–66); waterfalls from the side peaks; four red-trunk pines; scale-pattern waves with white foam.
Script: none on the painting.

copies.text: Many surviving court screens were repaired from the 1960s with non-traditional mounting methods and lost some original features.

facts.text: The screen was set behind the royal seat wherever the king appeared, indoors or out, and also in places holding the spirit tablets or royal portraits.
facts.quote: 왕이 임어하는 곳에는 실내외를 막론하고 어좌(御座) 뒤에
facts.quote_gloss: wherever the king was present, indoors or out, behind the throne

facts.text: Court records call it obongbyeong or obongsanbyeong ('five peaks screen'), without 'sun and moon', which suggests the mountains were the key element.
facts.quote_gloss: should be called obongbyeong

facts.text: Formats include 4/6/8-panel screens, single insert screens in stands, and four-leaf window panels.

Earlier, a metal sun-and-moon mirror (日月鏡) hung in the set; from Yeongjo's reign the sun and moon were painted in gold and silver, and from about the mid-19th century in red and white as on surviving screens.
facts.quote: painted with red and white colors

facts.text: In court event paintings of 1706–1902 the screen is often shown with only some elements; waterfalls appear from 1829, and the sun and moon are on the reversed sides in seven works of 1760–66.
Ceremonial five-peak screens were mounted with green silk borders and gilt floral ornament, graded by the status of each screen.
Pigment analysis of one 'Ilwol oakdo' found synthetic ultramarine, emerald green and lead white or titanium oxide, i.e. modern synthetic pigments.

examples.title: 일월오봉도병풍, 19th–early 20th c., eight-panel screen, color on silk
일월오봉도삽병 (insert screen in stand), 19th–early 20th c., color on silk
경기전 일월오봉도 (made with the 1872 portrait of King Taejo)

rows.name: Baeksu baekbokdo — 'hundred longevity, hundred fortune' character screens
rows.date_note: The Portland Art Museum screen is estimated 19th century (NMK conservation report); NPMK catalogues its screen only as 'Joseon'.
rows.what_it_is: Screens covered in rows of the characters 壽 (long life) and 福 (fortune), each written in a different archaic or decorative script (seal, bronze, bird, tadpole scripts…). A blessing-type character painting; many surviving examples are embroidered.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk; embroidered (NPMK 창덕6630; Portland) or painted.
Pigments/threads: colored silk threads, characters often in varied colors.
Mounting: 10-panel screens recorded; original mounting had teal/blue upper and lower borders and violet strips on each panel (Portland).
Iconography: grid of characters; NPMK: odd panels 壽, even panels 福, 36 per panel; Portland: 17 壽 and 16 福 per panel (33).
Script: archaic seal-script variants (籒文, 金文, 鍾鼎文, 小篆, 甲骨, 鳥篆, 蝌蚪篆 etc. per NPMK) — the characters are 壽 and 福 throughout, not names or marks.

copies.text: Chinese prints of the same motif exist (Met 2025.366, 'One Hundred Longevity Characters', woodblock, Suzhou), so the motif alone does not prove Korean origin.

facts.text: The NPMK embroidered screen has 36 characters per panel, 壽 on odd and 福 on even panels, in many seal-type scripts, with even spacing and tall rectangular characters.
facts.quote_gloss: 36 characters each: 壽 on odd panels, 福 on even panels

facts.text: The Portland Art Museum's ten-panel embroidered screen has 33 characters per panel (17 壽, 16 福) in different scripts and colors, and is estimated to be 19th century; it had been remounted in a modern style.
Blessing-type character pictures such as 百壽百福 萬壽無疆 form a class of munjado, and 'hundred longevity' character screens (백수전도) were also embroidered.
facts.quote: ‘백수백복 만수무강(百壽百福 萬壽無疆)’
facts.quote_gloss: 'hundred longevity, hundred fortune, boundless long life'

facts.text: Surviving examples are embroidered silk screens in both the NPMK and the Portland Art Museum.

rows.name: Buddhist and ritual folk images: gamnodo (sweet-dew rite painting), sansindo (mountain god), gammo yeojaedo (ancestral shrine painting)
rows.hanja: 甘露圖 · 甘露幀 · 甘露王圖 · 山神圖 · 感慕如在圖
rows.rr: gamnodo · gamnotaeng · gamnowangdo · sansindo · gammo yeojaedo
rows.mr: kamnodo · kamnot'aeng · kamnowangdo · sansindo · kammo yŏjaedo
rows.date_note: Gamnodo: earliest 1589 (Yakusenji, Japan), made until the early 20th c. (about 70 survive). Dated sansindo from 1788. Met's ancestral shrine painting is 19th c.
rows.what_it_is: Temple and household religious pictures that sit between Buddhist and folk painting: gamnodo show the rite of feeding hungry ghosts with the buddhas above and scenes of daily life below; sansindo show the mountain god (a folk deity taken into Buddhism) with his tiger, hung in temple shrines; gammo yeojaedo show an ancestral shrine and offering table, used by people who had no shrine.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk or paper; gamnodo are large (e.g. 195 × 169 cm, 208.5 × 208.5 cm).
Pigments: strong mineral colors; sansindo landscapes in blue-and-green.
Mounting: hanging temple paintings (taenghwa) or framed; Met sansindo framed.

Iconography: gamnodo three registers (buddhas, altar, hungry ghost and human life); sansindo: white-bearded old man in red robes leaning on a cat-like tiger, with pine, rocks and later longevity motifs; 20th-c. tigers roar and bare teeth.

Script: dated temple works naming their painter-monks are recorded (e.g. Haeinsa gamnowangdo, 1723, by Simgam, Sino and Deukchong, per the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture caption); folk shrine pictures are usually unsigned.

copies.text: From the 20th century tigers in mountain-god paintings take on a roaring, teeth-baring look under the influence of Japanese tiger painting.

facts.text: Gamnodo were used in rites to guide souls of the dead (e.g. suryukjae); the type formed in the 16th century and was made for about 400 years until the early 20th century; about 70 survive in Korea and abroad.
facts.quote_gloss: over about 400 years from the late 16th to the early 20th century

facts.text: In late-19th-century gamnodo from temples around Seoul the lower register shifts from scenes of death to lively everyday life (markets, trades, entertainment) — a sign of date.
The mountain god, long a folk deity, was absorbed into Buddhism; his paintings hang in temple samseonggak or sansingak; he usually appears as a white-bearded old man with a tiger.
facts.quote: later incorporated into the Buddhist pantheon

facts.text: Rough, brightly colored Buddhist paintings from small temples and shrines (sansingak, chilseonggak) are counted as minhwa in the wide sense, and folk elements entered Buddhist painting in the late 19th–early 20th century.
Ancestral shrine paintings (gammo yeojaedo) show a shrine with an offering table and were used as a substitute by people who had no shrine or were performing rites away from home.

examples.title: Mountain god with tiger (山神圖), late 19th c., ink and color on silk

examples.holder: Heungguksa, Namyangju (photo: Academy of Korean Studies, KOGL 1)
examples.title: 남양주 흥국사 감로왕도, 1868, color on silk, 195×169 cm
Ancestral shrine painting (感慕如在圖), 19th c., ink and color on paper

rows.name: Musindo — shaman (mudang) deity paintings
rows.period: Mainly 19th–20th century (older references from the 13th c.)
rows.date_note: Pigment analysis of 83 shaman paintings: Scheele's green in works dated c.1850s–1870s, emerald green widely used from the late 19th century to 1970 (Oh et al. 2015). Yi Gyu-bo's 13th-c. poem is the earliest textual reference.
rows.what_it_is: Portraits of the gods served by shamans — mountain gods, generals (Choe Yeong, Guan Yu), kings (Taejo), the smallpox goddess, Princess Bari, the Seven Stars, dragon kings — hung in shamans' shrines and village shrines. Painted by shamans skilled at painting, specialist painters and Buddhist painter-monks.
how_to_recognize: Support: usually fine cotton cloth (당목), sometimes hanji; finer sets on silk (Guksadang); later ones on paper.
Pigments: primary red, yellow and blue with white, black and green; 'Chinese colors' (당채) and opaque mineral colors (석채); copper-arsenic greens (Scheele's green, emerald green).
Mounting: hanging pictures about 60 × 110 cm; often unmounted or simply hung.
Iconography: single frontal deity, often with attendants; folk-style versus Buddhist-painting style depending on the maker.

Script: usually unsigned; an inscription on the painting can date it (one Guksadang painting is dated to the colonial period by the writing above the image); shrine repair records may name the painters (Bokgaedang, 1868).

copies.text: Later shaman paintings became cruder and were done on paper with water-based paint; recently offset-printed images on wood-free paper have been sold in Buddhist-supply shops.

facts.text: Musindo are typically painted on fine cotton (sometimes hanji), about 60 × 110 cm, in primary red, yellow and blue with white, black and green.
facts.quote_gloss: the deity is painted on fine-weave cotton

facts.text: Typical shaman paintings are found in central and northern Korea, where charismatic (spirit-possessed) shamans keep deity images; southern hereditary shamans do not use them; Hwanghae has the most varied paintings and costumes.
facts.quote_gloss: typical musindo are distributed in the central and northern regions

facts.text: Painters were skilled shamans, specialist musindo painters and temple painter-monks; folk-style versus Buddhist-painting-style musindo reflect who made them.
Copper-arsenic green pigments were found in 60 of 83 shaman paintings: Scheele's green indicates c.1850s–1870s, while emerald green was widely used from the late 19th century to 1970.
facts.quote_gloss: emerald green from the late 19th century to 1970

facts.text: Of the 21 Guksadang (Inwangsan, Seoul) shaman paintings, 12 on silk are thought to be by one late-Joseon painter; the rest are later and of lower quality, one on paper dated by its inscription to the colonial period.
facts.quote: 12점은 조선 말기에 같은 인물에 의하여 제작된 것으로 추정
facts.quote_gloss: 12 are thought to be by one person in late Joseon

facts.text: The earliest written evidence is Yi Gyu-bo's 'Old Shaman' poem: walls covered with brightly painted deities.
facts.quote_gloss: deities painted in colour filling the walls

examples.holder: Guksadang shrine, Inwangsan, Seoul — National Folklore Cultural Heritage (photo: Academy of Korean Studies, KOGL 1)
examples.title: 국사당 무신도 중 최영장군, color on silk, 65×110 cm
국사당 무신도 중 창부씨, color on silk, 57×93 cm
Bokgaedang (Mapo) shaman paintings, 13 works, c.1829–1868

rows.name: Byeongpung — folding screens: formats, mounting and folding
rows.period: Used throughout Joseon; most surviving folk and court screens 19th–20th century
rows.date_note: Oldest surviving Korean-mounted screen: the 16th-c. Xiaoxiang Eight Views screen taken to Japan in 1539 (Daiganji). Most screens on the market are 19th–20th century and many have been remounted.
rows.what_it_is: Paintings, calligraphy or embroidery pasted on wooden lattice frames covered with layers of paper, joined so they stand and fold. Screens divided rooms, kept out draughts, decorated walls and served as backdrops for weddings, birthdays, funerals and ancestral rites.
how_to_recognize: Support: the image (paper, silk or embroidery) is backed and pasted onto panels made of a wooden frame with several layers of paper.
Pigments: n/a (depends on the painting); border silks traditionally indigo/blue, with thin red, white and indigo bands; teal upper/lower borders and violet strips on a 19th-c. embroidered screen.

Mounting: tong-byeongpung (one board), gari-gae/gyeong-byeongpung (two boards), yeon-byeongpung (2–12 panels joined); 8 panels most common, then 12, 10, 4, 2. Panels joined by paper or cloth strips glued alternately on the edges ('hinge'/'paper-wing' method); short legs under each panel.
Iconography: one subject per screen, read right to left; two-sided screens (painting on both faces, or painting with calligraphy behind) became popular in the late 19th–early 20th c.
Script: a title slip (표제) may be pasted on the back; commemorative screens may carry lists of names.

copies.text: Original mountings rarely survive: the Portland 百壽百福 screen had been remounted in modern style; the Rothenbaum Museum's 'hundred fans' screen took its present form in 1980s repairs; court screens repaired from the 1960s lost original features through non-traditional methods.

facts.text: By number of boards: one board = tong-byeongpung; two boards = gari-gae or gyeong-byeongpung; two or more boards joined with paper strips = yeon-byeongpung; 8 panels is the most common.
facts.quote: 2개 이상의 판을 종이띠로 연결하여 만든 것을 연결 병풍
facts.quote_gloss: boards joined with paper strips make a linked screen

facts.text: Embroidered screens follow the same pattern: 8 panels most common, then 12, 10, 4 and 2; exceptionally 20 (e.g. commemorative 'ten thousand people' screens).
facts.quote_gloss: 8 panels most, then 12, 10, 4, 2

facts.text: Korean screens join panels with paper or cloth strips glued alternately to the panel edges (the 'hinge' or 'paper-wing' method), said in 1924 by Yamamoto Gen to be a Korean invention; hinges were formerly of hemp, good ones of silk, and today of cotton.
facts.quote: 예전에는 삼베로 하였고 좋은 것은 비단으로 하였으나 지금은 광목을 쓴다
facts.quote_gloss: formerly hemp, good ones silk, now cotton

facts.text: Korean screens have short legs under the panels, explained either by heated ondol floors (to stop the frame warping) or by outdoor use; the 16th-c. Daiganji screen has two legs per panel.
facts.quote_gloss: short legs made at the bottom of the screen

facts.text: Two-sided screens became noticeably popular in Korean houses in the 1800s–early 1900s, possibly inspired by Japanese double-sided screens; traditionally only one side carried images.

After 1910 Japanese mounting practice dominated: the Japanese word pyogu (表具) replaced janghwang after a Japanese mounter was hired for Emperor Sunjong's collection in 1926, and Korean mounters trained in Japanese shops; a mid-1970s antiques boom made mounting shops prosper.
facts.quote_gloss: in the mid-1970s, riding the boom, an antiques boom arose

examples.title: Painting of One Hundred Themes, late 1800s, ten-panel two-sided screen (album leaves front, calligraphy back)
Birds and Flowers, 19th c., eight panels mounted as two sets of four
소상팔경도 8곡병, 16th c., taken to Japan in 1539 (oldest Korean screen mounting)

rows.name: Court decorative painting vs folk painting — where the line is
rows.hanja: 宮中裝飾畵 · 民畵 · 圖畫署 · 畫員
rows.period: Late Joseon and Korean Empire (18th c.–1910) and after
rows.date_note: The distinction is sharpest in the 18th century; after the Dohwaseo was abolished (Korean Empire period) the court hired market painters and the line blurs (Seo Yoon-jung 2018).
rows.what_it_is: Many subjects (ten longevity symbols, peonies, chaekgeori, five peaks, Guo Ziyi's banquet) were first court decorative paintings made by court painters (hwawon) of the Dohwaseo and then imitated for private customers. Whether such court-style work is 'minhwa' depends on the author: some define minhwa broadly to include it, others keep 'minhwa' for anonymous popular work and call the rest 'decorative painting'.
how_to_recognize: Support: court and court-style screens are mostly silk; folk versions often paper.
Pigments: court work uses high-grade mineral pigments and gold; but late 19th-c. court items already contain imported synthetic pigments, so pigment alone does not separate court from folk.
Mounting: court ceremonial screens have green silk borders with gilt floral ornament, graded by status; very large sizes (2–3.6 m high).
Iconography: court versions keep full, standard compositions and fine detail; folk versions are smaller, flatter, crowd motifs, and add or drop elements to suit buyers.
Script: attributions to famous court painters (Kim Hong-do, Kim Deuk-sin, Shin Saimdang) on decorative screens are often later attributions, not evidence.

copies.text: Many paintings that went to Europe and America and are attributed to Kim Hong-do or Kim Deuk-sin are later works in their style; three overseas Guo Ziyi screens 'by Kim Deuk-sin' show his name circulated as a reputation more than as authorship.

facts.text: In the broad definition (Kim Cheol-sun), minhwa includes court-style practical paintings by Dohwaseo painters as well as naive work; others confine the term to popular anonymous painting.
facts.quote: 도화서 화풍의 생활화 · 실용화를 모두 가리킨다
facts.quote_gloss: refers to both … and Dohwaseo-style practical paintings

facts.text: After the Dohwaseo was abolished the court hired painters from the market; court styles spread to private painters through model books and drafts, so at the end of Joseon the boundary between court painting and court-style private painting becomes unclear and classification by materials, mounting or quality often fails.
facts.quote_gloss: the boundary becomes blurred

facts.text: Decorative screens of the 19th century were produced from full-size drafts (choebon) that fixed composition and colors; the NMK keeps drafts that match a Rothenbaum Museum screen exactly; c.1900 painting shops stood at Donghyeon (today's Euljiro) near the former Dohwaseo.
facts.quote_gloss: in the early 1900s shops selling paintings were here

facts.text: Court-made works are characterised by good materials and skilled execution (ten-longevity screens), and court ceremonial screens were mounted in green silk with gilt ornament according to strict, status-graded rules.
facts.quote_gloss: materials are good and workmanship excellent

facts.text: Middle-class buyers (market merchants, rich farmers) and, after the opening of the ports, Western buyers shaped new compositions and 'Korean', 'folk' and 'realistic' motifs on decorative screens; a German consul (Meyer) collected such screens 1890s–1905.
The Dohwaseo was the Joseon government office in charge of painting; its court painters (hwawon) made New Year paintings, ceremonial screens and records.

examples.title: Books and Scholars' Accoutrements (court style; hidden seal of Yi Taek-gyun), late 1800s, silk
Books and Scholarly Accoutrements (folk two-panel), 19th c., paper
The Banquet of Guo Ziyi, late 19th c., eight-panel screen, silk

rows.name: Nakhwa (pyrography) and hyeokpilhwa (leather-brush 'flying white' pictures)
rows.hanja: 烙畵 · 革筆畵 · 飛白書
rows.date_note: Cleveland: pyrography became widely popular in the 19th century; hyeokpilhwa is still made for tourists today.
rows.what_it_is: Two techniques of itinerant market painters. Nakhwa burns the design into paper or wood with a heated iron. Hyeokpilhwa (originally bibaekseo, 'flying-white writing') writes characters such as 孝悌忠信禮義廉恥 with a split stick or a strip of leather/felt dipped in several colors, turning the strokes into fish, crabs, shrimps and swallows.
how_to_recognize: Support: nakhwa on paper or wood; hyeokpilhwa on paper.
Pigments: nakhwa has scorch marks instead of ink; hyeokpilhwa has broad, streaky multicolored strokes.
Mounting: screens (Cleveland 1991.80 is a ten-panel screen) or single sheets.
Iconography: birds and flowers (nakhwa); character pictures with animal-shaped strokes (hyeokpilhwa).
Script: hanja virtues or names in hyeokpilhwa.

copies.text: Hyeokpilhwa, once sold at country markets, is now made on the spot for tourists in Insa-dong and the Korean Folk Village — the one minhwa still made and sold in the street.

facts.text: Nakhwa replaces brush strokes with scorch marks made by a heated metal tool; the technique became widely popular in the 19th century.

Yu Deuk-gong's Gyeongdo japji describes bibaekseo: a willow stick cut and split at the end, dipped in ink to write 孝悌忠信禮義廉恥, the strokes shaped into fish, crabs, shrimps and swallows; in modern times it became the colorful leather-strip hyeokpilhwa.
facts.quote: 버드나무의 가지를 깎아 그 끝을 갈라지게 하고
facts.quote_gloss: cut a willow branch and split its end

examples.title: Birds and Flowers, late 1800s, ten-panel screen, pyrography on paper (gift of Alan Carter Covell and Kyu J. Pak-Covell)

rows.name: Bojagi — wrapping cloths (incl. jogakbo patchwork and subo embroidered cloths)
rows.hanja: 褓 · 袱 · 繡褓 (조각보 has no fixed hanja)
rows.date_note: Oldest known: an embroidered cloth in the Jeonju City Museum, estimated late Goryeo (the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). Museums date many surviving jogakbo to the 19th–20th century (AIC 1996.372: 19th c.; AIC 1996.481: 1875/1925; Met 2007.149–.151: ca. 1950–80).
rows.what_it_is: Square cloths for wrapping, carrying, covering and storing things: everyday cloths, wedding cloths for gifts and documents, Buddhist offering cloths and special ritual cloths. Made single, lined, padded, oiled-paper, quilted, embroidered (subo) or pieced from scraps (jogakbo). Court cloths (gungbo) and commoners' cloths (minbo) are distinguished.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk (plain, gauze, damask), ramie, hemp, cotton; pieced jogakbo use leftover scraps.
Pigments/dyes: the five colors (blue, red, yellow, white, black) dominate embroidered wedding subo.
Mounting: unmounted cloths with ties at corners; many now framed by collectors/museums (Met 2007.149 framed).

Iconography: subo from Gangwon (Gwandong) center on a tree, with flowers, fruit, mandarin ducks, pomegranates; jogakbo are geometric patchwork; cloths are also classed by pattern (flower, tree, dragon, cloud), by color (blue, red, blue-red, five-color) and by material (gauze, plain silk, figured gauze, ramie).

Script: court cloths from Changdeok Palace often carry ink notes (on the cloth or a paper slip) giving contents, place of use, date, size or quantity — e.g. 紅真一畐半 and 梅真三畐 (畐 = 幅, loom widths) on NPMK phoenix cloths; painted court cloths (inmunbo) may bear 壽福, 康寧 or 子孫昌盛 characters.

copies.text: Western museums date several jogakbo to the mid-20th century (Met 2007.149–.151, ca. 1950–80; Met also holds 1980s–2000s examples), so a pieced cloth is not by itself old.

facts.text: The oldest known wrapping cloth is an embroidered cloth (subo) in the Jeonju City Museum, estimated late Goryeo, probably used to wrap sutras.
facts.quote: 현존하는 최고의 보자기로 알려진 것은 전주시립박물관에 소장된 수보
facts.quote_gloss: the oldest known bojagi is the subo in the Jeonju City Museum

facts.text: Jogakbo (patchwork cloths) began as a way of using up scraps; they are now admired for their modern-looking composition.
facts.quote_gloss: they arose from re-using waste material

facts.text: A folk belief linked 袱 (bok, wrapping cloth) with 福 (bok, good fortune): wrapping kept fortune in; dozens of cloths were made for a daughter's trousseau.
facts.quote_gloss: 袱 was believed to share meaning with 福

facts.text: A damask wrapping cloth from the Yi Hang-bok family was dated to the early 18th century by comparing the proportions of its cloud-and-treasure pattern with dated uigwe covers and tomb textiles — the method specialists use to date woven-pattern cloths.

Court wrapping cloths are documented in the Sangbang jeongnye (1752), in the 1882 records of the crown prince's wedding and in 13 'bobalgi' lists (wedding-related) in the Jangseogak, which record kind, material, size, quantity and price; 133 cloths survive from Changdeok Palace.

Court cloths include matbo (food covers with oiled paper attached, the most numerous survivors), inmunbo (cloths painted by court painters in bright 'Chinese colors', used to wrap screens, clothes and jewel boxes for royal weddings) and large single-layer gyajabo and jimbo for carrying goods.

Some NPMK court cloths carry ink notes of contents, place of use, date, size or quantity; a painted phoenix cloth (창덕7975) has a slip reading 紅真一畐半 ('red ground, one and a half widths'), another (창덕7968) 梅真三畐.
facts.quote_gloss: red ground, one and a half widths

facts.text: Court cloths were made through an approval chain: the Hojo asked the king, the Sanguiwon supplied fabric, the Sedapbang cut it and the Chimbang sewed it.
Nineteenth-century pieced silk wrapping cloths are in Western museums (AIC 1996.372, silk plain weave, pieced, with ribbon and cord).

rows.name: Jasu — embroidery, incl. embroidered screens (su-byeongpung), pouches and wedding robes
rows.hanja: 刺繡 · 繡屛風 · 刺繡屛風
rows.period: Embroidered screens mainly late Joseon (18th–early 20th c.); export 'oriental embroidery' 1950s–80s
rows.date_note: Met: embroidered screens were produced in greater number in the late Joseon period; most surviving rank badges are 18th c. or later (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 자수).
rows.what_it_is: Silk-thread (and gold-thread) embroidery on silk satin or damask, used for screens, rank badges, wedding robes (hwarot), pouches, pillow ends, spectacle cases and Buddhist textiles. Screens show flowers and birds most often, then longevity symbols and blessing characters, also Guo Ziyi's banquet, 'hundred boys', bronzes and books. Court workshops made the finest; women embroidered at home.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk; white or colored (blue, red) silk is most common, and screens also use black or indigo satin grounds.
Threads: twisted thread (kkon-sa) — fine until mid-Joseon, thicker later; loosely twisted floss (banpun-sa) for filling; gold thread couched down with silk.
Mounting: screens 8 panels most common; robes and pouches unmounted; badges often now mounted.

Stitches: jarit-su (mat-like stitch unique to Korea, frequent in older and Buddhist work), long-and-short (jaryeon-su), satin, outline, couching, knot and chain stitches; knot stitches and couching threads in the same color until mid-Joseon, contrasting primary colors later.
Script: Buddhist embroideries often carry donor inscriptions and cyclical dates; embroidered screens may include characters (壽, 福, texts beside bronzes).

copies.text: After 1910 Japanese embroidery flooded in and a painterly style called 'dongyang jasu' (Oriental embroidery) prevailed; after 1945 Western embroidery arrived; in the 1950s–80s traditional embroidery was promoted as an export product and a home side-job for women, and this export 'oriental embroidery' was eclectic to suit foreign taste.

A black-satin embroidered grasses-and-insects screen traditionally attributed to Shin Saimdang (1504–1551) cannot be firmly attributed to her; it is better seen as the embroidery closest to the 'Shin Saimdang' insect-painting style praised from the late 17th century.

facts.text: Embroidered screens are the representative Joseon embroidery; by subject, flowers-and-birds are most common, then ten longevity symbols and longevity-fortune characters; other subjects include the hundred boys, bronzes, Guo Ziyi's banquet, chaekgado and commemorative 'praise of virtue' screens.
facts.quote: 화조(花鳥)가 가장 많고 다음으로 십장생(十長生)과 수복(壽福)류
facts.quote_gloss: flowers-and-birds most, then ten longevity and su-bok

facts.text: Embroidered screens were produced in greater number in the late Joseon period; the Met's gold-embroidered bronzes screen (late 19th c.) is attributed to court workshops on the quality of materials and execution, while Cleveland considers its Guo Ziyi screen likely the work of an amateur woman embroiderer.
Twisted thread was fine until mid-Joseon and thicker from late Joseon; loosely twisted floss (banpun-sa) was used for filling large areas.
facts.quote: 조선 중기까지는 실올이 가는 꼰사가, 조선 후기 이후에는 굵은 꼰사가
facts.quote_gloss: fine twisted thread until mid-Joseon, thick twisted thread from late Joseon

facts.text: Gold thread was laid on the surface and tied down with silk (couching).
Until mid-Joseon, knot stitches and tying-down threads matched the surrounding color; later embroiderers used strong primary colors to make them stand out.
facts.quote: 후대로 내려오면서는 원색조의 강한 색사를 사용하여
facts.quote_gloss: in later periods strong primary-colour threads were used

facts.text: Under-drawings were done in ink lines on the cloth, stamped from woodblocks, moved with shell-white, or cut from paper and stitched over.
Wedding robes (hwarot) were communal: repeatedly repaired and passed down for decades, with the paper on collar and cuffs renewed for each bride.

Birds and Flowers (花鳥圖 刺繡 屛風), late 19th c., ten-panel embroidered screen

Ancient Chinese Bronzes, late 1800s, ten-panel screen, gold silk embroidery on black silk
Pouch, late 19th–early 20th c., embroidered silk

rows.name: Hyungbae — rank badges
rows.date_note: Introduced 1454 (Danjong 2) for officials of the 3rd rank and above; extended to the 9th rank in Yeongjo's reign; the late Joseon double/single crane and double/single tiger system lasted until 1910. Surviving badges are mostly 18th century or later.
rows.what_it_is: Square embroidered (earlier woven) panels sewn on the chest and back of an official's black robe (heukdallyeong) to show rank: cranes for civil officials, tigers for military officials, qilin and other beasts for princes; women of yangban and royal families wore phoenix, peony or 壽-character badges in some periods.
how_to_recognize: Support: silk satin or damask ground in the color of the robe (red grounds in the 17th–18th c.); about 17–26 cm square.
Threads: colored silks and gilt-metal-wrapped thread couched down; chain, knot, satin and stem stitches.
Mounting: originally sewn to robes; often now loose or mounted in pairs.

Iconography: civil — two cranes for senior (dangsang) officials, one crane for lower (dangha) officials (system from the late 18th c.); military — two/one tigers; main motif white from the 18th c.; from the late 18th c. cranes hold peony, peach or lingzhi, settling on lingzhi in the 19th c.; clouds, rocks, three peaks, waves and spray below.
Script: none; a 'tiger' badge with a taegeuk between the tigers is catalogued by the NPMK as military dangsang.

copies.text: Commoners were allowed to wear an official's robe with a double- or single-crane badge as a bridegroom (seopseong custom), so a crane badge does not by itself show that an ancestor held office.

facts.text: Rank badges were introduced in 1454 at Yang Seong-ji's proposal for civil and military officials of the 3rd rank and above, on the Ming model (peacock, cloud-crane, silver pheasant for civil 1st–3rd ranks; tiger-leopard and bear for military).
facts.quote_gloss: in 1454, on the proposal of Yang Seong-ji

facts.text: From the late 18th century civil badges were double crane for senior (dangsang) and single crane for lower (dangha) officials; military badges became double and single tiger from Sunjo's reign, a system used until 1910.
facts.quote_gloss: kept as double crane for dangsang and single crane for dangha

facts.text: Cleveland's label for a pair of single-crane badges says the single crane was worn by civil officials of the fourth or higher ranks.

Main motifs were drawn realistically and in natural colors in early Joseon but rendered in white from the 18th century; from the late 18th century cranes hold a peony, peach or lingzhi, and from the 19th century lingzhi only.
facts.quote_gloss: from the 19th century it settled on holding lingzhi

facts.text: Bird badges can be identified by head and tail: crane (red crown, black tail), peacock (round crest, eyed tail), wild goose (plain crown, simple tail, brown body), silver pheasant (long crest and tail), egret (long crest, simple tail, white body).
Older surviving badges are larger and embroidered in subtle twisted threads; later ones are generally smaller and use primary-color threads.
facts.quote: 후대의 것들은 대체로 규격이 작고 원색실을 사용해서
facts.quote_gloss: later ones are generally smaller and use primary-colour thread

facts.text: Badges were embroidered on satin damask with silk and gilt-metal-strip-wrapped thread in chain, knot, satin and stem stitches with couching.

rows.name: Norigae — women's pendant ornaments (single and three-part)
rows.hanja: (native word; 三作노리개 for the three-part set)
rows.date_note: No source dates the start precisely; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture links it to earlier belt pendants; surviving and illustrated items are mostly 19th–20th century.
rows.what_it_is: A pendant hung from the tie of the jacket (jeogori) or the skirt band: a top ring (ttidon), cord, the main ornament (one = danjak, three = samjak), decorative knots (maedeup) and long tassels. Ornaments are of gold, silver, jade, jadeite, coral, amber, pearl, enamel or embroidery, in auspicious shapes. Worn from court to commoners and handed down as heirlooms.
how_to_recognize: Support/materials: gold, silver, gilt silver, white jade, jadeite, purple agate, coral, amber (hobak and milhwa), pearl, tortoiseshell, enamel (chilbo/paran), embroidery, incense.
Colors: knots and tassels based on red, blue and yellow, with pink, light green, purple, violet, jade-blue.
Mounting: ttidon (square, round, flower or butterfly shapes) at top; knots above and tassels (strawberry, bong, cord, bell types) below; museum examples measure about 33–57 cm long.

Iconography: animals (bats, butterflies, fish, turtles), plants (eggplant, chilli, grapes, pomegranate, Buddha's hand citron), items (gourd bottle, pouch, lock, axe, knife, bells); characters such as 富貴多男 or 不老長生 pierced in silver.
Script: auspicious characters as decoration; no maker's marks reported in the sources read.

facts.text: A norigae consists of a top ring (ttidon), cord, the main ornament(s), knots and a tassel; one ornament makes a danjak, three a samjak norigae.
facts.quote: 주체가 되는 패물(三作 또는 單作) · 매듭(每緝) · 술(流蘇)
facts.quote_gloss: the main ornament (three or single), knots and tassels

facts.text: Samjak sets were graded large, medium and small: large (dae-samjak) for court ceremonial dress, medium for court and upper class, small for young women and girls; they were also named by material (gold, silver, jade, agate, amber) or shape.

The court dae-samjak combined a coral branch larger than a palm, a white-jade butterfly and an amber (milhwa) Buddha's-hand citron on long tassels; commoners mostly wore silver samjak, used at weddings and then stored wrapped in paper and silk.
facts.quote: 손바닥 크기가 넘는 산호가지와 백옥나비 · 밀화불수
facts.quote_gloss: a coral branch bigger than a palm, a white jade butterfly and an amber Buddha's hand

facts.text: Seasonal rules recorded by King Heonjong's consort Gyeongbin Kim (Sajeol boksaek jajang yoram): jade and beads in spring/summer/autumn, agate and amber (milhwa) and incense pendants in winter.
facts.quote_gloss: in winter they wore samjak of purple agate and amber

facts.text: Norigae were received from one's own family and in-laws and passed on to children, so they were regarded as family heirlooms.
facts.quote_gloss: were handed down and regarded as heirlooms

facts.text: Some pendants were practical: incense cases (thought to repel snakes and used as medicine), needle cases and small knives (jangdo); incense beads were strung like a rosary and worn under the skirt.
A LACMA norigae (19th c.) is of carved amber, coral and jade with knotted and metal-wrapped threads.
