rows.name: Binyeo — hairpins, with dwikkoji, cheopji and tteoljam head ornaments
rows.hanja: 簪 · 笄 · 釵 (binyeo itself is a native word); 疊紙 (첩지)
rows.period: Ancient to 20th century; variety boomed after the late-18th/19th-century hair reforms
rows.date_note: Bans on wig-based hairstyles under Yeongjo and Jeongjo and the general adoption of the chignon (jjok) by the mid-Sunjo reign (early 19th c.) made hairpins the main hair ornament; most surviving decorated pins are 19th–20th century.
rows.what_it_is: Long pins through a married woman's chignon (or to fix crowns and wigs). Named by material (gold, silver, white bronze, brass, jade, jadeite, coral, wood, bamboo, horn, bone) and by the head ornament (phoenix, dragon, mandarin duck, plum-and-bamboo, peony, pomegranate, mushroom, bean…). Dwikkoji are extra ornaments stuck in behind the chignon (ear-picks, comb-cleaners, flower heads); cheopji sat on the parting at court and ceremonial dress; tteoljam were court head ornaments with trembling spring-mounted butterflies and birds.
how_to_recognize: Materials: gold, silver, gilt silver, white bronze, brass, jade, jadeite, coral, agate, pearl, enamel; wood, bamboo, horn and bone for commoners.
Construction: a shaft with a decorated head; two-pronged silver auxiliary pins hidden under wigs or bridal crowns.

Iconography: phoenix and dragon heads for queen and crown princess (and phoenix for commoners' weddings); seasonal heads (dragon in winter, peony in spring, plum-and-bamboo in summer/autumn at court).
Cheopji: gilt dragon (empress), gilt phoenix (queen/consorts), gilt or black-horn frog (other ranked women).
Script: auspicious meanings are in the motifs; no maker's marks reported in the sources read.

facts.text: Wig-based hairstyles were banned under Yeongjo and Jeongjo; by the mid-Sunjo reign the chignon was general and luxury moved from wigs to hairpins, which became one of the representative crafts of the time.
facts.quote: 순조 중엽에 와서는 얹은머리 대신 쪽찐머리가 일반화
facts.quote_gloss: by the mid-Sunjo reign the chignon replaced the piled-up hairstyle

facts.text: Precious-material pins (gold, silver, jewels) were for the upper class; commoners used wood, horn and bone.
facts.quote: 서민계급의 부녀자는 나무［木］ · 뿔［角］ · 뼈［骨］ 등으로 만든 비녀
facts.quote_gloss: commoner women used pins of wood, horn and bone

facts.text: Phoenix and dragon pins were worn by the queen and crown princess for ceremonies; ordinary women wore a phoenix pin at their wedding.
facts.quote: 일반 부녀자는 혼례 때에 봉잠을 사용하였다
facts.quote_gloss: ordinary women used the phoenix pin at weddings

facts.text: Two-pronged silver auxiliary pins were hidden in the hair to fix wigs, bridal crowns (jokduri) or other ornaments.
Cheopji: the empress used a gilt dragon, queens and consorts a gilt phoenix, and other titled women a gilt or black-horn frog; the body is 7–8 cm long.
facts.quote: 도금 또는 흑각(黑角)으로 만든 개구리첩지
facts.quote_gloss: frog cheopji of gilt metal or black horn

facts.text: Tteoljam, court head ornaments worn with large ceremonial hairstyles, carry butterflies and birds on fine silver springs that tremble; they may derive from Ming China.
facts.quote: 은사로 가는 용수철을 만들어 나비와 새 모양의 장식
facts.quote_gloss: fine springs of silver wire bearing butterfly and bird ornaments

facts.text: Hairpins, like norigae, were treasured as heirlooms passed to descendants.

rows.name: Ornament materials: jade and jadeite, coral, amber (hobak and milhwa), silver, enamel; the silver knife (eunjangdo)
rows.hanja: 玉 · 翡翠 · 珊瑚 · 琥珀 · 蜜花 · 銀 · 七寶 · 銀粧刀
rows.hangul: 옥 · 비취 · 산호 · 호박 · 밀화 · 은 · 칠보 · 파란 · 은장도
rows.rr: ok · bichwi · sanho · hobak · milhwa · eun · chilbo · paran · eunjangdo
rows.mr: ok · pich'wi · sanho · hobak · milhwa · ŭn · ch'ilbo · p'aran · ŭnjangdo
rows.date_note: Sumptuary rules on silver and amber are recorded from 1498 and later; most surviving ornaments are 19th–20th century.
rows.what_it_is: The materials that signal rank and season on Korean ornaments: jade and jadeite, coral (an import), amber (hobak and the cloudy honey-colored milhwa), agate, pearl, tortoiseshell, gold (often gilt silver), silver, and enamel (chilbo and paran). The silver knife (eunjangdo) was both an ornament and a woman's means of self-defence.
how_to_recognize: Amber: light (SG 1.0–1.1), soft (hardness 2–2.5), melts at 287 °C and burns with a characteristic smell; honey-yellow, waxy yellow to red-brown (the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture).
Silver and gilt: even at court rings were mostly gilt or silver; silver samjak norigae for commoners; enamel (paran) on silver for eggplants, butterflies etc.
Coral: branches and beads in court dae-samjak, pins and hat strings; Met's munbangdo essay notes coral was not native to the peninsula.

Eunjangdo: silver hilt and sheath, steel blade, sometimes with silver chopsticks; blades may bear the characters 一片丹心 (일편단심, 'single-hearted loyalty') as decoration; worn on the tie (paedo) or in a pouch (nangdo).
Script: 一片丹心 on knife blades; auspicious characters pierced in silver norigae.

facts.text: Amber is fossil resin with hardness 2.0–2.5 and specific gravity 1.0–1.1 that melts at 287 °C, burning with a characteristic smell; in Korea it was one of the 'seven treasures', used for norigae and rings, and commoners were forbidden amber hat-strings and hat ornaments.
facts.quote: 287℃에서 녹고 불꽃을 내고 타며 특유한 냄새가 난다
facts.quote_gloss: melts at 287 °C and burns with a flame and a distinctive smell

facts.text: Amber and milhwa (honey-amber) are listed among the precious materials of norigae, and amber, tortoiseshell and agate were used for men's headband buttons and hat ornaments.

Headband buttons (gwanja) showed rank: gold and jade for high officials, bone, horn, tortoiseshell, agate or amber for the 3rd rank and below; in late examples, the higher the rank, the plainer the button.
facts.quote: 신분이 높을수록 금 · 옥 조각이 없는 간소한 관자를 사용
facts.quote_gloss: the higher the status, the plainer the button without gold or jade carving

facts.text: Even at court, rings were mostly gilt or silver; jade, agate, amber, jadeite, pearl and enamel rings were worn by season (gold in winter, jade in summer).
facts.quote: 도금 또는 은을 많이 사용하고 있는데, 이는 궁중에서도 마찬가지
facts.quote_gloss: mostly gilt or silver were used, and the same at court

facts.text: Silver knives (eunjangdo) were worn by men and women from the Mongol period; sumptuary laws of 1498 and 1670 banned commoners from wearing them; for women they were also a means of self-defence and a symbol of chastity; blades were sometimes engraved with 일편단심.
facts.quote_gloss: the blade was sometimes engraved with the words ilpyeon dansim as a pattern

facts.text: Coral, like peacock feathers and citrons, is not native to the Korean peninsula; it appears in court ornaments such as the dae-samjak coral branch.
facts.quote: not indigenous to the Korean peninsula

facts.text: Earrings, common in earlier periods, largely disappeared after a royal order of 1572 criticising ear-piercing; late-Joseon earrings were hooked over the ear rather than pierced.

rows.name: 20th-century market production and modern reproductions — telling them from 19th-century work
rows.hanja: 印刷屛風 · 輸出用民畵 · 模寫 · 創作民畵 · 東洋刺繡
rows.hangul: 인쇄 병풍 · 수출용 민화 · 모사 · 창작민화 · 동양자수
rows.rr: inswae byeongpung · suchulyong minhwa · mosa · changjak minhwa · dongyang jasu
rows.mr: inswae pyŏngp'ung · such'ullyong minhwa · mosa · ch'angjak minhwa · tongyang chasu
rows.date_note: Printed screens 1920s–1980s; export minhwa workshops and export embroidery boomed in the 1970s; amateur copying of old minhwa from templates since the 1990s.
rows.what_it_is: What an owner may have instead of a 19th-century original: printed screens (1920s–80s), paintings from 1970s export workshops, 1950s–80s export embroidery, offset-printed shaman pictures, tourist hyeokpilhwa, faithful modern copies made from templates by today's minhwa painters, and old works remounted in modern materials.
how_to_recognize: Support: printed screens and offset prints are printed, not painted (Park 2016; Kim Tae-gon); a modern remounting does not make the painting modern (and vice versa).

Pigments: emerald green or synthetic ultramarine shows a date after the mid-19th century, Scheele's green suggests c.1850s–1870s; their absence is consistent with, but does not prove, an earlier date, since traditional pigments stayed in use alongside them; emerald green was used until about 1970, so it cannot by itself separate a late-19th-century painting from a 1960s one.
Mounting: Japanese mounting practice strongly influenced Korean mounting from the colonial period; many old screens were remounted in the 1960s–80s.
Iconography: 20th-century Japanese influence — printed bird-and-flower screens with Japanese-style compositions (pine and crane, peony and peacock, eagles), roaring teeth-baring tigers.
Script: names of famous painters on decorative screens are not proof (see court_vs_folk).

copies.text: Offset-printed shaman pictures on wood-free paper are sold in Buddhist-supply shops.
Today's minhwa classes teach by copying old minhwa exactly from templates (choebon), producing reproductions; 'creative minhwa' grew from the mid-2010s.

facts.text: Printed bird-and-flower screens, introduced via Japan, were distributed nationwide by the 1920s and used, mainly as folding screens at weddings and 60th birthdays, until the 1980s; they replaced folk painting as popular art and folk painters borrowed their motifs.

The traditional minhwa lineage broke between 1945 and the Korean War; the contemporary minhwa scene began in the 1960s–70s with people from painting conservation and from the 'export minhwa workshops' that boomed in the 1970s.
facts.quote_gloss: the so-called 'export minhwa workshops' that boomed in the 1970s

facts.text: The 1970s were a commercial boom for old-style art: export minhwa workshops prospered and a mid-1970s antiques boom made mounting shops thrive.

In the 1950s–80s traditional embroidery was promoted by the state as an export product and a side-job for women; export 'oriental embroidery' was eclectic to suit foreign taste; after 1910 Japanese painterly 'Oriental embroidery' had already spread.

Emerald green and synthetic ultramarine (yangnok, yangcheong) were imported from Europe after the mid-19th century: Oh et al. dated a celestial-chart screen painted only in traditional pigments to after the mid-18th century and two using the new pigments to after the mid-19th, one of them mixing old and new; emerald green was used in shaman paintings until 1970; a synthetic copper-arsenic green is on King Gojong's late-19th-c. robe and synthetic ultramarine and emerald green on an analyzed sun-moon-peaks painting.
facts.quote: 19세기 중엽 이후 유럽에서 유입된 합성 무기안료
facts.quote_gloss: synthetic inorganic pigments imported from Europe after the mid-19th century

facts.text: Twentieth-century work shows Japanese pictorial influence: Japanese-style compositions on printed bird-and-flower screens and roaring, teeth-baring tigers in mountain-god paintings.
Western museums date some Korean folk textiles to the later 20th century (Met jogakbo ca. 1950–80; AIC ramie cloth 1875/1925), showing that traditional forms continued to be made.

disputed.item: Chaekgeori vs chaekgado vs munbangdo as names

positions.view: Chaekgeori (책거리) is the broader term including works without shelves; chaekgado is the shelf type
Munbangdo (文房圖) is the historical umbrella term; chaekgeori and chaekgado should be kept for the bookshelf type

disputed.item: Which ten objects make up the 'ten longevity symbols'

positions.view: Sun, clouds, mountains, water, rocks, crane, deer, turtle, pine, lingzhi (bamboo and peach often added)
Ten chosen from thirteen (sun, moon, clouds, mountains, rocks, water, crane, deer, turtle, pine, bamboo, lingzhi, peach)
Yi Saek's Goryeo list includes clouds; Seong Hyeon's early-Joseon list has the moon instead of clouds

disputed.item: Hyungbae size over time

positions.view: Older surviving badges are larger; later ones generally smaller with primary-color thread
Badges became larger from the mid-17th century

disputed.item: Spelling of the sixth munjado virtue

positions.view: 禮儀 (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 문자도)
禮義 (Yu Deuk-gong's Gyeongdo japji as quoted in the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture 혁필화)

disputed.item: Name of painted court wrapping cloths

positions.view: Called dangchaebo (당채보, 'Chinese-color cloth'), e.g. 모란문당채보 in the encyclopedia's media list
Historical name is inmunbo (引紋袱/인문보, 'cloth with drawn patterns'); 'dangchaebo' is a later misnomer

disputed.item: Who painted shaman paintings

positions.view: Thought to be Buddhist painters (geumeo), confirmed by shamans and painters' testimony
Three groups: shamans skilled at painting, specialist musindo painters (folk style) and painter-monks (Buddhist style)

disputed.item: Materials of shaman paintings

positions.view: Usually fine cotton (dangmok), sometimes hanji
The best late-Joseon Guksadang set is on silk
